# FND-PRG-106 · Code Reading and Debugging without Assistance

- Track: Data & AI Foundations
- Path: [Programming and Software Practice](https://sdaiaacademy.github.io/en/paths/FND-PRG.md)
- Level: Level 100 · Explain
- Format: Workshop: two days of drills and a supervised practical
- Total hours: 12 h
- Audience: beginner
- Status: In development

## Description

Participants practise reading unfamiliar code and finding faults without help, the skills most at risk when practice is delegated to an assistant. Through predict-the-output drills, hand tracing, Parsons problems and seeded-bug hunts in a small data-processing codebase, they learn a repeatable method: reproduce, isolate, hypothesise, test, fix, and add a regression check.

## Learning outcomes

By the end, the participant can:

- Read unfamiliar code and state its output, including the effects of aliasing, scope and mutation.
- Explain what a traceback or failing assertion reveals about where and what a fault is.
- Apply the reproduce, isolate, hypothesise, test and fix method to locate defects, keeping a log.
- Use a step debugger, breakpoints and targeted logging to inspect program state.
- Distinguish assistant use that keeps debugging skill, such as asking for explanations, from use that erodes it.

## Prerequisites

- [FND-PRG-101 · Python Programming for Data and AI](https://sdaiaacademy.github.io/en/courses/FND-PRG-101.md)
- Runs terminal commands; Git commands are supplied

## Topics

### Reading and structured practice

- Predict-the-output and hand tracing
- Parsons problems with distractor lines
- Faded worked examples
- Explaining code aloud
- Finding entry points and call paths in a multi-file codebase

### A debugging method

- Reproduce and shrink the failing case
- Isolate by halving input and code
- Fix, then add a regression check
- Bisecting history

### Tools without assistants

- Tracebacks and error messages
- Step debugger and breakpoints
- Assertions and logging

### Assistants afterwards

- Evidence on skill loss from delegation
- Verifying a suggested fix

---

# FND-MTH-101 · Linear Algebra for Machine Learning

- Track: Data & AI Foundations
- Path: [Mathematics and Statistics](https://sdaiaacademy.github.io/en/paths/FND-MTH.md)
- Level: Level 100 · Explain
- Format: Extended: 8 weeks part-time, one session and one lab a week, weekly graded problem sets and a capstone
- Total hours: 45 h
- Audience: beginner
- Status: In development

## Description

Participants compute each idea of linear algebra twice: by hand on small cases and in array code on real data. They treat data as vectors, matrices as transformations, least squares as projection, and eigen and singular value decompositions as ways to find structure. Labs use public embeddings and images and a synthetic link graph. The capstone is a low-rank analysis of a public dataset, defended orally.

## Learning outcomes

By the end, the participant can:

- Explain the geometric meaning of vectors, dot products, norms, projections and matrix products.
- Describe what rank, eigenvalues and singular values reveal about a matrix and name one machine learning use of each.
- Identify ill-conditioned or rank-deficient systems and explain their effect on a least-squares fit.
- Compute products, inverses, projections and decompositions by hand for small matrices and in array code for large ones.
- Implement least squares through QR factorisation and compare it with the normal equations.
- Apply the singular value decomposition to build low-rank approximations and principal components.

## Prerequisites

- School algebra: solving equations and reading graphs of functions
- Writes short Python programs with lists, loops and functions (FND-PRG-101 or equivalent)

## Next courses

- [FND-MTH-102 · Calculus and Optimisation for Machine Learning](https://sdaiaacademy.github.io/en/courses/FND-MTH-102.md)
- [SPC-MOD-304 · Optimisation and Operations Research for Decisions](https://sdaiaacademy.github.io/en/courses/SPC-MOD-304.md)

## Topics

### Vectors and similarity

- Vectors as data points and directions
- Dot product, norms and cosine similarity
- Embeddings and distance in high dimensions
- Attention scores as a matrix of dot products

### Matrices as transformations

- Matrix products as composition of maps
- Span, independence, basis and rank
- Linear systems
- Counting floating-point operations (FLOPs) and memory

### Orthogonality and least squares

- Orthogonal projection
- QR factorisation
- Least squares, normal equations and conditioning

### Eigenvalues and singular values

- Eigenvectors of symmetric matrices
- Covariance and principal component analysis (PCA)
- Power iteration and link ranking
- Singular value decomposition (SVD) and low-rank structure in recommenders and model adaptation

### Working numerically

- Vectorisation and broadcasting
- Floating-point limits
- Checking code against hand computation

---

# FND-MTH-102 · Calculus and Optimisation for Machine Learning

- Track: Data & AI Foundations
- Path: [Mathematics and Statistics](https://sdaiaacademy.github.io/en/paths/FND-MTH.md)
- Level: Level 100 · Explain
- Format: Extended: 8 weeks part-time, one session and one lab a week, weekly graded problem sets and a capstone
- Total hours: 45 h
- Audience: beginner
- Status: In development

## Description

Participants work through the calculus that trains models: derivatives as local linear approximations, gradients, Jacobians and the chain rule on computational graphs. They backpropagate by hand, then write a small reverse-mode automatic differentiation engine and check it against a framework. They run batch, stochastic and momentum gradient descent, read loss curves, and handle convexity and constraints. The capstone trains a small network with their own engine; tensor-level differentiation and modern optimisers follow in SPC-DLR-302.

## Learning outcomes

By the end, the participant can:

- Explain derivatives, partial derivatives, gradients and Jacobians as local linear approximations.
- Distinguish convex from non-convex objectives and describe how saddle points and step size shape gradient descent.
- Explain how a constraint moves the optimum of a small problem, using the Lagrangian and the meaning of its multiplier.
- Compute gradients of a composite function by applying the chain rule backwards through a computational graph.
- Implement reverse-mode automatic differentiation for scalar operations and verify it with finite-difference checks.
- Apply batch, stochastic and momentum gradient descent and diagnose divergence or slow convergence from loss curves.

## Prerequisites

- [FND-MTH-101 · Linear Algebra for Machine Learning](https://sdaiaacademy.github.io/en/courses/FND-MTH-101.md)
- School calculus: derivatives of polynomials and exponentials, or the pre-work refresher
- Writes short Python programs with functions and loops (FND-PRG-101 or equivalent)

## Topics

### Change and approximation

- Derivatives and the tangent-line approximation
- Partial derivatives, gradients and Jacobians
- Taylor expansions and finite differences

### The chain rule on graphs

- Computational graphs
- Forward and reverse mode
- Backpropagation by hand
- The chain rule with vectors and matrices

### Gradient-based optimisation

- Gradient descent and step size
- Stochastic and mini-batch gradients
- Momentum and adaptive step methods
- Learning-rate warm-up and decay
- Reading loss curves

### Shape and constraints

- Convexity, local minima and saddle points
- Curvature, the Hessian and the largest stable step
- Numerically stable softmax and log-sum-exp
- Regularisation as a penalty
- Lagrange multipliers and projected gradients

---

# FND-MTH-103 · Probability for Data and AI

- Track: Data & AI Foundations
- Path: [Mathematics and Statistics](https://sdaiaacademy.github.io/en/paths/FND-MTH.md)
- Level: Level 100 · Explain
- Format: Extended: 8 weeks part-time, one session and one lab a week, weekly graded problem sets and a capstone
- Total hours: 45 h
- Audience: beginner
- Status: In development

## Description

Participants build probabilistic reasoning from conditional probability to random variables, distributions, expectation and the limit theorems, checking every analytic answer with a seeded simulation. Screening and alert scenarios show base rates at work, categorical sampling shows how a language model picks tokens, and likelihood and cross-entropy connect probability to training losses. The capstone is a simulation model of a queue or alert system whose analytic and simulated answers must agree.

## Learning outcomes

By the end, the participant can:

- Explain conditional probability, independence and Bayes rule, and identify base-rate errors in worded claims.
- Describe the common discrete and continuous distributions and identify which fits a described process.
- Explain the law of large numbers and the central limit theorem and identify where the normal approximation fails.
- Compute expectations, variances and conditional probabilities analytically and confirm them by seeded simulation.
- Implement reproducible Monte Carlo simulations that report each estimate with its standard error.
- Compute likelihood, entropy, cross-entropy and Kullback-Leibler divergence and relate them to training losses.

## Prerequisites

- School algebra and reading graphs of functions; area under a curve is introduced in the pre-work
- Writes short Python programs with lists, loops and functions (FND-PRG-101 or equivalent)

## Next courses

- [FND-MTH-104 · Statistics by Simulation: Variation, Estimation and Testing](https://sdaiaacademy.github.io/en/courses/FND-MTH-104.md)

## Topics

### Events and conditioning

- Sample spaces and events
- Conditional probability and independence
- Bayes rule, base rates and likelihood ratios
- Updating a proportion with a beta prior

### Random variables and distributions

- Bernoulli, binomial, geometric, Poisson and categorical
- Uniform, normal and exponential
- Joint, marginal and conditional distributions
- Expectation, variance and covariance

### Limit theorems and simulation

- Pseudo-random generators and seeds
- Monte Carlo estimation and its error
- Law of large numbers and central limit theorem

### Probability inside models

- Likelihood and maximum likelihood
- Entropy, cross-entropy and Kullback-Leibler divergence
- Sampling with temperature
- Calibrated probabilities versus scores

---

# FND-MTH-104 · Statistics by Simulation: Variation, Estimation and Testing

- Track: Data & AI Foundations
- Path: [Mathematics and Statistics](https://sdaiaacademy.github.io/en/paths/FND-MTH.md)
- Level: Level 100 · Explain
- Format: Extended: 8 weeks part-time, one session and one lab a week, weekly graded problem sets and a capstone
- Total hours: 45 h
- Audience: beginner
- Status: In development

## Description

Participants approach inference by simulation before formulas. They draw repeated samples to see variation, build bootstrap intervals for means, medians, differences and slopes, run permutation tests, and report effect sizes with intervals rather than bare p-values. They find multiple-testing and forking-path problems in reported results. Each lab ends with a note on how the result was checked, and the capstone is an analysis brief on a public dataset, defended orally. Power analysis and study design follow in SPC-STA-201 and SPC-EXP-201.

## Learning outcomes

By the end, the participant can:

- Distinguish population, sample, parameter, statistic and sampling distribution, and explain what a standard error measures.
- Explain what p-values and confidence intervals mean and identify misreadings of them.
- Identify multiple-testing, forking-path and confounding problems in a reported analysis.
- Compute bootstrap intervals for means, medians, group differences and regression slopes.
- Implement permutation tests and report each result as an effect size with an interval.
- Apply family-wise and false-discovery-rate corrections and measure by simulation how often uncorrected tests produce false findings.

## Prerequisites

- [FND-MTH-103 · Probability for Data and AI](https://sdaiaacademy.github.io/en/courses/FND-MTH-103.md)
- Probability shown in the placement test is accepted in place of FND-MTH-103
- Computes group summaries with a DataFrame library (FND-DAT-102 or the pre-work notebook)

## Next courses

- [SPC-STA-201 · Statistical Inference by Simulation](https://sdaiaacademy.github.io/en/courses/SPC-STA-201.md)
- [SPC-EXP-201 · Designing and Reading Experiments](https://sdaiaacademy.github.io/en/courses/SPC-EXP-201.md)

## Topics

### Describing data

- Centre and spread, median and interquartile range
- Distribution shape and outliers
- Missing data and summaries

### Sampling variation

- Populations, samples and sampling frames
- Sampling distributions and standard error by simulation
- Observational versus experimental data, confounding and Simpson's paradox

### Estimation

- The bootstrap and its assumptions
- Interval coverage checked by simulation
- Intervals for differences and slopes

### Testing

- Null models and permutation tests
- What p-values do not mean
- Type I and Type II errors, and a first look at power
- Effect size and practical significance

### Honest reporting

- Multiple testing and false discoveries
- Forking paths and pre-specified analyses
- Recording how each result was checked

---

# FND-MTH-105 · Discrete Mathematics and Logic for Computing

- Track: Data & AI Foundations
- Path: [Mathematics and Statistics](https://sdaiaacademy.github.io/en/paths/FND-MTH.md)
- Level: Level 100 · Explain
- Format: Extended: 7 weeks part-time, one session and one lab a week, weekly graded problem sets and a capstone portfolio
- Total hours: 40 h
- Audience: beginner
- Status: In development

## Description

Participants practise the discrete mathematics and proof that computing degrees assume: sets, relations, logic, proof, counting and graphs. Code tests each claim on generated cases before it is proved, so the gap between testing and proof is visible. Labs link relations to joins, logic to rule checking, counting to collision and re-identification risk, and graphs to pipeline dependencies. Algorithms on graphs follow in FND-PRG-103.

## Learning outcomes

By the end, the participant can:

- Identify whether a relation is a function, an equivalence or an order, and which properties it has.
- Distinguish valid from invalid arguments and translate plain-language rules into propositional and predicate logic.
- Describe direct, contradiction and induction proofs and identify the gap in a flawed proof.
- Apply induction and loop invariants to prove simple claims about integers, sets and recursive code.
- Compute counts of arrangements, selections and collisions and verify them by enumeration.
- Use a graph model of dependencies to find cycles and compute a topological order.

## Prerequisites

- School algebra
- Writes short Python programs with lists, loops, functions and recursion (FND-PRG-101 or equivalent)

## Topics

### Sets, functions and relations

- Sets and Cartesian products
- Injective, surjective and bijective functions
- Equivalence relations and orders
- Joins as relation composition

### Logic

- Propositional logic and truth tables
- Normal forms and Boolean satisfiability (SAT)
- Predicates and quantifiers

### Proof

- Direct proof, counterexample and contradiction
- Mathematical and structural induction
- Loop invariants
- Testing a claim versus proving it

### Counting

- Sum and product rules
- Permutations and combinations
- Pigeonhole and inclusion-exclusion

### Graphs and growth

- Graphs, trees and directed acyclic graphs
- Paths, cycles and topological order
- Recurrences and growth of functions

---

# FND-DAT-101 · SQL and Relational Data

- Track: Data & AI Foundations
- Path: [Data Handling](https://sdaiaacademy.github.io/en/paths/FND-DAT.md)
- Level: Level 100 · Explain
- Format: Intensive: 4 teaching days and a capstone day, with guided pre-work and a tracked follow-up task
- Total hours: 30 h
- Audience: beginner
- Status: In development

## Description

Participants query relational data in SQL and check that the answers are right. In an embedded analytical engine on a laptop they move from keys and constraints through joins, grouping and common table expressions to window functions. They predict results before running queries, catch the silent errors that joins and NULLs cause, and test assistant-written SQL against known answers. The capstone answers a stakeholder brief on an unseen dataset.

## Learning outcomes

By the end, the participant can:

- Explain the relational model: tables, keys, constraints, NULL and the grain of a table.
- Identify the output of joins, grouping and NULL comparisons before running them.
- Write queries with filters, joins, grouping, subqueries and common table expressions that answer business questions.
- Apply window functions to rank rows, compare periods and compute running and moving totals.
- Implement a small schema with keys and constraints, load raw files into it and report rejected rows.
- Identify silent errors in assistant-written SQL, such as join fan-out, wrong grain and missing business rules.

## Prerequisites

- Comfortable with spreadsheets: filters, sorting and simple formulas
- No programming experience required

## Next courses

- [DEV-DAT-201 · Modern Data Engineering](https://sdaiaacademy.github.io/en/courses/DEV-DAT-201.md)
- [DEV-DAT-301 · Data Modelling: Conceptual to Semantic](https://sdaiaacademy.github.io/en/courses/DEV-DAT-301.md)
- [SPC-ANL-203 · Metrics, Semantic Models and Dashboards](https://sdaiaacademy.github.io/en/courses/SPC-ANL-203.md)
- [SPC-ANL-204 · Data Acquisition, Preparation and Quality for Analysis](https://sdaiaacademy.github.io/en/courses/SPC-ANL-204.md)

## Topics

### The relational model

- Tables, types, keys and constraints
- Grain and cardinality
- Normal forms in brief, and why analytical tables are wider
- Embedded versus client-server engines

### Querying one table

- Filters, sorting, and expressions on text and dates
- CASE expressions and set operations
- NULL and three-valued logic
- Grouping and having

### Combining tables

- Inner, outer, semi and anti joins
- Join fan-out and double counting
- Subqueries and common table expressions

### Window functions

- Partitions and ordering
- Ranking, lag and lead
- Running and moving aggregates

### Building and checking

- Loading files into constrained tables
- Insert, update and delete inside a transaction
- Views that limit what is exposed
- Reading a query plan and the effect of an index
- Testing queries against known answers

# FND-DAT-102 · Data Wrangling with DataFrames

- Track: Data & AI Foundations
- Path: [Data Handling](https://sdaiaacademy.github.io/en/paths/FND-DAT.md)
- Level: Level 100 · Explain
- Format: Intensive: 4 teaching days and a capstone day, with guided pre-work and a tracked follow-up task
- Total hours: 30 h
- Audience: beginner
- Status: In development

## Description

Participants turn messy raw files into analysis-ready tables with a DataFrame library. They type data, handle missing values, parse dates, normalise Arabic and English text, reshape between wide and long forms, join with cardinality checks and aggregate, writing each step as a small tested function in a notebook that reruns from the raw files. Labs use a synthetic bilingual service-request register; the capstone documents a fresh extract.

## Learning outcomes

By the end, the participant can:

- Describe tidy data and identify the reshaping operation that makes a given table tidy.
- Distinguish the ways data can be missing and explain how dropping, filling or flagging changes a summary.
- Implement a cleaning pipeline as chained, tested functions for types, dates, duplicates and categories.
- Apply joins with declared cardinality and reconcile row counts before and after each join.
- Normalise Arabic and English text fields for matching and measure the effect on match rates.
- Identify defects in assistant-written wrangling code, such as wrong types, dropped rows and many-to-many joins.

## Prerequisites

- Writes short Python programs with functions, lists and dictionaries (FND-PRG-101 or equivalent)
- Runs a notebook and installs a package in a provided environment

## Next courses

- [FND-DAT-103 · Data Formats, Interfaces and Quality Checks](https://sdaiaacademy.github.io/en/courses/FND-DAT-103.md)
- [SPC-ANL-201 · Exploratory Analysis and Visualisation](https://sdaiaacademy.github.io/en/courses/SPC-ANL-201.md)
- [SPC-ANL-204 · Data Acquisition, Preparation and Quality for Analysis](https://sdaiaacademy.github.io/en/courses/SPC-ANL-204.md)
- [SPC-MOD-201 · Machine Learning for Tabular Data: Baselines and Validation](https://sdaiaacademy.github.io/en/courses/SPC-MOD-201.md)

## Topics

### Loading and typing

- Delimited, spreadsheet and columnar files
- Spreadsheet traps: serial dates, leading zeros, merged headers
- Nullable, string and categorical types
- Copy behaviour and method chaining

### Cleaning

- Missing values: causes and treatments
- Duplicates and keys
- Range and plausibility checks
- Dates, periods, and Hijri and Gregorian calendars

### Text, including Arabic

- String methods and regular expressions
- Arabic letter variants, diacritics, elongation and digit forms
- Names and addresses across scripts

### Reshaping, joining and aggregating

- Tidy data, melt and pivot
- Joins with validated cardinality
- Group-by and window-style operations
- Eager and lazy engines

### Reproducible notebooks

- Rerunning from raw files
- Functions, assertions and parameters
- Data dictionaries and cleaning logs

# FND-DAT-103 · Data Formats, Interfaces and Quality Checks

- Track: Data & AI Foundations
- Path: [Data Handling](https://sdaiaacademy.github.io/en/paths/FND-DAT.md)
- Level: Level 100 · Explain
- Format: Workshop: two days with labs, a short pre-work task and a tracked follow-up task
- Total hours: 16 h
- Audience: beginner
- Status: In development

## Description

Participants move data between files, interfaces and tables without losing or corrupting it. They compare delimited, JSON Lines and columnar files, repair encoding and time-zone faults, write a paginated API client with retries, flatten nested JSON and declare a schema whose checks stop a bad batch from loading.

## Learning outcomes

By the end, the participant can:

- Compare delimited, JSON Lines and columnar files on size, read time and type fidelity.
- Explain how encodings, byte order marks and time zones corrupt data, and identify each symptom.
- Implement an API client that follows cursor pagination, respects rate limits, retries with backoff and keeps raw responses.
- Convert nested JSON into typed tables written as partitioned columnar files.
- Implement validation checks that stop a load when a batch breaks the declared schema.

## Prerequisites

- [FND-DAT-102 · Data Wrangling with DataFrames](https://sdaiaacademy.github.io/en/courses/FND-DAT-102.md)
- Writes Python functions and handles exceptions (FND-PRG-101 or equivalent)

## Topics

### File formats

- Delimited dialects and quoting
- JSON (JavaScript Object Notation) and JSON Lines
- Columnar files, partitions and in-memory interchange

### Text and time

- UTF-8 and legacy Arabic encodings
- Offsets and Coordinated Universal Time (UTC)
- Time zones and daylight saving

### Interfaces

- Status codes and errors
- Offset and cursor pagination
- Rate limits, retries and backoff
- Rerunnable loads and checkpoints

### Schema and validation

- Declared types, ranges and keys
- Failing a load versus quarantining rows
- Data contracts, which follow in DEV-DAT-204

---

# FND-AIC-101 · How Machine Learning Works

- Track: Data & AI Foundations
- Path: [AI Concepts and Responsible Practice](https://sdaiaacademy.github.io/en/paths/FND-AIC.md)
- Level: Level 100 · Explain
- Format: Intensive: 4 teaching days and a capstone day, with guided pre-work and a tracked follow-up task
- Total hours: 30 h
- Audience: beginner
- Status: In development

## Description

Participants work out how supervised learning turns labelled examples into predictions, by hand first and then in code. They fit a nearest-neighbour rule and a linear model on paper, make a model overfit on purpose, choose a decision threshold from error costs and base rates, and hunt leaks seeded in a pipeline. Labs run on a laptop with small public or synthetic tabular data, and the capstone is an honest modelling report with a model card, defended in person.

## Learning outcomes

By the end, the participant can:

- Explain how a supervised learner fits a prediction rule by minimising a loss.
- Distinguish training, validation and test data, and identify overfitting and underfitting from plotted curves.
- Identify target, duplicate, preprocessing and temporal leakage in modelling pipelines.
- Implement a train, validate and test workflow comparing a baseline, a linear model and a decision tree.
- Compute confusion-matrix metrics and choose a threshold from error costs and the base rate.
- Draft a one-page model card with intended use, data, metrics by subgroup and known limits.

## Prerequisites

- [FND-PRG-101 · Python Programming for Data and AI](https://sdaiaacademy.github.io/en/courses/FND-PRG-101.md)
- Writes short Python functions and loops; a passed placement exercise is accepted instead of FND-PRG-101
- Uses school algebra; the derivative of a squared error is taught in the pre-work

## Next courses

- [DEV-LLM-202 · Applied Natural Language Processing Engineering](https://sdaiaacademy.github.io/en/courses/DEV-LLM-202.md)
- [DEV-MLE-201 · Machine Learning Engineering: Baselines, Validation and Pipelines](https://sdaiaacademy.github.io/en/courses/DEV-MLE-201.md)
- [DEV-INF-201 · Machine Learning Systems on One Machine](https://sdaiaacademy.github.io/en/courses/DEV-INF-201.md)
- [SPC-MOD-201 · Machine Learning for Tabular Data: Baselines and Validation](https://sdaiaacademy.github.io/en/courses/SPC-MOD-201.md)

## Topics

### Learning from examples

- Features, labels and prediction rules
- Loss and gradient descent
- Nearest neighbours and linear models by hand

### Generalisation

- Training, validation and test sets
- Model complexity, overfitting and regularisation
- Cross-validation and learning curves

### Measuring a model

- Confusion matrix, precision and recall
- Thresholds, error costs and base rates
- Regression errors against a naive baseline

### Data and leakage

- Encoding, scaling and missing values
- Pipelines fitted on training data only
- Target, duplicate and temporal leakage

### Model families and limits

- Trees, linear models and small neural networks
- Distribution shift and subgroup error gaps
- Where language models fit (FND-AIC-102)

---

# FND-AIC-102 · How Language Models Work

- Track: Data & AI Foundations
- Path: [AI Concepts and Responsible Practice](https://sdaiaacademy.github.io/en/paths/FND-AIC.md)
- Level: Level 100 · Explain
- Format: Workshop: two days with labs and a tracked follow-up task
- Total hours: 16 h
- Audience: beginner
- Status: In development

## Description

Participants test language model behaviour with small logged experiments. They count Arabic and English tokens, read next-token probabilities from a small open-weight model, vary sampling, probe long-context recall, write a minimal tool-calling loop and measure what extra reasoning effort buys. The output is a behaviour sheet for one model, each claim backed by a run.

## Learning outcomes

By the end, the participant can:

- Explain how a model generates text by repeated next-token prediction and how sampling settings change the output.
- Measure token counts for parallel Arabic and English text across two tokenisers.
- Describe how pretraining, post-training and reasoning effort shape an assistant's answers, and what a knowledge cut-off limits.
- Implement a minimal tool-calling loop and mark which steps the model and the program each perform.
- Identify typical failure modes in model transcripts and name a check that catches each.

## Prerequisites

- Runs a Python notebook and edits short scripts (FND-PRG-101 or equivalent)

## Next courses

- [SPC-MOD-303 · Text and Unstructured Data for Data Science](https://sdaiaacademy.github.io/en/courses/SPC-MOD-303.md)

## Topics

### Tokens and prediction

- Tokenisers and Arabic script
- Transformers and attention in outline
- Next-token probabilities and sampling
- Tokens as cost and context

### How models are made

- Pretraining and post-training
- Reasoning effort and test-time compute
- Knowledge cut-off

### Context and tools

- Context windows and recall
- Tool calls that a program executes
- Retrieval as fresh context

### Failure modes

- Fabrication and sycophancy
- Injection through retrieved text
- Jagged capability

---

# FND-AIC-103 · Reading AI Evidence: Benchmarks, Claims and Statistics

- Track: Data & AI Foundations
- Path: [AI Concepts and Responsible Practice](https://sdaiaacademy.github.io/en/paths/FND-AIC.md)
- Level: Level 100 · Explain
- Format: Workshop: one day with labs and short guided pre-reading
- Total hours: 8 h
- Audience: beginner
- Status: In development

## Description

Participants read the numbers behind AI decisions: benchmark scores, leaderboard ranks, launch claims, adoption figures and model cards. They rescore an agent run as partial credit and as finished tasks, test whether a reported gain exceeds its noise, list what changed between two runs of one benchmark, and reconcile adoption figures that range from about 20% to 90%. The day ends with an evidence brief.

## Learning outcomes

By the end, the participant can:

- Explain what a benchmark measures and name threats to its validity, such as contamination, saturation and invalid items.
- Identify why two reported scores are not comparable: partial credit, attempts, harness, token budget or grader.
- Compute an interval for a reported accuracy difference and decide whether it exceeds sampling noise.
- Explain how adoption and productivity figures differ by denominator, time window and self-reported or measured effect.
- Draft an evidence brief that separates what a published AI claim shows from what it asserts, using its model card.

## Prerequisites

- Reads percentages and chart axes and writes a spreadsheet formula; no programming is required

## Topics

### Benchmarks

- Construct, items and scoring
- Contamination, saturation and audits
- Leaderboards built on pairwise votes

### Comparing results

- Partial credit against completed tasks
- 50% and 80% reliability time horizons
- Same model, different harness
- Cost per completed task
- Intervals and paired comparisons

### Claims about use and value

- Denominators and time windows
- Self-report against randomised trials
- What model and system cards omit

---

# FND-AIC-104 · Responsible Data and AI Practice for Builders

- Track: Data & AI Foundations
- Path: [AI Concepts and Responsible Practice](https://sdaiaacademy.github.io/en/paths/FND-AIC.md)
- Level: Level 100 · Explain
- Format: Workshop: one and a half days with labs and a tracked follow-up task
- Total hours: 12 h
- Audience: beginner
- Status: In development

## Description

Participants make a synthetic build, a complaint-triage assistant that calls a language model, responsible before it is written: they classify its data, decide what may go to an external model service, check licences, turn ethics principles into checks, clean a seeded repository and write the user disclosure. DEV-SEC-201 and DEV-SEC-303 go deeper.

## Learning outcomes

By the end, the participant can:

- Explain the data protection principles that shape a build, from lawful basis to transfer and breach notice.
- Classify project data by sensitivity and decide what may go to an external model service.
- Analyse model and dataset licences, including attribution and non-commercial terms, against a stated use.
- Identify the build check and user disclosure that each AI ethics principle requires.
- Apply security hygiene to a repository: remove secrets, pin and audit dependencies, validate model output.

## Prerequisites

- Has run a small Python project under version control (FND-PRG-102 or equivalent)

## Topics

### Data protection and classification

- Personal data in prompts, logs and training
- Lawful basis, minimisation, retention, transfer
- Classification and external services
- Pseudonymisation and its limits

### Licences and provenance

- Open-weight and dataset licences
- Attribution and use restrictions
- Ownership of generated content

### Ethics principles as build checks

- Subgroup fairness tests
- Transparency and disclosure
- Human oversight and ownership
- Risk tiers setting the depth of checks

### Security hygiene

- Secrets, keys and dependency pinning
- Untrusted input, output and logs

---

# FND-AIC-105 · Classical AI: Search, Planning and Knowledge Representation

- Track: Data & AI Foundations
- Path: [AI Concepts and Responsible Practice](https://sdaiaacademy.github.io/en/paths/FND-AIC.md)
- Level: Level 100 · Explain
- Format: Intensive: 4 teaching days and a capstone day, with guided pre-work and a tracked follow-up task
- Total hours: 30 h
- Audience: beginner
- Status: In development

## Description

Participants solve problems with the methods that predate machine learning and still run timetables, routes, configurations and rule checks. They implement heuristic search on an open road map, model a timetable for a constraint solver, run a classical planner, and encode eligibility rules in logic to find conflicts, then compare each result with a language-model-only attempt. The course suits career changers bridging to degree-level AI foundations and engineers who give agents solvers and planners as tools.

## Learning outcomes

By the end, the participant can:

- Describe a problem as states, actions, goal and costs, and distinguish when search, constraints, planning or logic fits it.
- Implement uniform-cost and A* search with an admissible heuristic and measure the nodes each expands.
- Implement a constraint model of a timetabling problem with hard rules and soft preferences.
- Explain how a classical planner derives a plan from action definitions and why each step can be checked.
- Implement eligibility rules in logic and use an inference engine to answer queries and expose conflicts.
- Compare a classical method and a language-model-only attempt for correctness, verifiability, cost and explanation.

## Prerequisites

- [FND-PRG-101 · Python Programming for Data and AI](https://sdaiaacademy.github.io/en/courses/FND-PRG-101.md)
- Writes Python functions over lists and dictionaries; FND-PRG-103 or FND-MTH-105 helps but is not required

## Topics

### Search

- State spaces and problem formulation
- Uninformed search, heuristics and A*
- Local search and simulated annealing
- Game search and Monte Carlo tree search in brief

### Constraint satisfaction

- Variables, domains, hard and soft constraints
- Backtracking and propagation
- SAT and constraint-programming solvers
- Where integer programming takes over (SPC-MOD-304)

### Planning

- Actions with preconditions and effects
- Planning domain definition language
- Plan validation and replanning

### Logic and knowledge representation

- Propositional and first-order logic
- Forward and backward chaining
- Ontologies in brief (DEV-DAT-304)

### Where classical methods still win

- Guarantees and audit trails
- Models that propose and solvers that check
- Solvers and planners as agent tools

---

# FND-AIC-106 · Technical Writing for Data and AI Work

- Track: Data & AI Foundations
- Path: [AI Concepts and Responsible Practice](https://sdaiaacademy.github.io/en/paths/FND-AIC.md)
- Level: Level 100 · Explain
- Format: Workshop: one and a half days of writing labs and a tracked follow-up review
- Total hours: 12 h
- Audience: beginner
- Status: In development

## Description

Participants write the documents that data and AI work runs on: a README, a design document, a decision memo, an experiment report and a model or system card. Each starts from a repository, a model comparison or an evaluation log and ends with a peer test; one draft is unassisted, another is revised with an assistant, and every claim is checked.

## Learning outcomes

By the end, the participant can:

- Identify the reader, purpose and required sections of five common technical document types.
- Draft a README that lets a stranger install, run and check a small project.
- Draft a one-page decision memo with options, trade-offs, a recommendation and the conditions that would change it.
- Prepare an experiment report and a model card that state uncertainty, results by data slice and known limits.
- Compare an unassisted draft with an assisted revision for accuracy, clarity and invented content.

## Prerequisites

- Has a small data or code project, own or provided, to document

## Topics

### Writing for a reader

- Reader, purpose and decision
- Bottom line first
- Arabic and English glossaries
- Uncertainty in plain words
- Rubric-based peer review

### Documents for systems and evidence

- README, design document, decision record
- Experiment reports
- Model and system cards
- Diagrams as text

### Writing with assistance

- AI-off first drafts
- Typical errors of assisted revision
- Verification logs and disclosure
- Context files for coding agents

# FN-101 · Python for Data and AI Work

- Track: Data & AI Foundations
- Path: [Shared Foundations: the entry courses for both badge tracks](https://sdaiaacademy.github.io/en/paths/FN-100.md)
- Level: Level 100 · Explain
- Format: Intensive: 4 teaching days of four sessions and a capstone day, with guided pre-work and a tracked follow-up task
- Total hours: 26 h
- Audience: beginner
- Status: Available
- Open the course: https://sdaiaacademy.github.io/fn-101/
- The whole course in one file: https://sdaiaacademy.github.io/fn-101/llms-full.txt
- Practice questions: https://sdaiaacademy.github.io/fn-101/practice.html

## Description

Participants write Python the way data and AI work needs it: small typed functions over collections and files, errors that fail loudly, and code moved out of notebooks into scripts that rerun. The case is a fictional regional water utility with synthetic meter readings in comma-separated values (CSV) files and bilingual service tickets in JavaScript Object Notation (JSON) Lines. Each day opens with an AI-off drill in reading, tracing or debugging code by hand, and the labs grow into a command-line tool that validates readings, flags anomalies and writes a summary report. Arabic text normalisation and SQL are left to FN-104, version control to FN-102.

## Learning outcomes

By the end, the participant can:

- Explain what a short program prints, step by step, including name binding, shared mutable lists and dictionaries, and scope.
- Distinguish when a notebook, a script or an importable module is the right home for a piece of code.
- Implement typed functions that load, validate and aggregate records with lists, dictionaries, sets and comprehensions.
- Apply exception handling and input validation so that each bad record is reported with a reason instead of crashing or passing silently.
- Use a repeatable debugging method: reproduce, shrink the input, form a hypothesis, test it, fix, and add a regression check.
- Prepare a command-line tool from an exploratory notebook, with an entry point, arguments and a written report.

## Prerequisites

- Has written and run a short program in any language, or completed the guided pre-work on values, conditions and loops

## Next courses

- [FN-102 · Command Line, Git and Reproducible Projects](https://sdaiaacademy.github.io/en/courses/FN-102.md)
- [FN-103 · Mathematics for Machine Learning: Vectors, Gradients and Probability](https://sdaiaacademy.github.io/en/courses/FN-103.md)
- [FN-104 · SQL and Data Wrangling](https://sdaiaacademy.github.io/en/courses/FN-104.md)
- [FN-105 · How Machine Learning and Language Models Work](https://sdaiaacademy.github.io/en/courses/FN-105.md)
- [FN-106 · Responsible Data and AI Practice in the Kingdom](https://sdaiaacademy.github.io/en/courses/FN-106.md)
- [AE-201 · Machine Learning Foundations and Model Evaluation](https://sdaiaacademy.github.io/en/courses/AE-201.md)
- [AE-203 · Building Applications on Language Models](https://sdaiaacademy.github.io/en/courses/AE-203.md)
- [AE-204 · Software Engineering with Coding Agents](https://sdaiaacademy.github.io/en/courses/AE-204.md)
- [DS-201 · Statistical Inference by Simulation](https://sdaiaacademy.github.io/en/courses/DS-201.md)
- [DS-202 · Data Acquisition, Preparation and Quality](https://sdaiaacademy.github.io/en/courses/DS-202.md)
- [DS-203 · Exploratory Analysis and Visualisation](https://sdaiaacademy.github.io/en/courses/DS-203.md)

- [DS-206 · Analysis with AI Assistants: Delegate, Verify, Reproduce](https://sdaiaacademy.github.io/en/courses/DS-206.md)

## Format and days

- Values, names and references
- Functions with clear contracts
- Type hints and a checker
- Parsons problems

- Dictionaries for counting and grouping

- Comprehensions and generators
- Records as data classes

- Exceptions that explain
- A debugging method

- What notebooks hide
- Scripts, modules and an entry point
- Tests as a safety net
- Learning with an assistant without losing the skill

### Day 5: Capstone project presentations


## Topics

### Reading and tracing code

- Values, names and references
- Mutation and aliasing
- Scope and the call stack
- Predict-the-output and Parsons problems

### Functions and types

- Decomposing a task into small functions
- Type hints and a type checker
- Docstrings and doctests
- Modules and the standard library

### Collections for data

- Lists, tuples, dictionaries and sets
- Comprehensions and generators

# FN-102 · Command Line, Git and Reproducible Projects

- Track: Data & AI Foundations
- Path: [Shared Foundations: the entry courses for both badge tracks](https://sdaiaacademy.github.io/en/paths/FN-100.md)
- Level: Level 100 · Explain
- Format: Intensive: 3 teaching days of four sessions and a capstone day, with guided pre-work and a tracked follow-up task
- Total hours: 21 h
- Audience: beginner
- Status: Available
- Open the course: https://sdaiaacademy.github.io/fn-102/
- The whole course in one file: https://sdaiaacademy.github.io/fn-102/llms-full.txt
- Practice questions: https://sdaiaacademy.github.io/fn-102/practice.html

## Description

Participants take a working but fragile analysis project and make it something another person can rebuild, review and trust. The case is a fictional public library network whose monthly loans report sits in one folder with hard-coded paths, no history, unpinned packages and a key in a configuration file. Over three days they script the shell, put the project under version control, review and merge through pull requests, lock the environment, add tests that run on every push, and write a README that reports measured results. A peer then rebuilds it on a clean machine.

## Learning outcomes

By the end, the participant can:

- Explain what a commit, a branch, a merge and a pull request record, and how each can be undone safely.
- Identify where secrets, personal data, large outputs and machine-specific paths leak into a project.
- Use shell pipelines, redirection and exit codes to inspect and summarise files without writing a program.
- Use branches, pull requests and review comments to integrate a change, resolving a merge conflict without losing either side's work.
- Configure a project environment with declared dependencies and a lock file so that it installs identically on a clean machine.
- Implement tests that run in continuous integration and a README that reports measured results with the command that produced them.

## Prerequisites

- [FN-101 · Python for Data and AI Work](https://sdaiaacademy.github.io/en/courses/FN-101.md)
- Opens a terminal and runs a Python script with arguments

## Next courses

- [AE-203 · Building Applications on Language Models](https://sdaiaacademy.github.io/en/courses/AE-203.md)
- [AE-204 · Software Engineering with Coding Agents](https://sdaiaacademy.github.io/en/courses/AE-204.md)
- [AE-205 · Deploying AI Services: Containers, Serving and Monitoring](https://sdaiaacademy.github.io/en/courses/AE-205.md)
- [AE-306 · Modern Data Engineering](https://sdaiaacademy.github.io/en/courses/AE-306.md)
- [DS-311 · Data Quality, Labelling and Pipelines for Analysis](https://sdaiaacademy.github.io/en/courses/DS-311.md)

## Format and days

### Day 1: Shell and history

- Working in the shell
- Pipelines over text
- First commits
- Reading and undoing history

### Day 2: Collaborate and lock

- Branches and pull requests
- Merge conflicts
- Environments and lock files
- Secrets and large files

### Day 3: Test, automate, report

- Tests for calculations
- Continuous integration
- A README that reports results
- Reproduction from a README

### Day 4: Capstone: a reproducible repository and its defence


## Topics

### The shell

- Paths, permissions and environment variables
- Pipes, redirection and filters
- Exit codes and short scripts
- Remote login with secure shell (SSH) keys

### Version control and review

- Commits, staging and history
- Branches, merges and conflicts
- Pull requests and review etiquette
- Undoing mistakes without rewriting shared history

### Reproducible environments

- Virtual environments
- Declared dependencies and lock files
- Pinned interpreter versions
- Data and outputs kept outside the code

### Tests and continuous integration

- Unit tests for calculations
- Small synthetic test data
- A pipeline that runs on every push

### Hygiene and reporting

- Secrets out of history: rotate, then clean
- Ignore files and pre-commit hooks
- A README that reports results
- A change log and a tagged release

# FN-103 · Mathematics for Machine Learning: Vectors, Gradients and Probability

- Track: Data & AI Foundations
- Path: [Shared Foundations: the entry courses for both badge tracks](https://sdaiaacademy.github.io/en/paths/FN-100.md)
- Level: Level 100 · Explain
- Format: Intensive: 4 teaching days of four sessions and a capstone day, with guided pre-work and a tracked follow-up task
- Total hours: 26 h
- Audience: beginner
- Status: Available
- Open the course: https://sdaiaacademy.github.io/fn-103/
- The whole course in one file: https://sdaiaacademy.github.io/fn-103/llms-full.txt
- Practice questions: https://sdaiaacademy.github.io/fn-103/practice.html

## Description

Participants learn the minimum mathematics both badges assume and compute every idea twice: by hand on a small case and in array code. The case is a fictional desalination plant with synthetic pump and sensor readings. Vectors and matrices describe the readings and their similarity; least squares and principal components find structure; derivatives, the chain rule and gradient descent fit an energy curve; conditional probability, distributions and seeded simulation explain alarm rates and the uncertainty of an estimate. The capstone ties the three strands into one short analysis.

## Learning outcomes

By the end, the participant can:

- Explain dot products, norms, matrix products and rank as operations on data, and predict the shape of each result.
- Compute cosine similarity, a least-squares fit and principal components with array code, checking each against a hand calculation.
- Describe derivatives, gradients and the chain rule on a computational graph, and trace one backward pass by hand.
- Implement gradient descent for a small model and identify step-size problems from the loss curve.
- Compute the probability that an alarm signals a real fault with Bayes rule, and confirm it by seeded simulation.
- Use simulation to estimate an expectation and its Monte Carlo error, and show how the error shrinks with sample size.

## Prerequisites

- [FN-101 · Python for Data and AI Work](https://sdaiaacademy.github.io/en/courses/FN-101.md)
- Solves a linear equation and reads a function graph at secondary-school level

## Next courses

- [FN-105 · How Machine Learning and Language Models Work](https://sdaiaacademy.github.io/en/courses/FN-105.md)
- [AE-201 · Machine Learning Foundations and Model Evaluation](https://sdaiaacademy.github.io/en/courses/AE-201.md)
- [AE-202 · Deep Learning and Generative AI Fundamentals](https://sdaiaacademy.github.io/en/courses/AE-202.md)
- [DS-201 · Statistical Inference by Simulation](https://sdaiaacademy.github.io/en/courses/DS-201.md)
- [DS-204 · Machine Learning for Tabular Data: Baselines and Validation](https://sdaiaacademy.github.io/en/courses/DS-204.md)

## Format and days

### Day 1: Data as vectors

- Vectors and similarity
- Matrices as transformations
- Loops versus vectorised code
- Rank and redundant sensors

### Day 2: Structure and fit

- Projection and least squares
- When least squares misbehaves
- Covariance and principal components
- Language models use the same algebra

### Day 3: Gradients

- Derivatives as local slopes
- The chain rule on a graph
- Gradient descent
- Penalties and their effect

### Day 4: Probability and simulation

- Conditional probability and base rates
- Distributions for counts and measurements
- Expectation and Monte Carlo error
- Probability inside models

### Day 5: Capstone: a second plant and the oral check


## Topics

### Vectors and matrices as data

- Dot products, norms and cosine similarity
- Matrix products as transformations
- Shapes, broadcasting and vectorised code
- Rank and linear independence

### Structure in data

- Projection and least squares
- Covariance and principal component analysis (PCA)
- Eigenvectors and singular values in brief
- Floating-point limits and conditioning

### Change and optimisation

- Derivatives and partial derivatives
- Gradients and the chain rule on a graph
- Automatic differentiation as the chain rule in code
- Gradient descent and step size
- Convexity, local minima and penalties

### Probability

- Conditional probability and Bayes rule
- Binomial, Poisson, normal and categorical distributions
- Expectation, variance and covariance
- Likelihood and cross-entropy as training losses

### Simulation

- Seeds and pseudo-random generators
- Monte Carlo estimates and their error
- Law of large numbers and the central limit theorem

# FN-104 · SQL and Data Wrangling

- Track: Data & AI Foundations
- Path: [Shared Foundations: the entry courses for both badge tracks](https://sdaiaacademy.github.io/en/paths/FN-100.md)
- Level: Level 100 · Explain
- Format: Intensive: 4 teaching days of four sessions and a capstone day, with guided pre-work and a tracked follow-up task
- Total hours: 26 h
- Audience: beginner
- Status: Available
- Open the course: https://sdaiaacademy.github.io/fn-104/
- The whole course in one file: https://sdaiaacademy.github.io/fn-104/llms-full.txt
- Practice questions: https://sdaiaacademy.github.io/fn-104/practice.html

## Description

Participants answer questions from data and show the answers are right. The case is a fictional courier company with synthetic shipments, hubs, couriers and delivery attempts. In an embedded analytical database they write joins, grouping and window functions, predicting each result first and catching fan-out and NULL errors. In a dataframe library they type, clean, reshape and join raw exports. At the boundary they handle delimited, JSON and columnar files, legacy Arabic encodings, Hijri and Gregorian dates, time zones, and schema checks that stop a bad batch.

## Learning outcomes

By the end, the participant can:

- Identify the grain and keys of each table and predict the row count of a join before running it.
- Implement SQL queries with joins, grouping, common table expressions and window functions that answer operational questions.
- Prepare an analysis-ready table from raw exports with a dataframe library, handling types, missing values, duplicates, dates and reshaping.
- Apply Arabic text normalisation and encoding repair so that names and addresses match across sources.
- Configure schema and quality checks that reject or quarantine a bad batch with a reason.
- Compare delimited, JSON Lines and columnar formats by size, read speed, types preserved and fitness for exchange.

## Prerequisites

- [FN-101 · Python for Data and AI Work](https://sdaiaacademy.github.io/en/courses/FN-101.md)
- Writes Python functions that read files and loop over records

## Next courses

- [AE-201 · Machine Learning Foundations and Model Evaluation](https://sdaiaacademy.github.io/en/courses/AE-201.md)
- [AE-306 · Modern Data Engineering](https://sdaiaacademy.github.io/en/courses/AE-306.md)
- [DS-202 · Data Acquisition, Preparation and Quality](https://sdaiaacademy.github.io/en/courses/DS-202.md)
- [DS-203 · Exploratory Analysis and Visualisation](https://sdaiaacademy.github.io/en/courses/DS-203.md)
- [DS-206 · Analysis with AI Assistants: Delegate, Verify, Reproduce](https://sdaiaacademy.github.io/en/courses/DS-206.md)
- [DS-307 · Metrics, Semantic Models and Dashboards](https://sdaiaacademy.github.io/en/courses/DS-307.md)

## Format and days

### Day 1: Query with care

- Grain, keys and cardinality
- Filters and NULL
- Joins that do not double count
- Grouping and common table expressions

### Day 2: Windows and checks

- Ranking and top-N
- Change over time
- Sequences of events
- Testing queries

### Day 3: Wrangle with dataframes

- Loading and typing
- Missing values and duplicates
- Reshape and join
- Same result, two engines

### Day 4: Formats, text and validation

- Choosing a file format
- Encodings and Arabic text
- Dates and time zones
- Checks that stop a bad batch

### Day 5: Capstone: the operations brief and its live rerun


## Topics

### Relational querying

- Tables, keys, grain and cardinality
- Filters, NULL and three-valued logic
- Joins, fan-out and anti joins
- Grouping and common table expressions

### Window functions

- Partitions and ordering
- Ranking, lag and lead
- Running and moving aggregates
- Testing a query against known answers

### Dataframes

- Typed loading and nullable types
- Missing values and duplicates
- Tidy data: melt and pivot
- Joins with validated cardinality
- Eager and lazy engines

### Text, dates and encodings

- UTF-8 and legacy Arabic code pages
- Arabic letter variants, diacritics, elongation and digits
- Hijri and Gregorian dates
- Time zones and offsets

### Formats and validation

- Delimited, JSON Lines and columnar files
- Declared schemas and range checks
- Rejecting a load versus quarantining rows
- Data dictionaries and cleaning logs

# FN-105 · How Machine Learning and Language Models Work

- Track: Data & AI Foundations
- Path: [Shared Foundations: the entry courses for both badge tracks](https://sdaiaacademy.github.io/en/paths/FN-100.md)
- Level: Level 100 · Explain
- Format: Intensive: 3 teaching days of four sessions and a capstone day, with guided pre-work and a tracked follow-up task
- Total hours: 21 h
- Audience: beginner
- Status: Available
- Open the course: https://sdaiaacademy.github.io/fn-105/
- The whole course in one file: https://sdaiaacademy.github.io/fn-105/llms-full.txt
- Practice questions: https://sdaiaacademy.github.io/fn-105/practice.html

## Description

Participants find out how models are made and where they fail by doing the work in small steps. The case is the after-sales service of a fictional home-appliance retailer. They fit a nearest-neighbour rule and a line by hand, then train and validate a classifier that predicts which repair tickets need a second visit, overfit it on purpose and find planted leakage. They then count tokens in Arabic and English, sample from a small open-weight model, test recall across a long warranty document, and check a published model claim against its evidence.

## Learning outcomes

By the end, the participant can:

- Explain how a supervised model fits labelled examples by reducing a loss, and why its score on training data overstates its score on new data.
- Use a train, validation and test split and cross-validation to compare a baseline with two models.
- Analyse a pipeline for target, duplicate and temporal leakage and measure the score before and after each fix.
- Compute precision, recall and the cost of errors at several thresholds and choose one for a stated cost.
- Describe how a language model splits text into tokens, predicts and samples the next token, and uses its context window.
- Identify the limits of a model claim, including fabrication, knowledge cut-off, benchmark contamination and partial versus complete credit.

## Prerequisites

- [FN-101 · Python for Data and AI Work](https://sdaiaacademy.github.io/en/courses/FN-101.md)
- [FN-103 · Mathematics for Machine Learning: Vectors, Gradients and Probability](https://sdaiaacademy.github.io/en/courses/FN-103.md)
- Loads a table into a dataframe and computes a proportion

## Next courses

- [FN-106 · Responsible Data and AI Practice in the Kingdom](https://sdaiaacademy.github.io/en/courses/FN-106.md)
- [AE-201 · Machine Learning Foundations and Model Evaluation](https://sdaiaacademy.github.io/en/courses/AE-201.md)
- [AE-203 · Building Applications on Language Models](https://sdaiaacademy.github.io/en/courses/AE-203.md)
- [DS-204 · Machine Learning for Tabular Data: Baselines and Validation](https://sdaiaacademy.github.io/en/courses/DS-204.md)

## Format and days

### Day 1: Models from examples

- Learning by hand
- Training and testing
- Overfitting on purpose
- Thresholds and the cost of errors

### Day 2: Evaluation and leakage

- Cross-validation
- Finding leakage
- Error by subgroup
- Tokens and next-token prediction

### Day 3: Language models and their limits

- Sampling and variability
- Context and recall
- Fabrication and grounding
- Reading AI evidence

### Day 4: Capstone: the modelling report and its defence


## Topics

### Learning from examples

- Features, labels and loss
- Nearest neighbours and linear models by hand
- Trees and small neural networks in brief

### Generalisation and evaluation

- Train, validation and test sets
- Overfitting and learning curves
- Cross-validation
- Confusion matrix, precision, recall and thresholds

### Leakage and data

- Target, duplicate and temporal leakage
- Pipelines fitted on training data only
- Distribution shift and subgroup error

### How language models work

- Tokens and Arabic script
- Next-token probabilities and sampling
- Pretraining and post-training
- Context windows, tools and retrieval in brief

### Limits and evidence

- Fabrication and sycophancy
- Knowledge cut-off and model cards
- Benchmarks, contamination and harness effects
- Partial credit against completed tasks

# FN-106 · Responsible Data and AI Practice in the Kingdom

- Track: Data & AI Foundations
- Path: [Shared Foundations: the entry courses for both badge tracks](https://sdaiaacademy.github.io/en/paths/FN-100.md)
- Level: Level 100 · Explain
- Format: Intensive: 3 teaching days of four sessions and a capstone day, with guided pre-work and a tracked follow-up task
- Total hours: 21 h
- Audience: beginner
- Status: Available
- Open the course: https://sdaiaacademy.github.io/fn-106/
- The whole course in one file: https://sdaiaacademy.github.io/fn-106/llms-full.txt
- Practice questions: https://sdaiaacademy.github.io/fn-106/practice.html

## Description

Participants make one small build lawful and responsible: a parent-enquiry assistant for a fictional private school group that drafts replies from attendance and fee records with a language model. They map its personal data and minimise it under the Personal Data Protection Law (PDPL), classify each data set under the National Data Management Office (NDMO) policy, decide what may reach an external model, turn the SDAIA AI Ethics Principles into tests, assess risk with the National AI Risk Management Framework, and write the disclosure and records the build needs.

## Learning outcomes

By the end, the participant can:

- Explain the PDPL obligations that govern a build, from lawful basis and minimisation to rights, retention, transfer and breach handling.
- Distinguish what the data classification, data sharing and open data policies and the SDAIA Generative AI Guidelines each decide.
- Classify each data set of the build under the four NDMO classification levels and derive the rule for sending it to an external model service.
- Apply minimisation and pseudonymisation to the data the assistant sends, and test whether records can be re-identified.
- Prepare a risk assessment that places the assistant in an ethics risk tier and works through the four phases of the national risk framework.
- Test the assistant against the ethics principles for fairness across Arabic and English enquiries, transparency and human review, and draft the disclosure parents see.

## Prerequisites

- [FN-101 · Python for Data and AI Work](https://sdaiaacademy.github.io/en/courses/FN-101.md)
- [FN-105 · How Machine Learning and Language Models Work](https://sdaiaacademy.github.io/en/courses/FN-105.md)
- Reads a short Python program that calls a web API

## Next courses

- [AE-207 · Responsible and Secure AI Engineering Practice](https://sdaiaacademy.github.io/en/courses/AE-207.md)
- [DS-202 · Data Acquisition, Preparation and Quality](https://sdaiaacademy.github.io/en/courses/DS-202.md)
- [DS-206 · Analysis with AI Assistants: Delegate, Verify, Reproduce](https://sdaiaacademy.github.io/en/courses/DS-206.md)
- [DS-207 · Responsible Data Practice and Conduct in Analytical Work](https://sdaiaacademy.github.io/en/courses/DS-207.md)

## Format and days

### Day 1: Personal data and the law

- Where personal data flows in a build
- Lawful basis and minimisation
- Pseudonymisation and its limits
- Rights, retention and breaches

### Day 2: Classify, share and send

- Data classification levels
- What may reach an external model
- Sharing with another entity
- Licences and provenance

### Day 3: Ethics and risk in practice

- Principles into tests
- Testing the assistant
- Risk tier and risk register
- Disclosure and human review

### Day 4: Capstone: the responsible build pack


## Topics

### Personal data in a build

- Personal data in prompts, logs and stores
- Lawful basis, purpose and minimisation
- Rights, retention, transfer and breaches
- Records of processing activities

### Classification and sharing

- Four levels and impact assessment
- Handling rules for external services
- Sharing with another entity
- What may be published as open data

### Ethics principles as tests

- The seven SDAIA AI Ethics Principles
- Risk tiers from little or no risk to unacceptable
- Fairness across languages and groups, with the AI Bias Reference Guide
- Disclosure and human review

### Generative AI and risk

- Generative AI guidelines for government and public use
- The four phases of the national risk framework
- Likelihood, impact and treatment
- Licences of models and data

# DEV-SWE-201 · Software Engineering with Coding Agents

- Track: AI Engineering
- Path: [Software Engineering for AI Builders](https://sdaiaacademy.github.io/en/paths/DEV-SWE.md)
- Level: Level 200 · Apply
- Format: Intensive: 4 teaching days and a capstone day, with guided pre-work and a tracked follow-up task
- Total hours: 36 h
- Audience: practitioner
- Status: In development

## Description

Participants deliver working software by directing a coding agent through four steps: specify, plan, execute and verify. On a synthetic appointment-booking service with legacy code and thin tests, they study agent transcripts, write specifications an agent can follow, make the repository agent-ready, and review agent changes at a depth matched to risk. One supervised checkpoint is taken without AI assistance.

## Learning outcomes

By the end, the participant can:

- Explain how a coding agent searches code, spends its context and uses subagents, and identify its common failure modes.
- Prepare a specification and plan that split a feature into slices an agent can execute and a reviewer can verify.
- Configure an agent-ready repository with a context file, a skill, a check-running hook, a read-only protocol server and permission settings.
- Apply risk-based review to agent changes, setting review depth by blast radius.
- Analyse unfamiliar code and an agent diff without assistance, predicting behaviour and locating defects.
- Deliver a feature with a coding agent from specification to merged change, with tests and a review record.

## Prerequisites

- [FND-PRG-102 · Command Line, Git and Reproducible Environments](https://sdaiaacademy.github.io/en/courses/FND-PRG-102.md)
- Writes and debugs small Python programs without assistance
- Writes and runs unit tests

## Next courses

- [DEV-SWE-302 · Agent-Ready Engineering Organisations: Parallel Agents, Review and Governance](https://sdaiaacademy.github.io/en/courses/DEV-SWE-302.md)
- [DEV-SWE-303 · Shaping the Build: Product Sense and Forward-Deployed Practice](https://sdaiaacademy.github.io/en/courses/DEV-SWE-303.md)

## Topics

### How coding agents work

- The loop: read, plan, edit, run, observe
- Code search, context limits and compaction
- Progress notes for work that spans sessions
- Failure modes: over-engineering, stopping short, skipped verification, destructive actions

### Specify and plan

- Measurable acceptance criteria
- Agent-led questioning before work
- Choosing autonomy: steer, supervise or delegate
- When not to use an agent

### The agent-ready repository

- A short context file pointing into documentation
- Instruction files that grow long, stale or contradictory
- Skills and hooks
- Protocol servers, read-only first
- Architecture enforced by linters and tests

### Permissions and safety

- Allow, ask and deny settings
- Sandboxes and secrets out of reach
- Untrusted repositories: injected instructions and configuration that runs on open
- What may be sent to an external model

### Verify and review

- Tests as the acceptance gate
- Reading diffs for intent, scope and side effects
- Removing agent-made technical debt

---

# DEV-SWE-202 · Back-End Services and Interfaces for AI Applications

- Track: AI Engineering
- Path: [Software Engineering for AI Builders](https://sdaiaacademy.github.io/en/paths/DEV-SWE.md)
- Level: Level 200 · Apply
- Format: Intensive: 4 teaching days and a capstone day, with guided pre-work and a tracked follow-up task
- Total hours: 30 h
- Audience: practitioner
- Status: In development

## Description

Participants build the service between users and language models. On a synthetic citizen-enquiry assistant they define a typed API contract, stream model output, move batch summarisation onto a queue with retries and idempotency, add sign-in, per-user authorisation and quotas, and persist conversations and job state so the service survives restarts. A deterministic fake model with scripted latency keeps labs and the load test on a laptop; a small open-weight model serves end-to-end checks. Deployment continues in DEV-OPS-201.

## Learning outcomes

By the end, the participant can:

- Distinguish request-response, streaming and asynchronous job patterns and state which fits a given model call.
- Implement a typed API contract that validates model output and maps provider failures to stable error codes.
- Implement token streaming with cancellation and clean handling of client disconnects.
- Implement queued jobs with idempotency keys, retries with backoff and a status endpoint.
- Configure sign-in, per-user authorisation and quotas.
- Build a service that persists state, recovers from a restart and meets a latency budget under load.

## Prerequisites

- [FND-PRG-105 · Computer Systems and Cloud Essentials for AI Work](https://sdaiaacademy.github.io/en/courses/FND-PRG-105.md)
- Has called a language model API from Python
- Writes unit tests in Python
- Writes SQL against a relational database

## Next courses

- [DEV-SWE-301 · System Design for AI Products](https://sdaiaacademy.github.io/en/courses/DEV-SWE-301.md)

## Topics

### Contracts

- Resource design and versioning
- Validating model output at the boundary
- Error mapping for timeouts, refusals and outages
- Provider-neutral clients and gateways

### Streaming

- Server-sent events and WebSockets
- Time to first token
- Cancellation and disconnects
- Streaming tool-call events

### Asynchronous work

- Queues and workers
- Idempotency and at-least-once delivery
- Backoff, jitter and dead-letter queues
- Status endpoints and webhooks

### Identity, limits and state

- OpenID Connect and token validation
- Provider keys held server-side only
- Tenant isolation, quotas and spend caps
- Conversations and tool calls as stored data
- Retention and deletion

### Readiness

- Fake models for tests
- Load tests against a budget
- Structured logs and trace identifiers

# DEV-SWE-203 · Front Ends for AI Applications: Streaming, Chat and Generative Interfaces

- Track: AI Engineering
- Path: [Software Engineering for AI Builders](https://sdaiaacademy.github.io/en/paths/DEV-SWE.md)
- Level: Level 200 · Apply
- Format: Workshop: two days with labs and a short build project, with guided pre-work
- Total hours: 16 h
- Audience: practitioner
- Status: In development

## Description

Participants build the interface of an assistant and an agent against a provided back end that replays recorded event streams. They render streamed content, keep conversation state consistent through edits and reloads, show tool calls with approval prompts, and display agent-returned interactive components with a text fallback. Every lab is tested for accessibility, including screen readers and right-to-left Arabic. Interaction design for product teams is LDS-PRD-203.

## Learning outcomes

By the end, the participant can:

- Describe the events an agent sends to an interface and how an open agent-to-interface protocol carries them.
- Implement streamed rendering and conversation state that survive stops, retries, edits and reloads.
- Implement approval prompts that state an action, its target and its effect, with a fallback for interactive components.
- Test the interface for keyboard use, screen-reader announcement of streamed text and right-to-left layout.
- Build a chat and agent interface that streams, recovers from failure, gates actions on approval and passes the accessibility audit.

## Prerequisites

- Builds a small web application in a component framework
- Calls an HTTP API from the browser

## Topics

### Streaming

- Server-sent events and fetch streams
- Incremental Markdown and tables
- Sanitising model output: HTML, links and remote images
- Stop, retry and partial failure

### Conversation state

- The server as source of truth
- Edits, branches and resumption

### Tools and generative interfaces

- Approval prompts people read
- Agent-returned components and fallbacks
- Shared state and interrupts

### Accessible, bilingual interfaces

- Live regions and focus
- Right-to-left and mixed-direction text
- Disclosing AI-generated content

# DEV-SWE-204 · Testing and Verification of AI-Assisted Code

- Track: AI Engineering
- Path: [Software Engineering for AI Builders](https://sdaiaacademy.github.io/en/paths/DEV-SWE.md)
- Level: Level 200 · Apply
- Format: Workshop: two days with labs and a short build project, with guided pre-work
- Total hours: 16 h
- Audience: practitioner
- Status: In development

## Description

Participants build the checks that decide whether agent-written code is accepted. On a synthetic, mostly agent-written fee-calculation library, they write and protect acceptance tests before delegating, add property-based and mutation testing, wire code, dependency and secret scanning into continuous integration, and size review effort to agent volume. Application-level security is DEV-SEC-201.

## Learning outcomes

By the end, the participant can:

- Prepare acceptance tests before delegating and protect them from agent edits.
- Implement property-based tests that find defects example tests miss.
- Measure suite strength with mutation testing and kill surviving mutants.
- Configure code, dependency and secret scanning and triage findings.
- Build a verification pipeline that accepts a correct agent change and rejects faulty ones.

## Prerequisites

- [FND-PRG-104 · Software Testing, Code Review and Documentation](https://sdaiaacademy.github.io/en/courses/FND-PRG-104.md)
- Has used a coding agent

## Next courses

- [DEV-SWE-302 · Agent-Ready Engineering Organisations: Parallel Agents, Review and Governance](https://sdaiaacademy.github.io/en/courses/DEV-SWE-302.md)

## Topics

### Tests as the contract

- Test-first delegation
- Characterisation tests before agent refactoring
- Protected tests and hooks
- Agents that skip, weaken or hard-code tests

### Stronger tests

- Properties and shrinking
- Mutation testing: why coverage is not strength

### Security of generated code

- Common flaws in generated code
- Static analysis and secret detection
- Dependencies, licences and invented package names

### Review capacity

- Review depth by risk tier
- Small, stacked changes
- Agent review as a first pass only

# DEV-SWE-301 · System Design for AI Products

- Track: AI Engineering
- Path: [Software Engineering for AI Builders](https://sdaiaacademy.github.io/en/paths/DEV-SWE.md)
- Level: Level 300 · Develop
- Format: Intensive: 4 teaching days and a design-review day, with guided pre-work and a tracked follow-up task
- Total hours: 30 h
- Audience: practitioner
- Status: In development

## Description

Participants design AI products as systems rather than prompts. On a synthetic bilingual permit assistant that retrieves regulations, parses uploads, drafts decisions and files them after human approval, they decide what is plain code, workflow, model call or agent, place every piece of state, set latency and cost budgets per user task, and plan degradation when a model is slow, wrong or down. A walking skeleton with fault injection tests the design, and a panel review closes the course.

## Learning outcomes

By the end, the participant can:

- Explain how non-determinism, token-priced compute, provider limits and model changes alter service design.
- Prepare a latency and cost budget per user task, including time to first token and cost per successful task.
- Analyse the failure modes of a design and attach a detection signal and degradation response to each.
- Design the decomposition and state placement of an AI product.
- Build a walking skeleton whose degradation paths hold the budget under injected faults.
- Review a peer design and defend one's own when the panel changes a constraint.

## Prerequisites

- [DEV-SWE-202 · Back-End Services and Interfaces for AI Applications](https://sdaiaacademy.github.io/en/courses/DEV-SWE-202.md)
- [DEV-LLM-201 · Building Applications on Language Models](https://sdaiaacademy.github.io/en/courses/DEV-LLM-201.md)
- Has maintained a service with a database and an external API dependency

## Next courses

- [DEV-INF-404 · AI Solution Architecture and Decision Records](https://sdaiaacademy.github.io/en/courses/DEV-INF-404.md)

## Topics

### What AI components change

- Non-determinism, token pricing and provider limits
- Models that change or retire; keeping a provider exit
- Code first, workflows before agents

### Decomposition and state

- Boundaries between code, workflow, model call and agent
- Monolith or services, decided by experiment
- Where conversation, memory, documents and job state live
- Idempotent steps and event logs
- Caches and cache-aware prompt layout

### Budgets

- Quality targets and where evaluation runs
- Latency at the 95th percentile
- Cost per successful task
- Rate limits and model tiers

### Failure and degradation

- Failure-mode analysis
- Timeouts, circuit breakers and bulkheads
- Fallback models, cached answers and human hand-off
- Limiting the blast radius of actions

### Design reviews

- Decision records and trade-off tables
- Security, privacy and data-placement checklists
- Hand-offs to DEV-INF-404 and DEV-OPS-304

---

# DEV-SWE-302 · Agent-Ready Engineering Organisations: Parallel Agents, Review and Governance

- Track: AI Engineering
- Path: [Software Engineering for AI Builders](https://sdaiaacademy.github.io/en/paths/DEV-SWE.md)
- Level: Level 300 · Develop
- Format: Workshop: two days with labs and a short build project, with guided pre-work
- Total hours: 16 h
- Audience: practitioner
- Status: In development

## Description

Participants set up how a team works with coding agents. On a synthetic repository with twelve open issues, they run background agents in parallel, version and evaluate the shared harness of context files, skills and hooks, set permission tiers and release lanes, size review queues to capacity, and measure delivery honestly.

## Learning outcomes

By the end, the participant can:

- Configure parallel background agents on isolated workspaces with a merge and conflict policy.
- Configure permission tiers, sandboxing and an egress allowlist for team agents.
- Design a versioned team harness with an owner, a changelog and a regression task set.
- Design release lanes and a review-queue policy that route changes by risk and fit reviewer capacity.
- Evaluate claims about agent productivity using delivery measures with stated uncertainty.

- Reviews work in a team repository with continuous integration

### Parallel agents

- Steer, queue and notify
- Worktrees and containers per task
- Agents per reviewer

### The harness as a product

- Ownership and versioning
- Evaluating harness changes
- Removing instructions models no longer need

### Permissions and lanes

- Approval fatigue
- Sandboxes, egress control and audit trails
- Agentic, supervised and assisted lanes

### Review and measurement

- Risk-tiered queues
- Oversight in name only
- Why throughput counts mislead
- Token spend per merged change
