# DEV-SWE-303 · Shaping the Build: Product Sense and Forward-Deployed Practice

- Track: AI Engineering
- Path: [Software Engineering for AI Builders](https://sdaiaacademy.github.io/en/paths/DEV-SWE.md)
- Level: Level 300 · Develop
- Format: Workshop: two days of role-played engagement and a short build, with guided pre-work
- Total hours: 16 h
- Audience: practitioner
- Status: In development

## Description

Participants practise the engineer's side of forward-deployed work: deciding what to build with the people who will use it. In a role-played engagement with a fictional municipal licensing office, they interview staff, write the specification, test the riskiest assumption with a time-boxed prototype, cost the value case, and hand over a system the client can run alone. Product managers take LDS-PRD-201; full business cases are LDS-ADV-201.

## Learning outcomes

By the end, the participant can:

- Analyse a workflow from interviews to find where AI would change an outcome users care about.
- Design a specification with success metrics, non-goals, acceptance criteria written as evaluation cases, data needs and risks.
- Test the riskiest assumption with a time-boxed prototype and short user sessions.
- Decide whether to stop, iterate or build, backed by a value case with sensitivity.
- Deliver a hand-over package the client team can run and change alone.

## Prerequisites

- [DEV-SWE-201 · Software Engineering with Coding Agents](https://sdaiaacademy.github.io/en/courses/DEV-SWE-201.md)
- Has shipped a language model application

## Topics

### Discovery

- Interviews about past behaviour
- Workflows and their exceptions
- Saying no to a use case

### Specification as the deliverable

- Problem, users and non-goals
- Acceptance criteria as evaluation cases
- Data, permission and classification needs

### Minimum viable decisions

- Riskiest assumption first
- Reversible and irreversible choices
- Cost per successful task and break-even

### Hand-over

- Runbooks and evaluation sets
- Ownership and exit criteria
- Training the receiving team

# DEV-LLM-201 · Building Applications on Language Models

- Track: AI Engineering
- Path: [Language Model Application Engineering](https://sdaiaacademy.github.io/en/paths/DEV-LLM.md)
- Level: Level 200 · Apply
- Format: Intensive: 4 teaching days and a capstone day, with guided pre-work and a tracked follow-up task
- Total hours: 36 h
- Audience: practitioner
- Status: In development

## Description

Participants build a language model application from the API up: provider-neutral calls, prompts kept as versioned code, structured outputs that validate, tool calling with confirmation before side effects, and answers grounded in documents with citations, all measured on a first evaluation set. One synthetic case study, a bilingual permits help desk with a policy handbook and a case database, runs through all four days.

## Learning outcomes

By the end, the participant can:

- Distinguish the chat-message, item-list and provider-neutral response shapes of model APIs.
- Implement prompts as versioned templates that keep instructions apart from untrusted user text.
- Implement structured outputs that validate against a schema, with a bounded retry and a fallback.
- Configure tool calling with typed tools, recovery from tool errors and confirmation before state changes.
- Measure quality, latency and cost per request for three candidate models.
- Build a grounded answering feature that cites sources and declines when the documents hold no answer.

## Prerequisites

- Writes and tests Python that calls an HTTP API
- Explains tokens, context windows and sampling at the depth of FND-AIC-102

## Next courses

- [LDS-ADV-201 · AI Use-Case Feasibility and Business Cases](https://sdaiaacademy.github.io/en/courses/LDS-ADV-201.md)
- [DEV-SWE-301 · System Design for AI Products](https://sdaiaacademy.github.io/en/courses/DEV-SWE-301.md)
- [DEV-LLM-203 · Retrieval and Knowledge Engineering for Language Model Systems](https://sdaiaacademy.github.io/en/courses/DEV-LLM-203.md)
- [DEV-LLM-204 · Document Intelligence: Parsing, Extraction and Multimodal Retrieval](https://sdaiaacademy.github.io/en/courses/DEV-LLM-204.md)
- [DEV-LLM-205 · Voice and Conversational Applications](https://sdaiaacademy.github.io/en/courses/DEV-LLM-205.md)
- [DEV-LLM-301 · Model Adaptation for Applications: Fine-Tuning, Distillation and Small Models](https://sdaiaacademy.github.io/en/courses/DEV-LLM-301.md)
- [DEV-LLM-302 · Arabic and Multilingual Language Applications](https://sdaiaacademy.github.io/en/courses/DEV-LLM-302.md)
- [DEV-LLM-303 · Model Choice, Routing and Inference Economics](https://sdaiaacademy.github.io/en/courses/DEV-LLM-303.md)
- [DEV-AGT-301 · Agentic Systems Engineering: Loops, Context and Harnesses](https://sdaiaacademy.github.io/en/courses/DEV-AGT-301.md)
- [DEV-MLE-304 · Multimodal Systems Engineering](https://sdaiaacademy.github.io/en/courses/DEV-MLE-304.md)
- [DEV-OPS-302 · Operating Language Model Applications: Tracing, Evaluation Gates and Safe Releases](https://sdaiaacademy.github.io/en/courses/DEV-OPS-302.md)
- [DEV-OPS-304 · AI Cost Engineering: Gateways, Routing, Caching and Unit Economics](https://sdaiaacademy.github.io/en/courses/DEV-OPS-304.md)

## Topics

### Model APIs without lock-in

- Three API shapes and gateways
- Sampling, reasoning effort and token limits
- Streaming, retries and rate limits

### Prompts and structured outputs

- Templates, versions and diffs
- User and retrieved text as untrusted data
- Constrained decoding versus validate and retry

### Tools

- Tool schemas and tool errors
- Confirmation before side effects
- Fixed workflows before agents

### Grounding

- Prompt versus retrieval on demand
- Keyword and embedding search over a small corpus
- Citations and saying no answer exists

### Measuring and choosing

- Error analysis on the first traces
- A small evaluation set from real tasks
- Code checks and one model-graded check
- Open-weight versus hosted models and licences

# DEV-LLM-202 · Applied Natural Language Processing Engineering

- Track: AI Engineering
- Path: [Language Model Application Engineering](https://sdaiaacademy.github.io/en/paths/DEV-LLM.md)
- Level: Level 200 · Apply
- Format: Intensive: 3 teaching days and a capstone day, with guided pre-work and a tracked follow-up task
- Total hours: 30 h
- Audience: practitioner
- Status: In development

## Description

The Academy's Applied NLP course. Participants trace Arabic and English text through tokenisers, embeddings and attention, build semantic search, and solve routing and entity-extraction tasks three ways: a classical baseline, a prompted generative model and a fine-tuned encoder. They adapt a model with low-rank adapters in free notebook memory and ship a small service with a model card. The data is a stream of synthetic citizen requests to a municipality.

## Learning outcomes

By the end, the participant can:

- Explain how tokenisation, embeddings and attention turn a sentence into a prediction.
- Implement semantic search and measure recall at ten for two embedding models.
- Measure a classical baseline, a prompted generative model and a fine-tuned encoder against each other on a routing task.
- Implement a token-classification model that extracts named entities.
- Apply low-rank and quantised low-rank adapters to fit training into limited memory.
- Build a routing and extraction service with a demo interface and a model card.

## Prerequisites

- [FND-AIC-101 · How Machine Learning Works](https://sdaiaacademy.github.io/en/courses/FND-AIC-101.md)
- Trains a classifier in a notebook and reads precision, recall and F1

## Next courses

- [DEV-LLM-301 · Model Adaptation for Applications: Fine-Tuning, Distillation and Small Models](https://sdaiaacademy.github.io/en/courses/DEV-LLM-301.md)
- [DEV-LLM-302 · Arabic and Multilingual Language Applications](https://sdaiaacademy.github.io/en/courses/DEV-LLM-302.md)

## Topics

### Representing text

- Subword tokenisers
- Arabic script, diacritics and normalisation
- Embeddings, vector indexes and semantic search

### Inside the transformer

- Attention and positions
- Encoders and decoders
- Pretrained checkpoints and model cards

### Decision models

- Baselines first
- Classification and token-classification heads
- A prompted model as a zero-shot classifier
- Precision, recall and F1

### Adapting and shipping

- Labels, splits and leakage
- Fine-tuning an encoder
- Low-rank adapters
- CPU latency and a demo

# DEV-LLM-203 · Retrieval and Knowledge Engineering for Language Model Systems

- Track: AI Engineering
- Path: [Language Model Application Engineering](https://sdaiaacademy.github.io/en/paths/DEV-LLM.md)
- Level: Level 200 · Apply
- Format: Intensive: 4 teaching days and a capstone day, with guided pre-work and a tracked follow-up task
- Total hours: 36 h
- Audience: practitioner
- Status: In development

## Description

Participants build the retrieval layer of a language model system: lexical, dense and hybrid search with reranking over a bilingual corpus, an agent that chooses among search tools, a memory file kept across sessions, statistical answers through a semantic layer instead of free text-to-SQL, and filtering by the requester's permissions. The case study is a synthetic ministry knowledge base with a statistics warehouse. Retrieval evaluation in depth is in DEV-EVL-303, building semantic models in DEV-DAT-202, indexing pipelines in DEV-DAT-302 and graph retrieval in DEV-DAT-304.

## Learning outcomes

By the end, the participant can:

- Distinguish lexical, dense, hybrid, multi-vector and agentic retrieval and the query types each suits.
- Implement hybrid retrieval with rank fusion and a cross-encoder reranker.
- Configure an agent to choose among file listing, keyword, semantic and SQL search and to page large results.
- Implement assistant access to a warehouse through a provided semantic layer, with query validation, row limits and role checks.
- Implement permission filtering so retrieval returns only passages the requester may see.
- Build a knowledge assistant over documents, structured data and a memory file, and defend each choice with measurements.

## Prerequisites

- [DEV-LLM-201 · Building Applications on Language Models](https://sdaiaacademy.github.io/en/courses/DEV-LLM-201.md)
- Writes SQL with joins and grouping

## Topics

### Search fundamentals

- BM25 and inverted indexes
- Approximate nearest-neighbour indexes
- Rank fusion and reranking
- Arabic morphology in lexical search

### Preparing a corpus

- Chunking by structure
- Metadata, dates and deduplication
- Long context versus retrieval

### Agentic search and memory

- The cheapest tool that works first
- Query rewriting and decomposition
- Offloading large results to files
- Memory files and wikis: bloat and staleness

### Structured data

- Schema grounding
- Semantic layers and governed metrics
- Validating generated SQL

### Access and trust

- Permission filters before ranking
- Retrieved text as untrusted input
- Citations and source dates

---

# DEV-LLM-204 · Document Intelligence: Parsing, Extraction and Multimodal Retrieval

- Track: AI Engineering
- Path: [Language Model Application Engineering](https://sdaiaacademy.github.io/en/paths/DEV-LLM.md)
- Level: Level 200 · Apply
- Format: Workshop: two days with labs and a short build project, with guided pre-work
- Total hours: 16 h
- Audience: practitioner
- Status: In development

## Description

Participants turn scanned and digital documents into checked data. They compare parsers and vision models on Arabic and English pages, score parsing on its own, extract fields from forms and tables with validation rules, index page images beside parsed text, and send low-confidence fields to human review. The data is a synthetic set of tender forms, invoices and reports with tables, stamps and mixed scripts.

## Learning outcomes

By the end, the participant can:

- Compare pipeline parsers, small document models and general vision-language models for layout, tables and Arabic text.
- Measure parsing quality separately from extraction with edit distance and table-structure scores.
- Implement schema-based extraction with field rules and cross-field checks.
- Implement retrieval that indexes page images alongside parsed text.
- Build a pipeline that routes low-confidence fields to human review.

## Prerequisites

- [DEV-LLM-201 · Building Applications on Language Models](https://sdaiaacademy.github.io/en/courses/DEV-LLM-201.md)
- Validates model output against a schema in Python

## Topics

### Parsing

- Born-digital text layers versus scanned pages
- Character recognition, layout and reading order
- Right-to-left and mixed scripts
- Specialised versus general vision models

### Tables and forms

- Table structure
- Fields, checkboxes and stamps

### Extraction with validation

- Schemas and field rules
- Cross-field checks
- Confidence and abstention
- Hidden text and instructions in documents

### Retrieval and review

- Page images as retrieval units
- Human review queues and their cost

Participants build a voice agent fast enough to talk to. - Time to first audio

### Channels and Arabic speech

- Synthesis quality

# DEV-LLM-301 · Model Adaptation for Applications: Fine-Tuning, Distillation and Small Models

- Track: AI Engineering
- Path: [Language Model Application Engineering](https://sdaiaacademy.github.io/en/paths/DEV-LLM.md)
- Level: Level 300 · Develop
- Format: Intensive: 4 teaching days and a capstone day, with guided pre-work and a tracked follow-up task
- Total hours: 36 h
- Audience: practitioner
- Status: In development

## Description

Participants decide when adapting a model is worth it, then do it well. From error analysis of a failing extraction and function-calling feature, they build a tuning set from traces and teacher outputs, train low-rank adapters on a small open-weight model, distil a large model into it, evaluate it against the base and a larger prompted model, and serve it quantised with several adapters. Research-grade post-training is SPC-DLR-306; serving optimisation at scale is DEV-INF-401.

## Learning outcomes

By the end, the participant can:

- Decide whether to prompt, retrieve, fine-tune or distil to fix an application's failures.
- Prepare a tuning dataset with deduplication, decontamination, licence checks and personal-data removal.
- Implement supervised fine-tuning with low-rank adapters on a small open-weight model.
- Implement distillation of a teacher's behaviour into a student by generating, filtering and training on examples.
- Evaluate an adapted model against its base and a larger prompted model on task metrics, general ability and safety behaviour.
- Build a serving setup for a quantised small model with several adapters and measure its latency, throughput and cost.

## Prerequisites

- [DEV-LLM-201 · Building Applications on Language Models](https://sdaiaacademy.github.io/en/courses/DEV-LLM-201.md)
- [DEV-LLM-202 · Applied Natural Language Processing Engineering](https://sdaiaacademy.github.io/en/courses/DEV-LLM-202.md)
- Reads a PyTorch training loop and diagnoses a loss curve
- Compares two configurations on an evaluation set with a statistical test (DEV-EVL-301 recommended)

## Topics

### When to adapt

- Prompt, retrieve, tune or distil
- Tuning changes behaviour more than knowledge
- What small models do and do not do reliably
- Open-weight licences and terms of use

### Data for tuning

- Traces, teacher outputs and corrections
- Chat templates and tool-call formats
- Deduplication and decontamination

### Adapters and distillation

- Low-rank and quantised adapters
- Function-calling fine-tuning
- Teacher generation with verifier filtering

### Evaluating adapted models

- Paired comparison against the base
- Forgetting and regressions
- Safety behaviour after tuning
- Arabic and English slices

### Serving small models

- Quantised formats
- Several adapters on one base
- Cost per thousand requests

---

# DEV-LLM-302 · Arabic and Multilingual Language Applications

- Track: AI Engineering
- Path: [Language Model Application Engineering](https://sdaiaacademy.github.io/en/paths/DEV-LLM.md)
- Level: Level 300 · Develop
- Format: Intensive: 3 teaching days and a capstone day, with guided pre-work and a tracked follow-up task
- Total hours: 30 h
- Audience: practitioner
- Status: In development

## Description

Participants make a language model application work for Arabic speakers as well as it does in English. They measure what tokenisation costs in Arabic, normalise text and identify dialects, handle code-switching and romanised Arabic, compare Arabic-first and multilingual open models, and build and calibrate their own Arabic test set with cultural criteria. The case study is a synthetic citizen-service assistant used in Modern Standard Arabic, three dialects and mixed language. Annotation operations at scale are DEV-EVL-304; Arabic speech is DEV-MLE-302.

## Learning outcomes

By the end, the participant can:

- Measure how tokeniser fertility changes cost, usable context and chunk sizes for standard and dialectal Arabic across target models.
- Implement normalisation, romanised-Arabic detection and dialect identification.
- Test retrieval and prompting strategies for dialectal and code-switched queries.
- Design an application test set covering standard Arabic, dialects, code-switching and cultural items.
- Evaluate Arabic-first and multilingual open models on public benchmarks and on the custom set, and explain disagreements.
- Build a model-graded check for cultural appropriateness and calibrate it against native-speaker labels.

## Prerequisites

- [DEV-LLM-201 · Building Applications on Language Models](https://sdaiaacademy.github.io/en/courses/DEV-LLM-201.md)
- [DEV-LLM-202 · Applied Natural Language Processing Engineering](https://sdaiaacademy.github.io/en/courses/DEV-LLM-202.md)
- Reads Modern Standard Arabic, or works in a pair with someone who does

## Topics

### Arabic as data

- Morphology, diacritics and orthographic variation
- Romanised Arabic and bidirectional text
- Numerals, names and Hijri dates

### Tokenisation and dialects

- Fertility and context budgets
- Dialect identification
- Arabic-English mixing in queries

### Open Arabic models as cases

- Arabic-first open-weight models such as ALLaM
- Multilingual models
- Context limits and licences

### Benchmarks and cultural evaluation

- Arabic knowledge, exam and instruction-following benchmarks
- Contamination and translated test sets
- Cultural rubrics and grader calibration
- Bias across dialects

# DEV-LLM-303 · Model Choice, Routing and Inference Economics

- Track: AI Engineering
- Path: [Language Model Application Engineering](https://sdaiaacademy.github.io/en/paths/DEV-LLM.md)
- Level: Level 300 · Develop
- Format: Workshop: one and a half days with labs and a costed decision memo, with guided pre-work
- Total hours: 12 h
- Audience: practitioner
- Status: In development

## Description

Participants choose models with numbers. They score open and closed, small and large models at several reasoning settings on their own tasks, design a routing policy with tiers and fallbacks, arrange prompts for cache hits, and compute when self-hosting an open-weight model beats an API. The case study is a synthetic document-review application with a stated volume, quality floor and data-placement rule. Serving optimisation continues in DEV-INF-401 and production cost control in DEV-OPS-304.

## Learning outcomes

By the end, the participant can:

- Measure quality, latency and cost per successful task for four models at two reasoning settings.
- Design a cascade that escalates from a small model to a larger one on validation failure or low confidence, keeping quality above a floor.
- Configure prompt and tool layout for prefix caching and measure the effect.
- Compute the break-even volume between a hosted API and self-hosting.
- Decide on model choice and hosting for the case-study application.

## Prerequisites

- [DEV-LLM-201 · Building Applications on Language Models](https://sdaiaacademy.github.io/en/courses/DEV-LLM-201.md)
- Has compared two configurations of an application on an evaluation set

## Topics

### Choosing on own tasks

- Leaderboards versus own evaluations
- Licence, residency and deprecation risk
- Reasoning budgets

### Routing and tiers

- Cascades and difficulty routers
- Per-stage models
- Cache cost of switching models

### Caching

- Prefix caching and stable layouts
- Response caches and their risks

### Self-hosting economics

- Throughput and utilisation
- Batch versus interactive
- Break-even

---

# DEV-AGT-301 · Agentic Systems Engineering: Loops, Context and Harnesses

- Track: AI Engineering
- Path: [Agentic Systems](https://sdaiaacademy.github.io/en/paths/DEV-AGT.md)
- Level: Level 300 · Develop
- Format: Intensive: 4 teaching days and a capstone day, with guided pre-work and a tracked follow-up task
- Total hours: 40 h
- Audience: practitioner
- Status: In development

## Description

Participants build an agent the way the field now builds them: a model in a loop that calls typed tools inside a sandbox, with most of the engineering in the harness around it. They write the loop from scratch, treat context as a budget, add memory files, skills and Model Context Protocol servers, compare agent frameworks with their own harness, put human approval gates into a state graph, and finish with an agent that is traced, evaluated and contained. One synthetic case study runs through all four days, and the capstone is a research agent over a synthetic document corpus.

## Learning outcomes

By the end, the participant can:

- Distinguish a fixed workflow, a single agent in a loop and a multi-agent design, and state which one a given task needs.
- Implement an agent loop from scratch that calls typed tools, handles tool errors and stops on explicit completion criteria.
- Measure and reduce context use with compaction, offloading of large tool results to files and progressive disclosure of skills.
- Configure a protocol server and a skill so that an agent discovers and uses them without changes to the agent's code.
- Build a state-graph agent with checkpoints and a human approval gate before every irreversible action.
- Evaluate an agent with transcript and outcome graders over repeated trials and report consistency and cost per completed task.
- Defend the containment design of an agent that combines private data, untrusted content and a possible exfiltration path.

## Prerequisites

- [DEV-LLM-201 · Building Applications on Language Models](https://sdaiaacademy.github.io/en/courses/DEV-LLM-201.md)
- Writes and tests Python that calls an HTTP API and validates a JSON response against a schema
- Has built a small application that sends prompts to a language model and parses structured output
- Uses Git and runs code in a container from the command line

## Next courses

- [DEV-AGT-302 · Protocol Servers and Agent Integrations](https://sdaiaacademy.github.io/en/courses/DEV-AGT-302.md)
- [DEV-AGT-303 · Computer-Use and Browser Agents](https://sdaiaacademy.github.io/en/courses/DEV-AGT-303.md)
- [DEV-AGT-401 · Harness Engineering for Long-Running and Multi-Agent Systems](https://sdaiaacademy.github.io/en/courses/DEV-AGT-401.md)
- [DEV-AGT-402 · Agent Platforms: Sandboxes, Durable Execution and Identity](https://sdaiaacademy.github.io/en/courses/DEV-AGT-402.md)
- [DEV-AGT-403 · Agent System Design Reviews](https://sdaiaacademy.github.io/en/courses/DEV-AGT-403.md)
- [DEV-OPS-303 · Operating AI Agents: Durable Execution, Sandboxing and Replay](https://sdaiaacademy.github.io/en/courses/DEV-OPS-303.md)

## Topics

### From model to agent

- Three API shapes: chat messages, item lists and provider-neutral responses
- Structured outputs with validation
- Typed tool schemas and tool errors
- The agent loop written from scratch
- Completion criteria and step budgets

### Context engineering

- Context as a budget
- Retrieval for agents: the cheapest tool that works first
- Compaction, resets and offloading tool results to files
- Cache-aware layout of prompts and tools
- Instruction bloat and how to avoid it

### Memory, skills and protocols

- Repository context files and the nearest-file rule
- Skills loaded in stages
- Memory files: write, consolidate, retrieve, forget
- Model Context Protocol: hosts, clients, servers, tools and resources
- Agent-to-agent delegation at concept level

### Harness anatomy

- Tools, context, state and feedback as the harness
- Agent frameworks and hosted agents compared with an own loop
- Loop engineering and verification inside the loop
- Removing scaffolding when a newer model no longer needs it

### Graphs and human gates

- State graphs, checkpoints and interrupts
- Approval at defined risk thresholds
- Approval prompts nobody reads
- Subagents for isolation; when multiple agents pay

### Evaluating agents

- Tasks, trials, graders, transcripts and outcomes
- Success in at least one versus all of k trials
- Capability suites and regression suites
- A smoke evaluation in continuous integration

### Securing and shipping agents

- The agentic application risk list from the Open Worldwide Application Security Project (OWASP)
- Private data, untrusted content and exfiltration: remove one leg
- Sandboxes, egress control and least-privilege tools
- Tracing with the OpenTelemetry generative AI conventions, still in development
- Serving an agent behind an API

# DEV-AGT-302 · Protocol Servers and Agent Integrations

- Track: AI Engineering
- Path: [Agentic Systems](https://sdaiaacademy.github.io/en/paths/DEV-AGT.md)
- Level: Level 300 · Develop
- Format: Workshop: two days with labs and a short build project, with guided pre-work
- Total hours: 16 h
- Audience: practitioner
- Status: In development

## Description

Participants build, secure and test servers that expose an organisation's tools and data to any compliant agent, then connect agents across team boundaries. On a synthetic case-management system they design a stateless Model Context Protocol (MCP) server with typed tools and resources, run it over local and remote transports, add delegated authorisation with narrow scopes, write contract and hostile-input tests, place it behind a gateway with a registry entry, and expose one capability as an Agent2Agent (A2A) service with a signed agent card. Full attack-and-harden work on servers continues in DEV-SEC-301.

## Learning outcomes

By the end, the participant can:

- Explain what the current protocol revision changed and which deprecated features a new server must not depend on.
- Build a stateless protocol server with typed tools, resources and a stable tool order that an unmodified agent can list and call over local and remote transports.
- Configure delegated authorisation so that each tool call carries a short-lived token scoped to one user and one kind of action.
- Test a server with contract, error-path and hostile-input tests, including a tool description that changes after approval.
- Design the integration of several servers behind a gateway with a registry, allowlists, rate limits and audit logs.
- Implement an agent-to-agent service that accepts a delegated task through a signed capability card and reports task state, streamed updates and results.

## Prerequisites

- [DEV-AGT-301 · Agentic Systems Engineering: Loops, Context and Harnesses](https://sdaiaacademy.github.io/en/courses/DEV-AGT-301.md)
- Builds and tests an HTTP service with authentication
- Reads an OAuth 2 authorisation flow and explains the role of scopes and token audience

## Topics

### The protocol for server builders

- Hosts, clients and servers
- Tools, resources and prompts
- Capability discovery
- Extensions and their maturity stages
- Interactive interfaces returned by servers as an extension, with a text fallback
- How the specification changes and how long deprecated features last

### Stateless server design

- No sessions: every request stands alone
- Input and output schemas in JSON Schema
- Stable tool order for prompt caching
- Large results, pagination and links to files
- Asking the client for input without server-initiated requests
- Long-running work through the tasks extension

### Transports and deployment

- Local standard input and output
- Streamable HTTP for remote servers
- Packaging servers in containers
- Versioning a server without breaking clients

### Authorisation

- OAuth-based delegation and protected resource metadata
- Client registration now that dynamic registration is deprecated
- Token audience, scope minimisation and lifetimes
- Why token passthrough is forbidden
- Confused-deputy risk in authorisation proxies
- Request forgery during metadata discovery

### Testing servers

- The reference inspector and scripted clients
- Contract and error-path tests
- Tool poisoning and changes after approval
- Hostile text in tool results

### Gateways and registries

- Central gateways and allowlists
- Shadow servers and inventory
- Rate limits, audit logs and secrets
- Server descriptions for registries

### Agent-to-agent interoperation

- Agent cards, tasks, messages, parts and artefacts
- Protocol bindings: JSON-RPC, gRPC and HTTP with JSON
- Streaming and push notifications
- When to expose a tool server and when an agent service

---

# DEV-AGT-303 · Computer-Use and Browser Agents

- Track: AI Engineering
- Path: [Agentic Systems](https://sdaiaacademy.github.io/en/paths/DEV-AGT.md)
- Level: Level 300 · Develop
- Format: Workshop: two days with labs and a short build project, with guided pre-work
- Total hours: 16 h
- Audience: practitioner
- Status: In development

## Description

Participants build agents that act through graphical and web interfaces, and learn when not to. In a containerised desktop and a locally hosted synthetic services portal, they compare screenshot and page-structure observation, ground actions on interface elements, recover from unexpected dialogs, and fence the agent with a disposable browser profile, a domain allowlist and confirmation before irreversible actions. They measure partial and complete task success separately, price each completed task, and recommend whether an API or a scripted automation would do the job better.

## Learning outcomes

By the end, the participant can:

- Compare screenshot, accessibility-tree and document object model observation for cost, reliability and exposure to injected content.
- Implement a browser agent that completes multi-step form tasks with element grounding, waiting and error recovery.
- Measure partial and complete task success, consistency over repeated trials and cost per completed task.
- Configure containment for an interface agent with a disposable profile, a domain allowlist, no stored credentials, confirmation gates and a step budget.
- Diagnose the causes of failed interface-agent runs and redesign the agent or the task to remove the most frequent cause.
- Decide whether an interface agent, a scripted automation or an API integration fits a process, using measured cost, latency and risk.

## Prerequisites

- [DEV-AGT-301 · Agentic Systems Engineering: Loops, Context and Harnesses](https://sdaiaacademy.github.io/en/courses/DEV-AGT-301.md)
- Reads HTML and uses browser developer tools to inspect page elements
- Has run a containerised application with a mapped port

## Topics

### Acting through interfaces

- Observation: screenshots, accessibility trees and page structure
- Action spaces: click, type, scroll, keys, navigation
- Coordinate grounding and element grounding
- Labelled element overlays
- Why interface steps are slow and costly

### Browser agents

- Headed and headless browsers
- Waiting, synchronisation and dynamic pages
- Tabs, downloads and file uploads
- Test accounts only; no real credentials

### Desktop agents

- Virtual displays in containers and virtual machines
- Screen scaling and coordinate frames
- Legacy forms and dialogs

### Measuring success

- Partial credit versus completed tasks
- State-based checks on the back end
- Public interface benchmarks and their limits
- Consistency over repeated trials
- Cost and time per completed task

### Safety limits

- Page content as untrusted input
- Injection through visible text, hidden elements and pop-ups
- Confirmation before irreversible actions
- Payments, credentials and bot-detection challenges kept out of scope
- Human takeover and hand-back in the middle of a task
- Personal data in screenshots and recordings

### When an API is the better tool

- Scripted automation as the baseline
- Hybrid designs: API where it exists, interface where it does not
- Turning a successful agent run into a replayable script
- Maintenance cost when interfaces change

---

# DEV-AGT-401 · Harness Engineering for Long-Running and Multi-Agent Systems

- Track: AI Engineering
- Path: [Agentic Systems](https://sdaiaacademy.github.io/en/paths/DEV-AGT.md)
- Level: Level 400 · Evaluate
- Format: Intensive: 3 teaching days and a capstone day, with guided pre-work and a tracked follow-up ablation study
- Total hours: 36 h
- Audience: specialist
- Status: In development

## Description

Participants design and measure harnesses for agents that run for hours, hand work between roles and keep memory across sessions. They build planner, generator and evaluator roles with file-based hand-offs and completion criteria agreed before work starts, design a memory layer that writes, consolidates, retrieves and forgets, run asynchronous subagents that an orchestrator can steer, and make sessions survive restarts. Throughout, they hold the model fixed and remove harness components one at a time to find which still pay, and they finish with a harness design defended on measured evidence. Labs use scaled-down tasks and a course-provided call budget on hosted open-weight models; workflow engines and idempotent tools are taught in DEV-AGT-402.

## Learning outcomes

By the end, the participant can:

- Implement planner, generator and evaluator roles that exchange work through files and stop on completion criteria agreed before work starts.
- Design a memory layer that writes, consolidates, retrieves and forgets, and guards against stale notes, over-recording and concurrent overwrites.
- Build an orchestrator that runs asynchronous subagents it can steer, queue and be notified by, and that receives summaries rather than full transcripts.
- Build durable sessions whose event log is separate from the harness, so that a run resumes after the harness or sandbox is killed.
- Evaluate harness components by ablation with the model held fixed, reporting success over repeated trials, cost and wall-clock time per accepted task.
- Decide whether a multi-agent design or a single agent with subagents fits a task, and defend the choice with measured coordination cost.

## Prerequisites

- [DEV-AGT-301 · Agentic Systems Engineering: Loops, Context and Harnesses](https://sdaiaacademy.github.io/en/courses/DEV-AGT-301.md)
- [DEV-EVL-302 · Evaluating Agents: Trajectories, Simulation and Consistency](https://sdaiaacademy.github.io/en/courses/DEV-EVL-302.md)
- Has built and evaluated an agent with tools, memory and a state graph
- Computes a confidence interval for a pass rate and runs a paired comparison

## Topics

### Long-running agents

- Task length at a given reliability and the limits of that measure
- Premature wrap-up near the context limit
- Agents that praise their own work
- Cost and time per accepted task

### Role separation

- Planner, generator and evaluator
- Agreed completion criteria before work
- File-based hand-offs
- When a separate evaluator pays and when it does not
- Evaluators that find a bug and then excuse it

### Context over long horizons

- Compaction versus context reset
- Progressive disclosure and tool search
- Subagents for isolation, and why pulling their transcripts back undoes the benefit
- Cache-aware layout and model switches at natural boundaries

### Memory design

- Notes written in session
- Offline consolidation against transcripts
- A small injected index
- Agent-maintained knowledge bases plus search
- Dating, distrusting and forgetting facts
- Concurrent writers

### Asynchronous and multi-agent work

- Steer, queue and notify
- Coordination topologies: orchestrator-worker, pipeline, peer
- Inter-agent message design
- Delegation across organisations by protocol
- No trust or privilege escalation through delegation
- Cascading failures between agents

### Durable sessions

- Session log, harness and sandbox as replaceable parts
- Resuming from the log after a crash
- Checkpoints at hand-offs
- Background and overnight runs and their review load

### Harness ablation and maintenance

- Holding the model fixed
- Ablation design and repeated trials
- Confidence intervals and practical significance
- Retesting the harness after every model upgrade
- The harness as a versioned product with an owner

---

# DEV-AGT-402 · Agent Platforms: Sandboxes, Durable Execution and Identity

- Track: AI Engineering
- Path: [Agentic Systems](https://sdaiaacademy.github.io/en/paths/DEV-AGT.md)
- Level: Level 400 · Evaluate
- Format: Intensive: 3 teaching days and a capstone day, with guided pre-work and a tracked follow-up task
- Total hours: 30 h
- Audience: specialist
- Status: In development

## Description

Participants build the platform layer that lets many teams run agents safely: isolated execution, state that survives failure, tools that are safe to retry, and an identity for every agent acting on a person's behalf. On a provided Linux lab host with a single-node cluster they compare isolation tiers, enforce egress allowlists, move credentials out of the sandbox into a proxy, run agent sessions on a durable workflow engine with replay, make tools idempotent, issue scoped, short-lived delegated tokens at each hop, and run the platform for several synthetic tenants with quotas, kill switches and cost attribution. Day-to-day operation, trace replay and agent versioning continue in DEV-OPS-303.

## Learning outcomes

By the end, the participant can:

- Measure start-up time and density of process, container, user-space kernel and micro virtual machine isolation for one agent workload, and compare the attack surface each tier exposes.
- Design a sandbox with an egress allowlist, scoped mounts and a credential-holding proxy so that generated code never sees a secret.
- Build durable agent sessions on a workflow engine with checkpointed state, replay and idempotent tool calls.
- Build delegated authorisation in which each hop exchanges its token for a narrower, short-lived one and no access decision rests on nested actor claims.
- Design multi-tenant operation with per-tenant isolation, quotas, rate limits, kill switches and cost attribution.
- Audit an agent platform design against a control checklist covering isolation, state, identity, monitoring and human escalation.

## Prerequisites

- [DEV-AGT-301 · Agentic Systems Engineering: Loops, Context and Harnesses](https://sdaiaacademy.github.io/en/courses/DEV-AGT-301.md)
- [DEV-OPS-201 · Deploying AI Services: Containers, Serving and Monitoring](https://sdaiaacademy.github.io/en/courses/DEV-OPS-201.md)
- Deploys a containerised service with configuration and secrets kept out of the image
- Explains an OAuth 2 token's audience, scopes and lifetime
- Applies and inspects container cluster manifests from the command line

## Topics

### Platform shape

- Session log, harness and sandbox as separate replaceable parts
- Control plane and execution plane
- What the platform owns and what agent teams own
- Managed agent runtimes and self-hosted platforms compared

### Execution isolation

- Isolation tiers: process, container, user-space kernel, micro virtual machine
- Read-only, read-write and no-delete mounts
- Resolving symbolic links before path checks
- An egress allowlist is a capability grant
- Snapshots and reset between tasks
- Isolation that blinds endpoint monitoring

### Secrets and tool proxies

- Credentials never inside the sandbox
- Proxies holding vaulted tokens
- Custom proxies as the weak part

### Durable execution

- Event history, checkpoints and replay
- Determinism constraints on workflow code
- Timers and waits for human approval
- Changing code while workflows are running

### Safe tools

- Idempotency keys
- Exactly-once effects and the outbox pattern
- Compensation for steps that cannot be undone
- Dry runs and previews

### Agent identity and delegated authorisation

- Workload identity for agents
- Token exchange at every hop
- Narrow scopes and short lifetimes
- Consent records for actions on a person's behalf
- Revoking an agent's access mid-run
- The state of agent identity standards

### Multi-tenant operation

- Quotas, rate limits and noisy neighbours
- Kill switches and step budgets
- Cost attribution per tenant and per accepted task
- Audit logs and action-level monitoring
- Placement driven by data classification

# DEV-AGT-403 · Agent System Design Reviews

- Track: AI Engineering
- Path: [Agentic Systems](https://sdaiaacademy.github.io/en/paths/DEV-AGT.md)
- Level: Level 400 · Evaluate
- Format: Studio: six weeks part-time of coached review rounds, ending in a written review and a panel defence
- Total hours: 30 h
- Audience: specialist
- Status: In development

## Description

Participants review agent system designs the way an architecture board should: first asking whether an agent is needed at all, then setting the autonomy level, tracing failure and cost, and writing a review the design owner can act on. In coached rounds on design dossiers built from public engineering write-ups and synthetic proposals, each participant reviews several designs with peers, then leads a full written review of one design and defends it before a panel that includes an experienced agent engineer.

## Learning outcomes

By the end, the participant can:

- Decide whether a proposed system needs an agent, a fixed workflow or no model at all, from the task's environment, context and verifiability.
- Evaluate a design's autonomy level, task horizon, persistent state and authority, and set human oversight proportionate to the risk.
- Diagnose likely failure modes and compounding risks using a published agentic failure taxonomy and risk list.
- Evaluate the cost of a design per accepted task, including retries, reasoning tokens, cache behaviour and human review time.
- Review the evaluation and release plan of a design for outcome grading, consistency over trials and regression gates.
- Defend a written design review before a panel and revise it in response to challenge.

## Prerequisites

- [DEV-AGT-301 · Agentic Systems Engineering: Loops, Context and Harnesses](https://sdaiaacademy.github.io/en/courses/DEV-AGT-301.md)
- Has completed DEV-AGT-401 or DEV-AGT-402, or has shipped an agent system to real users
- Writes a structured technical document such as an architecture decision record

## Topics

### The design review as a practice

- Review versus approval
- Roles: owner, reviewer, panel
- Decision records
- Writing findings the owner can act on

### Is an agent needed

- Fixed workflow, agent or deterministic code
- Environment, context and verifiability as predictors
- The task contract: goal, environment, permitted actions, observations, completion criteria

### Autonomy and oversight

- Levels of autonomy
- Horizon, state and authority as exposures
- Risk-tiered human oversight
- Approval theatre and fatigue
- Kill switches and escalation paths

### Failure analysis

- Agentic failure taxonomies
- Compounding error over many steps
- Goal hijack, tool misuse and privilege abuse
- Memory poisoning and cascading failures
- Recovery paths

### Cost and capacity

- Cost per accepted task, not per token
- Token mix: cache reads, reasoning, retries
- Model tiering and routing
- Latency budgets
- Energy use of agentic workloads

### Evidence a design must bring

- Evaluation plans and consistency metrics
- Harness ablation evidence
- Containment and identity evidence
- Operational readiness and runbooks

### Governance fit

- Data classification and personal data
- Documentation of tool access and operational limits
- Accountability for agent actions
- Mapping a design to a risk management framework

---

# DEV-EVL-301 · Evaluation-Driven Development for Language Model Applications

- Track: AI Engineering
- Path: [Evaluation and Quality Engineering for AI Systems](https://sdaiaacademy.github.io/en/paths/DEV-EVL.md)
- Level: Level 300 · Develop
- Format: Intensive: 4 teaching days and a capstone day, with guided pre-work and a tracked follow-up task
- Total hours: 28 h
- Audience: practitioner
- Status: In development

## Description

Participants learn to treat evaluation as the specification of a language model application. They read traces of a working but unreliable assistant, name its failure modes, turn them into code-based checks and calibrated model-graded checks, and wire the suite into a regression gate. The course uses one synthetic case study from start to finish, and every number a participant reports comes from a run they executed.

## Learning outcomes

By the end, the participant can:

- Distinguish code-based checks, model-graded checks and human review, and state when each is the cheapest reliable instrument.
- Carry out open and axial coding of application traces to produce a failure taxonomy with counts.
- Implement code-based evaluators for structure, grounding and policy rules.
- Calibrate a model-graded evaluator against human labels and report its agreement with a confidence interval.
- Decide between two candidate configurations of an application using a statistically sound comparison.
- Build a regression gate that blocks a change when a critical failure mode gets worse.

## Prerequisites

- Has called a language model API from Python and parsed a structured response
- Reads a confusion matrix and computes precision and recall

## Next courses

- [DEV-EVL-302 · Evaluating Agents: Trajectories, Simulation and Consistency](https://sdaiaacademy.github.io/en/courses/DEV-EVL-302.md)
- [DEV-EVL-303 · Evaluating Retrieval and Grounded Generation](https://sdaiaacademy.github.io/en/courses/DEV-EVL-303.md)
- [DEV-EVL-401 · Evaluation Programmes and Release Gates](https://sdaiaacademy.github.io/en/courses/DEV-EVL-401.md)

## Topics

### Why evaluation is the specification

- Non-determinism and the three gulfs between intent, prompt and behaviour
- Benchmarks versus application evaluations
- What leaderboards do and do not tell you

### Error analysis

- Collecting and sampling traces
- Open coding and axial coding
- Failure taxonomies and saturation
- Prioritising by frequency and severity

### Evaluators

- Assertions and reference-based metrics
- Model-graded checks: binary criteria over rating scales
- Calibrating a grader against human labels
- Correcting observed pass rates for grader error

### Comparing systems

- Paired comparisons and bootstrap intervals
- Sample size and minimum effect of interest
- Cost, latency and quality as one decision

### Evaluation in the delivery pipeline

- Golden sets, versioning and data leakage
- Regression gates in continuous integration
- From offline suites to online monitoring
- Human review queues

### Responsible evaluation

- Subgroup and language slices, including Arabic and English
- Privacy of traces and labelled data
- Documenting limits in a system card

---

# DEV-EVL-302 · Evaluating Agents: Trajectories, Simulation and Consistency

- Track: AI Engineering
- Path: [Evaluation and Quality Engineering for AI Systems](https://sdaiaacademy.github.io/en/paths/DEV-EVL.md)
- Level: Level 300 · Develop
- Format: Workshop: two days with labs and a short evaluation project, with guided pre-work
- Total hours: 16 h
- Audience: practitioner
- Status: In development

## Description

Participants evaluate a tool-using agent for a synthetic travel-booking service. They grade the sandbox's final state and the transcript, drive dialogues with a simulated user holding a hidden goal, repeat tasks to measure consistency and cost per completed job, and repair evaluations that mislead.

## Learning outcomes

By the end, the participant can:

- Implement final-state outcome checks and transcript checks on tool use, side effects and policy.
- Configure a simulated user with a persona, a hidden goal and a stop rule, and measure its fidelity.
- Compute one-success and every-success rates over k trials with small-sample intervals, and the cost per completed job.
- Diagnose and repair an agent evaluation that gives a misleading score.
- Build capability and regression suites for an agent and defend which metric should gate its release.

## Prerequisites

- [DEV-EVL-301 · Evaluation-Driven Development for Language Model Applications](https://sdaiaacademy.github.io/en/courses/DEV-EVL-301.md)
- Has built a tool-calling agent, for example in DEV-AGT-301
- Computes a proportion and its confidence interval

## Next courses

- [DEV-AGT-401 · Harness Engineering for Long-Running and Multi-Agent Systems](https://sdaiaacademy.github.io/en/courses/DEV-AGT-401.md)

## Topics

### Grading agents

- State, tool, side-effect and policy checks
- Several valid paths, not one reference trajectory
- Capability versus regression suites

### Simulated users and environments

- Persona, hidden goal, stop rule and goal leakage
- Mock tools with resettable state

### Consistency and cost

- Pass at k versus pass to the power k (75% per trial: about 42% for three of three)
- Task-level intervals; cost and turns per completed job

### When evaluations mislead

- State leaking between trials
- Agents reading answer keys or version history
- Infrastructure noise and ambiguous tasks

---

# DEV-EVL-303 · Evaluating Retrieval and Grounded Generation

- Track: AI Engineering
- Path: [Evaluation and Quality Engineering for AI Systems](https://sdaiaacademy.github.io/en/paths/DEV-EVL.md)
- Level: Level 300 · Develop
- Format: Workshop: one and a half days with labs and a short evaluation project, with guided pre-work
- Total hours: 12 h
- Audience: practitioner
- Status: In development

## Description

Participants evaluate a retrieval-augmented assistant over a synthetic bilingual corpus of public-service regulations. They extend a test set with graded relevance judgements, measure retrieval apart from generation, check that answers are supported, cited and complete, test abstention on unanswerable questions, and attribute failures to parsing, retrieval or generation.

## Learning outcomes

By the end, the participant can:

- Design a retrieval test set covering Arabic and English, dialect and spelling variants, and unanswerable and multi-passage questions.
- Compute rank-aware retrieval metrics for two retrievers and compare them with a paired interval.
- Implement claim-level support, citation and completeness checks and calibrate the model-graded step against human labels.
- Diagnose the main source of failure in a grounded-generation system and decide which component to change first.

## Prerequisites

- [DEV-EVL-301 · Evaluation-Driven Development for Language Model Applications](https://sdaiaacademy.github.io/en/courses/DEV-EVL-301.md)
- Has built or operated a retrieval-augmented application, for example in DEV-LLM-203

## Topics

### Measuring retrieval

- Graded relevance and pooling
- Recall at k, reciprocal rank, discounted gain
- Evaluating agentic search steps

### Building test sets

- Real, written and filtered synthetic queries
- Unanswerable, multi-passage and time-sensitive questions
- Dialect, spelling-variant and Latin-script Arabic queries against Modern Standard Arabic text

### Grounding and citations

- Supported versus correct and complete
- Citation precision and recall
- Abstention

### Attributing failures

- Parsing measured on its own
- Retrieval ceiling
- Permission leaks

---

# DEV-EVL-304 · Annotation, Golden Data and Human Review Operations

- Track: AI Engineering
- Path: [Evaluation and Quality Engineering for AI Systems](https://sdaiaacademy.github.io/en/paths/DEV-EVL.md)
- Level: Level 300 · Develop
- Format: Workshop: two days with labs and a short design project, with guided pre-work
- Total hours: 16 h
- Audience: practitioner
- Status: In development

## Description

Participants write a labelling guideline, pilot it on synthetic Arabic and English responses, measure agreement and adjudicate, then build a versioned golden set, test whether a model labeller is reliable enough to share the work, and design and cost a review queue.

## Learning outcomes

By the end, the participant can:

- Draft a labelling guideline with definitions, decision rules and edge cases, and revise it after a pilot.
- Compute chance-corrected agreement by category and rater to find ambiguous categories.
- Measure a language model labeller's reliability against adjudicated labels before and after a prompt change.
- Design a golden evaluation set with a sampling plan, adjudication, versioning and leakage safeguards.
- Design and cost a human review queue: sampling rules, capacity, quality checks and a route into the evaluation set.

## Prerequisites

- Computes proportions, confusion matrices and confidence intervals
- Has evaluated a model or application with labelled data

## Topics

### Guidelines and raters

- Label types: binary, categorical, span, pairwise
- Decision rules and versions
- Rater training and qualification

### Agreement and adjudication

- Cohen's and Fleiss' kappa, Krippendorff's alpha
- Disagreement as signal; adjudication methods

### Golden data and model labellers

- Stratified sampling for rare failure modes
- Separation from training and prompts
- Model labellers: reliability and drift

### Review operations

- Random, risk-targeted and low-confidence sampling
- Gold items, spot audits, cost per item
- Rater welfare and dialect expertise

---

# DEV-EVL-401 · Evaluation Programmes and Release Gates

- Track: AI Engineering
- Path: [Evaluation and Quality Engineering for AI Systems](https://sdaiaacademy.github.io/en/paths/DEV-EVL.md)
- Level: Level 400 · Evaluate
- Format: Intensive: 4 teaching days and a capstone day, with guided pre-work and a tracked follow-up task
- Total hours: 30 h
- Audience: specialist
- Status: In development

## Description

Participants design how an organisation decides that an AI system is fit to release and stays so. For a synthetic public-service agency with a citizen assistant, a document-triage model and an internal coding agent, they tier systems by risk, back-test release criteria, audit a public benchmark, plan monitoring and brief a mock risk committee. Pipeline implementation is in DEV-OPS-302; benchmark science is in SPC-TRU-301.

## Learning outcomes

By the end, the participant can:

- Design a risk-tiered evaluation policy stating the suites, sample sizes, human review and sign-off each tier requires.
- Design release criteria with blocking thresholds, non-inferiority margins and re-evaluation triggers fixed in advance, and back-test them.
- Audit a public benchmark or vendor claim for validity, contamination, harness sensitivity and dependence on token budget.
- Design a monitoring plan linking production signals to offline suites and turning incidents into regression cases.
- Analyse the running cost of an evaluation programme across grader calls, review hours and infrastructure, and allocate it by tier.
- Defend a release recommendation, presenting the evidence with its uncertainty and residual risk.

## Prerequisites

- [DEV-EVL-301 · Evaluation-Driven Development for Language Model Applications](https://sdaiaacademy.github.io/en/courses/DEV-EVL-301.md)
- Has run an evaluation suite as a gate in continuous integration
- Reads paired comparisons, confidence intervals and power calculations

## Topics

### Evaluation as an organisational system

- Inventory and owners; tiering by impact, autonomy and reach
- Evidence per tier: capability, regression, adversarial, subgroup, human review, monitoring
- Shared harness, dataset registry and grader calibration records

### Release criteria

- Blocking and advisory checks; criteria fixed in advance
- Non-inferiority margins, noise floors and many checks at once
- Change classes: prompt, model, retrieval, tool, provider upgrade
- Sign-off, exceptions and their expiry

### Auditing benchmarks and claims

- Construct validity and task ambiguity
- Contamination and models that recognise a benchmark
- Harness, token budget and infrastructure effects on rankings

### Monitoring after release

- Sampled grading of production traffic
- Drift, feedback and guardrail-trigger signals with named owners
- Incidents turned into regression cases

### Reporting and governance

- Scorecards that show uncertainty and residual risk
- System cards and evaluation records
- Mapping tiers and gates to a risk management framework

---

# DEV-MLE-201 · Machine Learning Engineering: Baselines, Validation and Pipelines

- Track: AI Engineering
- Path: [Machine Learning Engineering](https://sdaiaacademy.github.io/en/paths/DEV-MLE.md)
- Level: Level 200 · Apply
- Format: Intensive: 4 teaching days and a capstone day, with guided pre-work and a tracked follow-up task
- Total hours: 36 h
- Audience: practitioner
- Status: In development

## Description

Participants engineer a tabular model the way production will judge it. They climb a baseline ladder from a constant predictor to tuned boosted trees and an automated challenger, choose validation that mirrors use, hunt seeded leaks, calibrate probabilities and set a cost-based threshold, then package it as a configuration-driven pipeline an assessor re-runs from a clean checkout. Data is public or synthetic, with repeated entities and time stamps that make naive validation fail. The data-science counterpart is SPC-MOD-201; conformal intervals and explanation methods are SPC-MOD-301.

## Learning outcomes

By the end, the participant can:

- Explain why a validation estimate turns optimistic when splits ignore groups, time order or duplicate entities.
- Implement a baseline ladder from a constant predictor through a regularised linear model to gradient-boosted trees tuned under a fixed budget, then test an automated or pretrained challenger.
- Configure a grouped or time-ordered validation scheme and report its gap to a naive random split.
- Analyse a training pipeline for target, temporal, preprocessing and entity leakage and remove each source.
- Calibrate predicted probabilities and choose a decision threshold from stated error costs.
- Build a reproducible training pipeline that another engineer re-runs to the same metrics.

## Prerequisites

- [FND-AIC-101 · How Machine Learning Works](https://sdaiaacademy.github.io/en/courses/FND-AIC-101.md)
- Writes Python functions with unit tests and works with DataFrames
- Uses Git to branch, commit and request a review
- Reads a bootstrap interval and a confusion matrix (FND-MTH-104 or equivalent)

## Next courses

- [DEV-MLE-202 · Deep Learning Engineering](https://sdaiaacademy.github.io/en/courses/DEV-MLE-202.md)
- [DEV-MLE-203 · Feature, Training-Data and Labelling Pipelines](https://sdaiaacademy.github.io/en/courses/DEV-MLE-203.md)
- [DEV-MLE-303 · Recommender and Ranking Systems Engineering](https://sdaiaacademy.github.io/en/courses/DEV-MLE-303.md)

## Topics

### The baseline ladder

- Framing target and metric
- Constant, rule and linear baselines
- Gradient-boosted trees, tuning budgets and simple ensembles
- Automated and pretrained tabular models as challengers

### Validation and leakage

- Grouped, stratified and time-ordered splits
- Nested tuning and the untouched test set
- Leakage types and fitting transforms inside folds
- Feature availability at prediction time

### Probabilities and decisions

- Calibration curves, Platt and isotonic methods
- Thresholds from error costs
- Error and calibration by subgroup

### Engineering the pipeline

- Pipeline objects and configuration files
- Seeds, locked environments and data hashes
- Schema, invariance and minimum-performance tests
- Model card and prediction interface for hand-off to DEV-OPS-301

---

# DEV-MLE-202 · Deep Learning Engineering

- Track: AI Engineering
- Path: [Machine Learning Engineering](https://sdaiaacademy.github.io/en/paths/DEV-MLE.md)
- Level: Level 200 · Apply
- Format: Intensive: 4 teaching days and a capstone day, with guided pre-work and a tracked follow-up task
- Total hours: 36 h
- Audience: practitioner
- Status: In development

## Description

Participants make neural networks train, tell a bug from a hard problem, and spend accelerator time well. They check automatic differentiation by hand, write a training loop that checkpoints and resumes, diagnose seeded faults, fine-tune open-weight pretrained models against training from scratch, and raise throughput with mixed precision and better data loading. Labs debug on a laptop CPU first, then use a fixed budget of GPU hours on a free notebook service or Academy machines.

## Learning outcomes

By the end, the participant can:

- Compute gradients by reverse-mode automatic differentiation and estimate the memory held by saved activations.
- Implement a training loop with learning-rate scheduling, checkpointing, resumption and fixed seeds.
- Diagnose faults in broken training runs using overfit-one-batch tests, loss and gradient-norm curves and data checks.
- Apply transfer learning from an open-weight model, comparing frozen, partial and full fine-tuning with training from scratch.
- Measure throughput and peak memory, then apply mixed precision, data-loading and batch-size changes.
- Use experiment tracking to run a bounded hyperparameter search and report results across seeds.

## Prerequisites

- [DEV-MLE-201 · Machine Learning Engineering: Baselines, Validation and Pipelines](https://sdaiaacademy.github.io/en/courses/DEV-MLE-201.md)
- Writes Python classes and works with NumPy arrays
- Applies the chain rule to a small composite function (FND-MTH-102 or equivalent)

## Next courses

- [DEV-MLE-301 · Computer Vision Engineering](https://sdaiaacademy.github.io/en/courses/DEV-MLE-301.md)
- [DEV-MLE-302 · Speech and Audio Systems Engineering](https://sdaiaacademy.github.io/en/courses/DEV-MLE-302.md)
- [DEV-MLE-303 · Recommender and Ranking Systems Engineering](https://sdaiaacademy.github.io/en/courses/DEV-MLE-303.md)
- [DEV-MLE-305 · Geospatial and Earth-Observation AI Engineering](https://sdaiaacademy.github.io/en/courses/DEV-MLE-305.md)
- [DEV-INF-402 · Scaling Machine Learning Systems: Distributed Training and Fleets](https://sdaiaacademy.github.io/en/courses/DEV-INF-402.md)

## Topics

### Tensors and automatic differentiation

- Shapes, broadcasting and devices
- Reverse mode and gradient checking
- Memory held by saved activations
- Building blocks: linear, convolution, attention, normalisation, residual

### The training loop

- Loaders, losses and reductions
- Optimisers and learning-rate schedules
- Regularisation, early stopping and validation curves
- Checkpointing, resumption and determinism

### Debugging training

- Overfit one batch first
- Reading loss and gradient-norm curves
- Exploding, vanishing and dead units
- Data and label bugs

### Pretrained models and transfer

- Choosing an open-weight backbone and checking its licence
- Frozen, partial and full fine-tuning
- Adapters in brief (depth in DEV-LLM-301)

### Throughput and experiments

- Mixed precision, loss scaling and graph compilation
- Data-loading bottlenecks and gradient accumulation
- Profiling and GPU-hour accounting
- Seeds, bounded search and ablations; multi-device training is DEV-INF-402

# DEV-MLE-203 · Feature, Training-Data and Labelling Pipelines

- Track: AI Engineering
- Path: [Machine Learning Engineering](https://sdaiaacademy.github.io/en/paths/DEV-MLE.md)
- Level: Level 200 · Apply
- Format: Workshop: 2 days with labs and a short tracked follow-up task
- Total hours: 16 h
- Audience: practitioner
- Status: In development

## Description

Participants build the data side of a production model on a synthetic payments event log. They assemble training sets with point-in-time joins, define features once for training and serving, catch training-serving skew, and run a model-assisted labelling flow with human review and versioned labels.

## Learning outcomes

By the end, the participant can:

- Explain how point-in-time errors, stale features and training-serving skew enter a prediction system.
- Implement an as-of join that uses only feature values available at each label's time.
- Configure shared feature definitions with offline materialisation and online retrieval.
- Test a deployed model for training-serving skew by comparing logged and recomputed features.
- Build a labelling flow that samples by model uncertainty, pre-labels, routes to human review and versions the labels.

## Prerequisites

- [DEV-MLE-201 · Machine Learning Engineering: Baselines, Validation and Pipelines](https://sdaiaacademy.github.io/en/courses/DEV-MLE-201.md)
- Writes analytical SQL with joins and window functions

## Topics

### Features and point-in-time correctness

- Entities, keys and event time
- Batch, streaming and on-request features
- Offline and online stores, freshness and backfills
- As-of joins and late-arriving data

### Training-serving skew

- Causes: duplicated code, defaults, versions
- Logging served features
- Skew checks; monitoring is DEV-OPS-301

### Labelling flows

- Choosing what to label next
- Model pre-labels and anchoring bias
- Label provenance and versioning; guidelines and agreement are DEV-EVL-304

# DEV-MLE-301 · Computer Vision Engineering

- Track: AI Engineering
- Path: [Machine Learning Engineering](https://sdaiaacademy.github.io/en/paths/DEV-MLE.md)
- Level: Level 300 · Develop
- Format: Intensive: 4 teaching days and a capstone day, with guided pre-work and a tracked follow-up task
- Total hours: 36 h
- Audience: practitioner
- Status: In development

## Description

Participants build vision systems that survive field conditions. On public inspection images and street-scene video they audit annotations, fine-tune convolutional and transformer backbones, train detectors and segmenters, track and count objects, and fit a model to a latency budget. Every lab ends with a test under changed lighting, blur or camera position. Vision-language models are DEV-MLE-304; on-device runtimes are DEV-INF-303.

## Learning outcomes

By the end, the participant can:

- Prepare an image dataset by auditing labels, near-duplicates and leakage by site, and writing annotation guidelines.
- Apply transfer learning from convolutional and transformer backbones with a stated augmentation policy.
- Compute mean average precision over intersection-over-union thresholds and analyse detection errors by type.
- Build a video pipeline that detects, tracks and counts objects crossing a line.
- Optimise a vision model to a latency, memory and accuracy budget through resolution, export and quantisation.
- Evaluate a vision system under field conditions and decide whether it is fit for release.

## Prerequisites

- [DEV-MLE-202 · Deep Learning Engineering](https://sdaiaacademy.github.io/en/courses/DEV-MLE-202.md)
- Reads precision-recall curves and computes precision and recall by hand

## Topics

### Visual data

- Boxes, masks, keypoints and annotation formats
- Guidelines, agreement and label noise
- Near-duplicates and leakage by scene or site
- Augmentation and what it assumes; sensors are DEV-PHY-201

### Backbones and tasks

- Convolutional networks and vision transformers
- Self-supervised open-weight backbones and their licences
- Detection, semantic, instance and promptable segmentation
- Keypoints and pose in brief; document text is DEV-LLM-204
- Open-vocabulary detectors as zero-shot baselines

### Video

- Frame sampling against latency
- Tracking by detection and identity metrics
- Counting and event rules

### Evaluation and release

- Precision-recall, average precision and overlap metrics
- The gap between test and production
- Corruption and shift tests; monitoring camera drift

### Deployment constraints

- Resolution, batch size and numeric precision
- Export to an interchange format and quantisation
- Measuring latency and memory on CPU and accelerators

# DEV-MLE-302 · Speech and Audio Systems Engineering

- Track: AI Engineering
- Path: [Machine Learning Engineering](https://sdaiaacademy.github.io/en/paths/DEV-MLE.md)
- Level: Level 300 · Develop
- Format: Intensive: 3 teaching days and a capstone day, with guided pre-work and a tracked follow-up task
- Total hours: 30 h
- Audience: practitioner
- Status: In development

## Description

Participants build a speech pipeline end to end: they prepare audio and transcripts, benchmark and fine-tune open-weight recognisers, add voice activity detection and speaker diarisation, stream recognition within a latency budget, and test synthesised speech for read-back. Arabic is the main case, with Modern Standard Arabic, dialects, code-switching with English, and the normalisation rules that decide whether an error rate means anything. Voice agents and turn-taking are in DEV-LLM-205; training speech models from scratch is in SPC-GEN-303.

## Learning outcomes

By the end, the participant can:

- Prepare a speech dataset with segmentation, transcript normalisation rules and speaker-disjoint splits.
- Measure word and character error rates, real-time factor and latency by dialect, speaker group and channel.
- Optimise an open-weight recogniser for a target domain and dialect by fine-tuning, and decide whether the improvement justifies its cost.
- Implement voice activity detection and speaker diarisation, and compute the diarisation error rate.
- Test an open text-to-speech model with a recognise-back check and a small listening panel.
- Build a streaming transcription service that meets a latency budget and degrades gracefully under load.

## Prerequisites

- [DEV-MLE-202 · Deep Learning Engineering](https://sdaiaacademy.github.io/en/courses/DEV-MLE-202.md)
- Has containerised a small web service (DEV-OPS-201 or equivalent)
- Reads Arabic script, or brings another language with dialect variation for the labs

## Topics

### Speech fundamentals

- Spectrograms and log-mel features
- Encoder-decoder, connectionist temporal classification and transducer recognisers
- Self-supervised multilingual encoders
- Acoustic models, vocoders and voice cloning

### Arabic speech data

- Dialects and code-switching
- Normalising diacritics, letter variants and numerals
- Punctuation and inverse text normalisation
- Open corpora and their licences

### Recognition and diarisation

- Long-form segmentation
- Speaker embeddings and diarisation
- Adapters versus full fine-tuning
- Noise, reverberation and data augmentation
- Hallucinated text on silence

### Streaming and deployment

- Chunked and streaming decoding
- Real-time factor and batching
- Quantised models on CPU
- Monitoring channel and accent drift

### Evaluation and responsible use

- Error rates with intervals
- Listening tests
- Voice as biometric personal data

---

# DEV-MLE-303 · Recommender and Ranking Systems Engineering

- Track: AI Engineering
- Path: [Machine Learning Engineering](https://sdaiaacademy.github.io/en/paths/DEV-MLE.md)
- Level: Level 300 · Develop
- Format: Intensive: 3 teaching days and a capstone day, with guided pre-work and a tracked follow-up task
- Total hours: 30 h
- Audience: practitioner
- Status: In development

## Description

Participants build a two-stage recommender on a public interaction log: candidate generation with matrix factorisation, a two-tower model and an approximate nearest-neighbour index, then a learned ranker with business rules and diversity re-ranking. They evaluate offline with time-based splits, estimate a new policy's effect from logged data, and design an online test with guardrails. Cold start, popularity bias and feedback loops are treated as engineering problems with measurable controls. Experiment statistics in depth are in SPC-EXP-301, and policy learning in SPC-EXP-401.

## Learning outcomes

By the end, the participant can:

- Prepare an interaction dataset with implicit-feedback labels, time-based splits and leakage checks.
- Implement candidate generation with matrix factorisation and a two-tower model served from an approximate nearest-neighbour index.
- Build a learned ranking stage with business rules and diversity re-ranking over retrieved candidates.
- Compute an off-policy estimate of a new ranking policy from logged data, with its variance.
- Design an online experiment for a ranking change, with primary metric, guardrails, duration and feedback-loop risk.
- Diagnose cold-start and popularity-bias failures and select controls for new users, new items and long-tail exposure.

## Prerequisites

- [DEV-MLE-201 · Machine Learning Engineering: Baselines, Validation and Pipelines](https://sdaiaacademy.github.io/en/courses/DEV-MLE-201.md)
- [DEV-MLE-202 · Deep Learning Engineering](https://sdaiaacademy.github.io/en/courses/DEV-MLE-202.md)
- Writes SQL joins and window functions over event tables

## Topics

### Framing

- Explicit and implicit feedback
- Relevance, diversity, novelty and value
- Multi-stage architecture and latency per stage

### Candidate generation

- Matrix factorisation and item similarity
- Two-tower models and negative sampling
- Approximate nearest-neighbour indexes
- Sequence-aware and language-model-based retrieval

### Ranking

- Pointwise, pairwise and listwise losses
- Gradient-boosted rankers
- Re-ranking for diversity, freshness and rules

### Evaluation

- Time-based splits and leakage
- Recall, NDCG and coverage
- Why sampled-negative metrics mislead
- Position bias and click models
- Off-policy estimation
- Interleaving and guarded online tests

### Feedback loops and operations

- Cold start
- Popularity bias and exposure fairness
- Feature freshness and retraining cadence
- Detecting self-reinforcing loops

---

# DEV-MLE-304 · Multimodal Systems Engineering

- Track: AI Engineering
- Path: [Machine Learning Engineering](https://sdaiaacademy.github.io/en/paths/DEV-MLE.md)
- Level: Level 300 · Develop
- Format: Workshop: two days with labs and a tracked follow-up task
- Total hours: 16 h
- Audience: practitioner
- Status: In development

## Description

Participants build applications that read images and video with vision-language models: field extraction from inspection and retail photos, answers grounded with boxes and points, and time-stamped questions over sampled video frames. ## Learning outcomes

By the end, the participant can:

- Implement question answering and field extraction from images with schema validation.
- Use boxes and points returned by the model to check that each answer refers to the right region.

- Image prompts with structured outputs
- Grounding with boxes and points
- Pairing a general model with a specialist detector
- Keyframes and time-stamped answers

### Evaluation and limits

- Test sets from own images
- Object-existence and hallucination checks
- Arabic text in images
- Instructions hidden in images

- Fine-tuning open Earth-observation foundation models

- Spatial autocorrelation and blocked folds

# DEV-MLE-306 · Forecasting Systems in Production

- Track: AI Engineering
- Path: [Machine Learning Engineering](https://sdaiaacademy.github.io/en/paths/DEV-MLE.md)
- Level: Level 300 · Develop
- Format: Workshop: two days with labs and a tracked follow-up task
- Total hours: 16 h
- Audience: practitioner
- Status: In development

## Description

Participants turn forecasting methods into a running system. On a public many-series retail or energy dataset they build a rolling-origin backtest with a seasonal-naive floor, test statistical, gradient-boosted and pretrained zero-shot forecasters, reconcile forecasts across a hierarchy, and deploy a scheduled pipeline that writes probabilistic forecasts, monitors accuracy and triggers retraining.

## Learning outcomes

By the end, the participant can:

- Implement a rolling-origin backtest that scores point and quantile forecasts against naive floors.
- Test statistical, gradient-boosted and pretrained zero-shot forecasters under one backtest.
- Apply hierarchical reconciliation across product and region levels.
- Build a scheduled pipeline with input checks, versioned models and forecasts stored with their intervals.
- Design monitoring and retraining rules that catch accuracy decay and structural breaks without reacting to noise.

## Prerequisites

- [SPC-MOD-302 · Forecasting and Time Series](https://sdaiaacademy.github.io/en/courses/SPC-MOD-302.md)
- Has packaged a Python job in a container and run it on a schedule

## Topics

### Backtesting as the contract

- Rolling origins and horizons
- Scaled errors, pinball loss and coverage
- Information available at forecast time
- Moving holidays such as Ramadan and Eid

### Many series and hierarchies

- Global versus local models
- Intermittent and new series
- Hierarchical reconciliation

### Pretrained forecasters as baselines

- Zero-shot use with covariates
- When tuned statistical models still win
- Licences and overlap with test series

### Production

- Data-arrival checks
- Structural-break monitoring
- Retraining policies and human overrides
