# SPC-DLR-401 · Post-Training II: Reinforcement Learning for Language Models

- Track: Data Science
- Path: [Deep Learning and Model Development](https://sdaiaacademy.github.io/en/paths/SPC-DLR.md)
- Level: Level 400 · Evaluate
- Format: Extended: 10 weeks part-time, one seminar and one long lab a week on a provided multi-GPU node, four graded assignments, a supervised test and a reproduction capstone
- Total hours: 60 h
- Audience: specialist
- Status: In development

## Description

Participants train language models with reinforcement learning (RL) against rewards that can be checked. They write a policy-gradient loop with group-relative advantages and a divergence penalty, build verifiers for maths, code and structured outputs, train a small open model to reason, and find and close the reward hacks it discovers. They measure accuracy against test-time compute and train on verified agent trajectories from a sandboxed coding environment. Every result is compared at equal compute with a supervised or distillation baseline.

## Learning outcomes

By the end, the participant can:

- Build an RL training loop for a language model with group-relative advantages, clipping and a divergence penalty.
- Design verifiable reward functions for maths, code and format tasks that reject known exploits.
- Diagnose reward hacking and pathologies such as length inflation, format gaming and entropy collapse, and fix them.
- Evaluate test-time compute strategies and choose an allocation for a fixed inference budget.
- Decide whether RL, fine-tuning on filtered samples or distillation gives the largest improvement on a task at equal compute.
- Prepare verified agent trajectories from a sandboxed environment and use them for rejection-sampling fine-tuning.

## Prerequisites

- [SPC-DLR-306 · Post-Training I: Fine-Tuning, Preference Optimisation and Distillation](https://sdaiaacademy.github.io/en/courses/SPC-DLR-306.md)
- Explains policy gradients and value baselines at the depth of an introductory reinforcement learning course such as SPC-GEN-304
- Runs containers and writes unit tests

## Topics

### RL for language models

- Policy gradients, baselines and advantages
- Clipping, divergence control and critic-free estimators
- Rollout and training systems

### Rewards

- Verifiable rewards for maths, code and formats
- Outcome, process and learned reward models, and their limits
- Reward hacking and specification gaming

### Reasoning training

- Cold start with supervised data
- Curricula and difficulty filtering
- Whether written reasoning reflects the computation

### Test-time compute

- Best-of-n, voting and verifier reranking
- Sequential refinement and budget control
- Compute-optimal allocation and reporting

### Learning from agent trajectories

- Environments, sandboxes and task contracts
- Trajectory curation and credit assignment
- Multi-turn RL with tools

---

# SPC-DLR-402 · Efficient Deep Learning: Compression, Quantisation and Long Context

- Track: Data Science
- Path: [Deep Learning and Model Development](https://sdaiaacademy.github.io/en/paths/SPC-DLR.md)
- Level: Level 400 · Evaluate
- Format: Extended: 10 weeks part-time, one lecture and one long lab a week, four graded assignments, a supervised test and a compression capstone
- Total hours: 60 h
- Audience: specialist
- Status: In development

## Description

Participants make models smaller, faster and able to read longer inputs, and measure what each method costs in quality. They prune convolutional and transformer models, quantise weights, activations and the key-value cache to 8 and 4 bits after and during training, distil a compressed student, extend a model's context window, and train a small mixture-of-experts (MoE) layer. Each change is judged on a quality, latency and memory frontier measured on real hardware. Serving engineering is DEV-INF-401; on-device deployment is DEV-INF-303.

## Learning outcomes

By the end, the participant can:

- Apply magnitude, structured and semi-structured (N:M) pruning, and measure accuracy against sparsity and real speed-up.
- Build a post-training quantisation pipeline with calibration, per-channel and group scaling, and outlier handling.
- Diagnose quality loss after compression by locating sensitive layers and outliers, and repair it with mixed precision or quantisation-aware training.
- Build a long-context extension of a small model and evaluate it beyond single-fact retrieval tests.
- Implement a mixture-of-experts layer with routing and a load-balancing loss.
- Design a compression plan for a target device or budget and defend it with a measured frontier.

## Prerequisites

- [SPC-DLR-302 · Deep Learning from First Principles](https://sdaiaacademy.github.io/en/courses/SPC-DLR-302.md)
- [SPC-DLR-303 · Building a Language Model from Scratch](https://sdaiaacademy.github.io/en/courses/SPC-DLR-303.md)
- Profiles a training or inference step and reads the trace (SPC-DLR-304 recommended)
- Has run logit-level distillation (SPC-DLR-306 recommended)

## Topics

### Measuring efficiency

- Latency, throughput, memory and energy
- Quality, latency and memory frontiers
- Memory-bound decoding and what hardware accelerates

### Pruning and distillation

- Magnitude, structured and N:M sparsity
- Distilling compressed students
- Neural architecture search in brief

### Quantisation

- Integer and low-bit floating formats
- Calibration, group scaling and outliers
- Quantisation-aware training
- Key-value cache quantisation

### Long context

- Cost of attention with length
- Positional interpolation and rotary scaling
- Sliding-window, sparse and linear attention, and state-space hybrids
- Testing long context honestly

### Sparse experts

- Routing, load balancing and capacity
- Active against total parameters
- Consequences for serving

---

# SPC-GEN-301 · Diffusion and Flow Matching from Scratch

- Track: Data Science
- Path: [Generative, Multimodal and Embodied Models](https://sdaiaacademy.github.io/en/paths/SPC-GEN.md)
- Level: Level 300 · Develop
- Format: Extended: 10 weeks part-time, one two-hour session and one lab a week, weekly graded assignments and a capstone
- Total hours: 60 h
- Audience: specialist
- Status: In development

## Description

Participants build image generators from the equations up, treating diffusion and flow matching as one framework: a probability path from noise to data, a learned velocity or score field, and a differential equation solved at sampling time. They implement both objectives on toy distributions, train a U-Net and then a diffusion transformer on public image datasets, add classifier-free guidance, move into the latent space of an autoencoder, and finish with discrete diffusion for text. Every quality claim is backed by metrics on held-out data.

## Learning outcomes

By the end, the participant can:

- Explain diffusion, score-based and flow matching models as ways of learning a velocity field along a probability path.
- Implement flow matching and denoising score matching, and compare deterministic and stochastic samplers.
- Build a class-conditional image generator with a U-Net and then a transformer backbone, using classifier-free guidance.
- Design a latent generative model, choosing the autoencoder's compression for a compute budget.
- Implement a masked discrete diffusion model for short text and compare it with an autoregressive model of similar size.
- Evaluate a generator's quality, diversity and memorisation, and state where each metric misleads.

## Prerequisites

- [SPC-DLR-302 · Deep Learning from First Principles](https://sdaiaacademy.github.io/en/courses/SPC-DLR-302.md)
- Works with probability densities and multivariable calculus, at the depth of SPC-DLR-301

## Next courses

- [SPC-GEN-402 · World Models, Video and 3D Generation](https://sdaiaacademy.github.io/en/courses/SPC-GEN-402.md)

## Topics

### Probability paths

- Ordinary and stochastic differential equations for generation
- Velocity and score fields; conditional and marginal paths
- Flow matching, score matching and denoising as one loss family
- Noise schedules, prediction targets and loss weighting

### Sampling and conditioning

- Euler, higher-order and stochastic solvers
- Few-step sampling by distillation and consistency training
- U-Net and diffusion transformer backbones
- Classifier-free guidance and text conditioning by cross-attention

### Latent models

- Variational autoencoders
- Compression against reconstruction
- Latent diffusion at a fixed budget

### Discrete diffusion for text

- Masked and uniform corruption processes
- Diffusion against autoregressive language models

### Evaluation and release

- Fréchet distance, precision and recall, and their failure modes
- Memorisation and extraction checks
- Provenance, watermarking and labelling of synthetic media

---

# SPC-GEN-302 · Vision and Multimodal Foundation Models

- Track: Data Science
- Path: [Generative, Multimodal and Embodied Models](https://sdaiaacademy.github.io/en/paths/SPC-GEN.md)
- Level: Level 300 · Develop
- Format: Extended: 10 weeks part-time, one two-hour session and one lab a week, weekly graded assignments and a capstone
- Total hours: 60 h
- Audience: specialist
- Status: In development

## Description

Participants pretrain and probe the visual representations that multimodal models are built on. They train a small vision transformer with two of the contrastive, masked-image and self-distillation objectives on public images, then a contrastive image-text model, and assemble a small vision-language model from a frozen encoder, a trained projector and an open-weight language model, followed by instruction tuning. A final block fits neural radiance fields and Gaussian splatting to captured scenes. Application use of vision-language models is DEV-MLE-304; video and 3D generation is SPC-GEN-402.

## Learning outcomes

By the end, the participant can:

- Compare contrastive, masked and self-distillation objectives and explain the invariances each teaches an encoder.
- Implement two self-supervised objectives for a small vision transformer and measure them with linear probes and retrieval.
- Build a small vision-language model from a frozen encoder, a trained projector and an open-weight language model, then instruction-tune it.
- Evaluate a vision-language model for hallucinated objects, Arabic and English text reading, and prompt sensitivity.
- Fit a neural radiance field and a Gaussian splatting model to a captured scene and compare quality and speed.
- Design a pretraining and adaptation plan for a vision encoder in a new domain with few labels.

## Prerequisites

- [SPC-DLR-302 · Deep Learning from First Principles](https://sdaiaacademy.github.io/en/courses/SPC-DLR-302.md)
- Has trained an image classifier and uses linear algebra for rotations and projections

## Topics

### Self-supervised vision

- Vision transformers and patch embeddings
- Contrastive, masked and self-distillation objectives
- Probing, retrieval, dense-feature and fine-tuning evaluation

### Image-text models

- Contrastive image-text pretraining and zero-shot use
- Caption noise, filtering and inherited bias

### Vision-language models

- Encoder-projector designs against early-fusion native multimodal models
- Alignment pretraining and visual instruction tuning
- Resolution, tiling and visual token budgets

### Evaluating multimodal models

- Benchmarks and their limits
- Object hallucination and grounding
- Contamination and prompt sensitivity

### Three-dimensional representations

- Camera models and structure from motion
- Neural radiance fields and Gaussian splatting
- Depth and point clouds, in brief

# SPC-GEN-303 · Speech and Arabic Language Modelling

- Track: Data Science
- Path: [Generative, Multimodal and Embodied Models](https://sdaiaacademy.github.io/en/paths/SPC-GEN.md)
- Level: Level 300 · Develop
- Format: Extended: 10 weeks part-time, one two-hour session and one lab a week, weekly graded assignments and a capstone
- Total hours: 60 h
- Audience: specialist
- Status: In development

## Description

Participants train and adapt the models behind spoken and written Arabic. They fine-tune a self-supervised speech encoder and an encoder-decoder recogniser on public Arabic speech, report error rates by dialect, and fine-tune a text-to-speech model judged by listening tests. For text, they design an Arabic-aware tokeniser, continue pretraining and align a small open-weight model, and evaluate it against audited Arabic and cultural benchmarks. Applications are DEV-LLM-302 and DEV-MLE-302.

## Learning outcomes

By the end, the participant can:

- Explain how Arabic morphology, optional diacritics, dialects and code-switching affect tokenisation, recognition and evaluation.
- Fine-tune a speech encoder and an encoder-decoder recogniser for Arabic and report error rates by dialect.
- Fine-tune a pretrained text-to-speech model for Arabic and measure its intelligibility and naturalness.
- Design an Arabic and English tokeniser and justify its vocabulary by fertility and downstream loss.
- Build a continued-pretraining and alignment run that improves a small open-weight model in Arabic without losing English ability.
- Evaluate an Arabic model for knowledge, instruction-following, dialect and cultural appropriateness, and audit the benchmarks used.

## Prerequisites

- [SPC-DLR-302 · Deep Learning from First Principles](https://sdaiaacademy.github.io/en/courses/SPC-DLR-302.md)
- Has trained a small transformer language model end to end, as in SPC-DLR-303
- Reads Arabic script, or pairs with someone who does for error analysis

## Topics

### Speech recognition

- Self-supervised speech encoders
- Connectionist temporal classification and encoder-decoder models
- Error rates, normalisation and diacritics

### Speech synthesis

- Acoustic models, vocoders, codec tokens and speech language models
- Listening tests and objective proxies
- Voice cloning and consent

### Tokenisation and multilinguality

- Tokeniser fertility on Arabic
- Morphological segmentation
- Cross-lingual transfer and vocabulary extension

### Arabic pretraining and alignment

- Filtering, deduplication and dialect identification
- Mixing ratios and forgetting
- Preference data for cultural norms

### Arabic evaluation

- Knowledge, exam and instruction-following benchmarks
- Cultural and dialect evaluation sets
- Contamination and translated-benchmark artefacts

# SPC-GEN-304 · Reinforcement Learning and Decision Making

- Track: Data Science
- Path: [Generative, Multimodal and Embodied Models](https://sdaiaacademy.github.io/en/paths/SPC-GEN.md)
- Level: Level 300 · Develop
- Format: Extended: 12 weeks part-time, one two-hour session and one lab a week, graded assignments and a capstone
- Total hours: 80 h
- Audience: specialist
- Status: In development

## Description

Participants implement the main families of reinforcement learning from scratch and report results that hold across random seeds. They solve small Markov decision processes (MDPs) exactly, then build value-based, policy-gradient and actor-critic agents, a model-based agent that plans with a learned dynamics model, and an offline agent trained on logged data. They compare exploration strategies and close by setting reinforcement learning against optimisation and heuristic baselines on operations problems. Reinforcement learning for language models is SPC-DLR-401, robot learning SPC-GEN-401 and optimisation methods SPC-MOD-304.

## Learning outcomes

By the end, the participant can:

- Explain the Bellman equations, the policy gradient theorem and the bias-variance trade-off in return estimates.
- Implement value iteration, bandit exploration strategies, Q-learning and a deep Q-network with replay and target networks.
- Implement a policy-gradient agent, proximal policy optimisation and an off-policy actor-critic for continuous control.
- Build a model-based agent that plans with a learned dynamics model, and diagnose where model error limits it.
- Evaluate offline methods against behaviour cloning on datasets of different quality and recommend one per regime.
- Design a reinforcement learning experiment for a decision problem, with the reward, optimisation baselines and a sound comparison over seeds.

## Prerequisites

- [SPC-DLR-302 · Deep Learning from First Principles](https://sdaiaacademy.github.io/en/courses/SPC-DLR-302.md)
- Uses probability, expectations and gradient-based optimisation, at the depth of SPC-DLR-301

## Next courses

- [SPC-GEN-401 · Robot Learning and Vision-Language-Action Models](https://sdaiaacademy.github.io/en/courses/SPC-GEN-401.md)

## Topics

### Foundations

- MDPs, value functions and dynamic programming
- Bandits, regret and exploration

### Value-based methods

- Temporal-difference learning and Q-learning
- Deep Q-networks and overestimation

### Policy and actor-critic methods

- Policy gradients, baselines and advantage estimation
- Trust regions and proximal policy optimisation
- Off-policy actor-critic with entropy regularisation

### Model-based and offline learning

- Learned dynamics, model predictive control and tree search
- Behaviour cloning, distribution shift and conservative value methods
- Off-policy evaluation, in brief (full treatment in SPC-EXP-401)

### Experiments and applications

- Seeds, interquartile means and bootstrap intervals
- Reward design, reward hacking and constraints
- Comparison with optimisation and heuristics
- Multi-agent settings, in brief

---

# SPC-GEN-401 · Robot Learning and Vision-Language-Action Models

- Track: Data Science
- Path: [Generative, Multimodal and Embodied Models](https://sdaiaacademy.github.io/en/paths/SPC-GEN.md)
- Level: Level 400 · Evaluate
- Format: Extended: 10 weeks part-time, one two-hour session and one lab a week, with robot-arm lab days and a team capstone
- Total hours: 60 h
- Audience: specialist
- Status: In development

## Description

Participants train and evaluate learned robot policies in simulation and on low-cost open robot arms. They collect teleoperated demonstrations, train behaviour cloning, action-chunking and diffusion policies, fine-tune an open-weight vision-language-action (VLA) model, and measure success with intervals on held-out objects, positions and instructions. They narrow the simulation-to-hardware gap with domain randomisation and system identification. Engineering of deployed robot learning systems is DEV-PHY-302.

## Learning outcomes

By the end, the participant can:

- Implement behaviour cloning with action chunking and a diffusion policy, and compare them on the same demonstrations.
- Design a demonstration protocol and diagnose how number, diversity and operator quality of demonstrations affect success.
- Evaluate a fine-tuned open-weight VLA model against a policy trained from scratch on held-out objects, positions and instructions.
- Diagnose the gap between simulation and a real arm and measure how far randomisation and system identification close it.
- Review a published robot learning result for evaluation design and claimed generalisation.
- Configure workspace limits, speed limits and an emergency stop for a learned policy on a physical arm.

## Prerequisites

- [SPC-GEN-304 · Reinforcement Learning and Decision Making](https://sdaiaacademy.github.io/en/courses/SPC-GEN-304.md)
- Has trained a diffusion or flow model, as in SPC-GEN-301, or passes an entry exercise
- Fine-tunes a transformer model with adapters, as in SPC-DLR-306

## Topics

### Robot data

- Observation and action spaces, control rate and latency
- Teleoperation, public datasets and data cards

### Imitation learning

- Behaviour cloning and compounding error
- Action chunking
- Diffusion and flow policies for multimodal actions

### Vision-language-action models

- Backbones with action heads or action tokens
- Pretraining on data from many robot types
- Adapter fine-tuning, inference speed and action rate

### Simulation to reality

- Where simulators differ from hardware
- Domain randomisation and system identification

### Evaluation and safe operation

- Success rates, intervals and trial counts
- Generalisation splits; simulated evaluation as a proxy for hardware
- Workspace limits, emergency stop and supervision

# SPC-GEN-402 · World Models, Video and 3D Generation

- Track: Data Science
- Path: [Generative, Multimodal and Embodied Models](https://sdaiaacademy.github.io/en/paths/SPC-GEN.md)
- Level: Level 400 · Evaluate
- Format: Seminar: 8 weekly sessions of paper reading and discussion, a replication sprint and a closing review; rebuilt each term from current conference tutorials and workshops
- Total hours: 30 h
- Audience: specialist
- Status: In development

## Description

A research seminar on models that generate or simulate the world: video generators, interactive world models that predict what happens next given an action, and generators of 3D objects and scenes. Each week participants read and present papers, place their claims on a shared taxonomy and judge the evidence behind them. In a replication sprint each pair reproduces one small published result, such as a latent dynamics model in a classic control task or a small video prediction model, within a fixed GPU budget.

## Learning outcomes

By the end, the participant can:

- Describe the main families of video, world-model and 3D generative methods and the evidence each offers for physical consistency.
- Review a paper's claims about controllability, physical consistency and generalisation, and judge whether its evaluation supports them.
- Measure a pretrained video or world model's consistency under controlled prompts or actions with a small probe set.
- Reproduce one small published result and report where the reproduction agrees and differs.
- Defend a position on an open problem, such as how to evaluate interactive world models.

## Prerequisites

- [SPC-GEN-301 · Diffusion and Flow Matching from Scratch](https://sdaiaacademy.github.io/en/courses/SPC-GEN-301.md)
- Reads current machine learning papers and has trained a model on a GPU
- Reinforcement learning basics (SPC-GEN-304) and radiance fields (SPC-GEN-302) help in the world-model and 3D sessions

## Topics

### Video generation

- Video tokenisers, latent video diffusion and autoregressive generation
- Temporal consistency and long-horizon generation
- Measuring video quality and physical plausibility

### World models for agents

- Latent dynamics for planning and control
- Interactive, action-conditioned video world models
- World models as training environments for agents and robots

### 3D and 4D generation

- Objects and scenes as radiance fields, Gaussians or meshes
- Lifting 2D generators into 3D
- Multi-view consistency and its measurement

### Evidence and responsibility

- Benchmarks of physical understanding and their limits
- Compute, provenance and licences of training video
- Synthetic media labelling and deepfake risk

# SPC-TRU-301 · Evaluation Science for AI Models

- Track: Data Science
- Path: [Trustworthy AI Science](https://sdaiaacademy.github.io/en/paths/SPC-TRU.md)
- Level: Level 300 · Develop
- Format: Intensive: 4 teaching days and a capstone day, with guided pre-work and a tracked follow-up task
- Total hours: 40 h
- Audience: specialist
- Status: In development

## Description

Participants treat a benchmark score as a measurement and state what it measures, how precisely and at what cost. They audit a public benchmark for label errors and construct validity, test models for contamination, validate a model-based judge against human labels, report results with uncertainty and compute budgets, and build a small agent evaluation in a sandbox. Statistical depth is in SPC-EXP-402; evaluation of applications and agents for developers is in DEV-EVL-301 and DEV-EVL-302.

## Learning outcomes

By the end, the participant can:

- Explain the main threats to evaluation validity: construct mismatch, contamination, saturation, test awareness and grader error.
- Analyse a public benchmark for label errors and ambiguous items, and recompute model scores on the corrected set.
- Test models for training-data contamination with overlap search, perturbed item variants and completion probes.
- Evaluate a model-based judge against human labels, measure its position, length and self-preference biases, and decide where it may replace human graders.
- Design an agent evaluation that reports success over repeated trials, cost per solved task and failure categories.
- Build a new evaluation for a stated capability and report results with uncertainty, compute budget and known limits.

## Prerequisites

- Runs and scores open-weight language models from Python
- Computes bootstrap intervals and standard errors, as in SPC-STA-201
- Runs containers from the command line

## Next courses

- [SPC-TRU-303 · AI Safety and Alignment Engineering](https://sdaiaacademy.github.io/en/courses/SPC-TRU-303.md)

## Topics

### Measurement and benchmark design

- Constructs and what a score can claim
- Item writing, keys and adjudication
- Item response theory in brief
- Saturation; private and refreshed test sets
- Datasheets with Arabic and dialect coverage

### Contamination and test awareness

- Overlap search against training corpora
- Perturbed variants, canaries and dated test sets
- Models that detect tests

### Model-based judges

- Pointwise, pairwise and reference-guided judging
- Position, length and self-preference bias
- When a judge may replace people

### Reporting under a budget

- Clustered and paired comparisons
- Prompts, settings and seeds as conditions
- Rankings that shift with test-time compute

### Agent evaluations

- Sandboxes and programmatic checkers
- Repeated trials, transcripts and environment bugs

# SPC-TRU-302 · Interpretability of Neural Networks

- Track: Data Science
- Path: [Trustworthy AI Science](https://sdaiaacademy.github.io/en/paths/SPC-TRU.md)
- Level: Level 300 · Develop
- Format: Extended: 10 weeks part-time, a weekly lecture and lab, four graded assignments and a replication project
- Total hours: 60 h
- Audience: specialist
- Status: In development

## Description

Participants open up trained networks and test claims about how they compute. On small open-weight transformers and toy models, they cache activations, train linear probes, reverse-engineer induction and indirect-object circuits with activation patching, train a sparse dictionary on a residual stream and steer the model with its features. Every claim is tested by intervention, and the course spends as long on what explanations fail to show as on how to produce them. The project replicates and extends one published result.

## Learning outcomes

By the end, the participant can:

- Explain superposition, the linear representation hypothesis and the difference between correlational and causal evidence about model internals.
- Implement activation caching, the logit lens and linear probes, and compare probe accuracy with a control task.
- Diagnose the circuit behind a defined behaviour with activation and path patching, and test it by ablation.
- Build a sparse dictionary of model activations, evaluate its reconstruction, sparsity and interpretability, and steer behaviour with a chosen feature.
- Test two explanation methods for faithfulness with model randomisation, counterfactual inputs and a reasoning-trace consistency check.
- Deliver a reproduction and extension of a published interpretability result, and defend which conclusions the evidence supports.

## Prerequisites

- [SPC-DLR-302 · Deep Learning from First Principles](https://sdaiaacademy.github.io/en/courses/SPC-DLR-302.md)
- Implements a transformer block and training loop
- Uses projections, bases and singular value decomposition fluently

## Topics

### Foundations

- The residual stream view of a transformer
- Superposition and toy models
- Correlational versus causal evidence

### Probing

- Linear probes and control tasks
- Logit lens and tuned lens
- World-state probes in synthetic game models

### Circuits and causal interventions

- Activation, path and attribution patching
- Induction heads and in-context learning
- Ablation, faithfulness and completeness

### Feature dictionaries

- Sparse autoencoders and transcoders
- Dead features, feature splitting and reconstruction error
- Automated feature labelling and attribution graphs

### Steering and editing

- Steering vectors and persona directions
- Locating and editing factual associations
- Side effects of interventions

### Limits of explanation

- Sanity checks for attribution maps
- Interpretability illusions
- Faithfulness of reasoning-model traces
- What an audit can rest on

---

# SPC-TRU-303 · AI Safety and Alignment Engineering

- Track: Data Science
- Path: [Trustworthy AI Science](https://sdaiaacademy.github.io/en/paths/SPC-TRU.md)
- Level: Level 300 · Develop
- Format: Extended: 10 weeks part-time, a weekly lecture and lab, four graded labs and a safety case
- Total hours: 60 h
- Audience: specialist
- Status: In development

## Description

Participants judge whether an AI system could cause serious harm and design controls that do not depend on the model being trustworthy. They write threat models, build dangerous-capability evaluations from safe proxy tasks in a sandbox, measure propensities such as sycophancy, reward hacking and sandbagging, red-team an open model by hand and with an automated attacker, and design protocols in which a weaker trusted model monitors a stronger untrusted one. Alignment training methods are in SPC-DLR-306 and SPC-DLR-401; application red teaming is DEV-SEC-302; governance controls are LDS-AIG-302.

## Learning outcomes

By the end, the participant can:

- Compare misuse, misalignment and structural threat models, and describe how safety frameworks tie capability thresholds to safeguards.
- Draft a threat model naming actors, capabilities, harm pathways and the evidence that would rule each pathway in or out.
- Build a dangerous-capability evaluation from safe proxy tasks, with elicitation effort and thresholds fixed in advance.
- Evaluate sycophancy, reward hacking and sandbagging propensities, and test whether results change when the model can tell it is being evaluated.
- Design and stress-test a control protocol in which a trusted monitor reviews an untrusted model's actions.
- Defend a safety case that links each claim about a deployment to evaluation, red-team and monitoring evidence.

## Prerequisites

- [SPC-TRU-301 · Evaluation Science for AI Models](https://sdaiaacademy.github.io/en/courses/SPC-TRU-301.md)
- Fine-tunes a small open-weight language model with adapters, as in SPC-DLR-306 or DEV-LLM-301
- Has built a simple tool-using agent loop and read its transcripts

## Topics

### Threat models and safety frameworks

- Misuse, misalignment and structural risks
- Capability thresholds and safeguards
- Safety cases: claims, arguments and evidence

### Dangerous-capability evaluations

- Cyber and autonomy proxies in sandboxes
- Elicitation by scaffolding, fine-tuning and repeated attempts
- Handling hazardous information

### Propensity evaluations

- Sycophancy, deception and sandbagging
- Reward hacking and specification gaming
- Emergent misalignment after narrow fine-tuning
- Evaluation awareness

### Red teaming

- Manual and automated red teaming
- Limits of refusal training
- Turning findings into regression evaluations

### Monitoring and control

- Trusted and untrusted models
- Monitoring reasoning versus monitoring actions
- Audit budgets, resampling and deferral

# SPC-TRU-304 · Trustworthy Machine Learning: Robustness, Privacy and Fairness

- Track: Data Science
- Path: [Trustworthy AI Science](https://sdaiaacademy.github.io/en/paths/SPC-TRU.md)
- Level: Level 300 · Develop
- Format: Extended: 10 weeks part-time, a weekly lecture and lab, four graded labs and an evaluation paper
- Total hours: 60 h
- Audience: specialist
- Status: In development

## Description

Participants attack and defend machine learning models and measure what each defence buys. They evaluate adversarial defences without being misled by gradient masking, plant and detect backdoors, run membership-inference and extraction attacks on models trained on synthetic records, train with differential privacy and audit the guarantee, check whether unlearning removes what it claims, and examine fairness and uncertainty under distribution shift. De-identification and subgroup audits are in SPC-MOD-306, calibration basics in SPC-MOD-301 and pipeline privacy engineering in DEV-SEC-303.

## Learning outcomes

By the end, the participant can:

- Explain threat models for evasion, poisoning, privacy and fairness harms in terms of attacker knowledge, capability and goal.
- Evaluate an adversarial defence with adaptive attacks and certified bounds, and identify gradient masking.
- Implement a backdoor attack and two detection methods, and measure attack success against clean accuracy.
- Audit a model for training-data leakage, then train with differential privacy and compare measured leakage with the formal bound.
- Test whether an unlearning method removes a forget set, using a retrained model as the reference.
- Design a fairness and uncertainty evaluation that states its measurement assumptions and checks stability under distribution shift.

## Prerequisites

- [SPC-DLR-302 · Deep Learning from First Principles](https://sdaiaacademy.github.io/en/courses/SPC-DLR-302.md)
- Trains and evaluates an image or tabular classifier
- Reads probability and optimisation notation

## Topics

### Evaluation discipline

- Threat models
- Adaptive attacks and gradient masking
- Reporting at low false-positive rates

### Adversarial robustness

- Gradient-based attacks and adversarial training
- Certified defences by randomised smoothing
- Adversarial suffixes against language models

### Poisoning, backdoors and model theft

- Dirty-label and clean-label poisoning
- Poisoning of fine-tuning data
- Detection and removal
- Model stealing and output watermarks

### Privacy and unlearning

- Membership inference and training-data extraction
- Differentially private training and privacy accounting
- Empirical auditing of privacy guarantees
- Exact and approximate unlearning

### Uncertainty and fairness research methods

- Conformal prediction under distribution shift
- Out-of-distribution detection and selective prediction
- Fairness criteria and impossibility results
- Measurement error in labels and group attributes

# SPC-RSP-101 · Emerging Computing Paradigms for AI

- Track: Data Science
- Path: [Research Practice and Frontier](https://sdaiaacademy.github.io/en/paths/SPC-RSP.md)
- Level: Level 100 · Explain
- Format: Seminar: three half-day sessions of briefing, simulator labs and claim review; the claim set is refreshed every six months
- Total hours: 12 h
- Audience: specialist
- Status: In development

## Description

Participants examine three kinds of hardware proposed for learning workloads: quantum, neuromorphic, and optical or analogue computing. For each they learn the computational model, run a small simulation on a laptop, and sort published claims into demonstrated, plausible and unsupported. The seminar ends with a written assessment of an unseen announcement. It is an awareness course: it prepares specialists and technical leads to read hardware claims critically and to judge when a paradigm deserves monitoring or a pilot, not to build on these platforms.

## Learning outcomes

By the end, the participant can:

- Explain what a gate-based quantum computer, a spiking neural network and an analogue optical matrix multiplier each compute natively.
- Distinguish demonstrated results, plausible near-term results and unsupported claims for machine learning on each paradigm.
- Identify the bottlenecks that limit practical advantage: data loading, noise and error correction, precision and conversion costs, training methods and software maturity.
- Use a circuit simulator to train a two-qubit variational classifier and compare it with a classical baseline on the same data.
- Analyse an announcement of hardware advantage for AI and draft an assessment of its baseline, problem size, end-to-end cost and missing comparisons.

## Prerequisites

- Works with vectors and matrices at the level of FND-MTH-101; complex numbers are revised in session
- Runs a Python notebook and has trained a small model such as a linear classifier
- No physics background is assumed

## Topics

### Why new hardware for learning

- Energy and memory-bandwidth limits of digital accelerators
- What advantage means: speed, energy, sample efficiency, cost
- Reading a hardware claim: baseline, problem size, end-to-end time

### Quantum computing and learning

- Qubits, gates, measurement and circuits
- Variational circuits and quantum kernels
- Data loading, barren plateaus and dequantised algorithms
- Annealing and optimisation claims against classical solvers
- Error correction: what has been shown and what remains

### Neuromorphic computing

- Spiking neurons and event-based sensors
- Training spiking networks: surrogate gradients and conversion
- Where low-power event processing has been demonstrated

### Optical and analogue computing

- Matrix multiplication in light and in memory arrays
- Noise, precision and analogue-digital conversion costs
- Inference versus training on analogue hardware

### Judging claims

- Demonstrated, plausible, unsupported
- Signals worth monitoring
- When a pilot is justified

---

# SPC-RSP-301 · Research Practice Studio

- Track: Data Science
- Path: [Research Practice and Frontier](https://sdaiaacademy.github.io/en/paths/SPC-RSP.md)
- Level: Level 300 · Develop
- Format: Studio: eight weeks part-time with weekly coached clinics, an exchanged peer review and a final defence
- Total hours: 60 h
- Audience: specialist
- Status: In development

## Description

Participants practise a research group's working habits on one small question: structured paper reading, reproducing a published result on a small budget, a tracked follow-up experiment across seeds, sound statistics, a short paper, a peer review and an open-source contribution. They also supervise a research agent running overnight experiments and decide which of its results to accept.

## Learning outcomes

By the end, the participant can:

- Prepare a reading note that states a paper's claim, evidence, baselines, compute and threats to validity.
- Reproduce one figure or table from a published paper within a stated compute budget and explain any gap.
- Design and run a tracked follow-up experiment with a stated hypothesis, controls and a seed count justified by a power estimate.
- Compute the uncertainty of model comparisons across seeds and data splits, correcting for multiple comparisons.
- Review a peer's short paper for soundness, clarity, reproducibility and ethics.
- Audit a research agent's overnight experiment results, deciding for each whether to accept, rerun or reject it.

## Prerequisites

- Trains, evaluates and debugs a neural network or gradient-boosted model in Python, as in SPC-DLR-302 or SPC-MOD-201
- Computes a confidence interval and runs a two-sample test, as in FND-MTH-104 or SPC-STA-201
- Uses Git for daily work

## Next courses

- [SPC-RSP-401 · Reproduction Capstone: Reproduce and Extend a Published Result](https://sdaiaacademy.github.io/en/courses/SPC-RSP-401.md)

## Topics

### Reading and positioning

- Three-pass reading and reading notes
- Related work and citation checks
- Claims, evidence and threats to validity

### Reproduction and experiment design

- Configurations, seeds and environment capture
- Compute budgets; debugging on a CPU first
- Baselines, controls and ablations

### Tracking and statistics

- Experiment tracking and run metadata
- Seed variance, paired comparisons, bootstrap intervals
- Multiple comparisons and forking paths

### Supervising research agents

- Automated experiment loops and what they optimise
- Overfitting to the validation set by search
- Audit trails and acceptance rules

### Writing, review and open science

- Paper structure, figures, compute reporting and limitations
- Reviewing against a reproducibility and ethics checklist
- Authorship, AI disclosure, fabricated citations
- Contributing to open-source research code

---

# SPC-RSP-302 · Data Science Practicum

- Track: Data Science
- Path: [Research Practice and Frontier](https://sdaiaacademy.github.io/en/paths/SPC-RSP.md)
- Level: Level 300 · Develop
- Format: Practicum: about eight weeks part-time in teams of three or four, on a sponsor's decision question, with milestone reviews by experienced data scientists
- Total hours: 100 h
- Audience: specialist
- Status: In development

## Description

Teams of three or four take a decision question from a sponsoring organisation, such as where to place a service, which cases to inspect first or whether a pilot worked, and carry it to a recommendation the sponsor can act on. They frame the decision, audit the data, fix the analysis plan before seeing outcomes, build and validate the analysis and defend it to the sponsor and an Academy panel. SPC-MOD-307 and SPC-ANL-301 are recommended beforehand.

## Learning outcomes

By the end, the participant can:

- Design a decision question from a sponsor's request, with options, a success metric, constraints and the evidence that would change the decision.
- Prepare a data audit covering provenance, quality, classification, personal data and fitness for the question.
- Design an analysis plan matched to the question type (descriptive, predictive, causal or optimisation) and fix it before outcomes are examined.
- Build and validate the analysis with baselines, sensitivity checks and stated uncertainty for every number the recommendation relies on.
- Defend a recommendation and its limits to the sponsor and a technical panel, including what evidence would reverse it.
- Prepare a hand-over pack with a decision log, an analysis card, a monitoring suggestion and open risks.

## Prerequisites

- [SPC-STA-201 · Statistical Inference by Simulation](https://sdaiaacademy.github.io/en/courses/SPC-STA-201.md)
- [SPC-MOD-201 · Machine Learning for Tabular Data: Baselines and Validation](https://sdaiaacademy.github.io/en/courses/SPC-MOD-201.md)
- Writes analysis code in Python or R under version control
- Has designed or analysed an experiment or a before-and-after comparison, as in SPC-EXP-201
- Can commit about 12 hours a week for eight weeks

## Topics

### Framing and scoping

- Decision questions versus analysis requests
- Stakeholder interviews and success metrics
- Scope, timeline and team roles

### Data access and audit

- Sharing agreements and classification
- Anonymisation and synthetic substitutes
- Profiling and fitness for purpose

### Analysis design and delivery

- Matching method to question type
- Validation schemes fixed in advance
- Reproducible pipelines and code review
- AI-assisted analysis with verification notes

### Recommendation and hand-over

- Uncertainty in plain words
- Briefing a sponsor and answering challenge
- Analysis cards, decision logs and monitoring

# SPC-RSP-401 · Reproduction Capstone: Reproduce and Extend a Published Result

- Track: Data Science
- Path: [Research Practice and Frontier](https://sdaiaacademy.github.io/en/paths/SPC-RSP.md)
- Level: Level 400 · Evaluate
- Format: Studio: twelve weeks part-time, individual and coached, with proposal, mid-point and panel reviews
- Total hours: 100 h
- Audience: specialist
- Status: In development

## Description

Each participant chooses a result from a recent peer-reviewed paper, reproduces it within an agreed compute budget, extends it with one well-designed experiment, and reports both against a reproducibility checklist. A mid-point review checks the reproduction before extension starts. Credit goes to measurement quality, not agreement with the paper: a carefully measured failure to reproduce, with its likely causes tested, can earn full marks.

## Learning outcomes

By the end, the participant can:

- Defend the choice of a target result on feasibility, licence position and compute budget.
- Reproduce the target result, measuring variation across seeds and logging every deviation from the paper.
- Diagnose the causes of any gap between the reproduced and the published result.
- Design and run one extension that tests the claim beyond its original conditions, such as a new dataset, scale, language or ablation.
- Deliver a reproducibility report that meets a published checklist for code, data, compute, statistics and ethics.
- Defend the findings, including any negative result, under questioning from a panel.

## Prerequisites

- [SPC-RSP-301 · Research Practice Studio](https://sdaiaacademy.github.io/en/courses/SPC-RSP-301.md)
- Has completed a model development course at level 300, such as SPC-DLR-302, SPC-DLR-303 or SPC-GEN-301, or can show equivalent work
- Writes research-grade training code and profiles a training run

## Topics

### Choosing a target

- What makes a result reproducible within budget
- Licences of code, data and model weights
- Estimating compute from the paper

### Reproduction method

- Environment capture and the limits of determinism
- Seeds, variance and how many runs are enough
- Deviation logs and contacting authors

### Diagnosing gaps

- Unreported hyperparameters and preprocessing
- Evaluation mismatches and contamination
- Hardware and numerical precision effects

### Extension design

- Out-of-distribution and cross-lingual tests, including Arabic
- Ablations and scaling probes
- Plans and stopping rules fixed before the runs

### Reporting

- Reproducibility checklists
- Negative results that others can use
- Releasing artefacts responsibly

---

# SPC-RSP-402 · Frontier Seminar: Agent Research and Multi-Agent Systems

- Track: Data Science
- Path: [Research Practice and Frontier](https://sdaiaacademy.github.io/en/paths/SPC-RSP.md)
- Level: Level 400 · Evaluate
- Format: Seminar: six weekly sessions of reading, presentation and small replications, rebuilt each term from current conference tutorials and workshops
- Total hours: 24 h
- Audience: specialist
- Status: In development

## Description

A reading and replication seminar on open research problems in language-model agents: memory, long-horizon tasks, goal tracking and coordination among several agents. Each week participants read two or three current papers, present one, and run a small controlled experiment that tests a claim, such as whether a memory design helps once the model and token budget are fixed, or whether several agents beat one agent given the same compute. The seminar ends with a replication note and a research proposal. Building production agents is taught in DEV-AGT-301; this seminar studies them.

## Learning outcomes

By the end, the participant can:

- Explain the main open problems in agent research, namely memory, long horizons, goal drift, credit assignment and coordination, with the strongest current evidence on each.
- Review an agent paper's experimental design, including harness confounds, budget matching and sensitivity to task length.
- Design a controlled experiment that isolates one agent component while holding the model, tools and token budget fixed.
- Build a replication of a small published result on long-horizon or multi-agent behaviour, reporting success over repeated trials with intervals.
- Design a research proposal on one open problem, with hypotheses, an evaluation design and the result that would count as failure.

## Prerequisites

- Has built an agent loop with tool calling and memory, as in DEV-AGT-301, or equivalent
- Runs controlled experiments with seeds and reports intervals, as in SPC-RSP-301
- Reads machine learning papers fluently

## Topics

### Measuring agents fairly

- Harness, tools and budget as confounds
- Success over repeated trials and task-length curves
- Benchmark validity and contamination in agent tasks

### Memory and context

- Context as a budget: summarisation and retrieval memory
- Learned versus engineered memory
- Interference and stale state

### Long horizons and goal tracking

- Planning, replanning and goal drift
- Credit assignment and reinforcement learning on trajectories
- Self-verification and where it fails

### Multi-agent systems

- Debate, division of labour and coordination protocols
- Compute-matched comparison with a single agent
- Cascading errors, collusion and injected instructions between agents
- Game-theoretic and multi-agent reinforcement learning views

### Agents doing research

- Automated experiment loops and what they complete
- Where research judgement still fails
- Oversight of autonomous agents in experiments

# SPC-RSP-403 · Frontier Seminar: AI for Science

- Track: Data Science
- Path: [Research Practice and Frontier](https://sdaiaacademy.github.io/en/paths/SPC-RSP.md)
- Level: Level 400 · Evaluate
- Format: Seminar: six weekly sessions of reading, presentation and hands-on work with open-weight models, rebuilt each term from current conference tutorials and workshops
- Total hours: 24 h
- Audience: specialist
- Status: In development

## Description

A reading and hands-on seminar on scientific foundation models with open weights: protein, genomic, materials, weather and Earth-observation models. Each week participants read current papers, run an open model on public data and test one claim against a domain baseline and a fair split. The seminar trains the judgement scientific use needs: leakage through similar sequences or nearby places and times, physical baselines, uncertainty, and the gap between benchmark scores and laboratory or field validation.

## Learning outcomes

By the end, the participant can:

- Explain how scientific foundation models differ from language models in training data, inductive biases, outputs and validation.
- Use an open-weight scientific model to produce predictions on public data and compare them with a domain baseline.
- Design an evaluation split that prevents leakage through sequence similarity, spatial proximity or temporal overlap.
- Review a published AI-for-science claim for its baselines, its validation against experiment or observation, and its uncertainty.
- Design a validation plan for using a scientific model in a domain project, naming the experimental or field evidence required.

## Prerequisites

- Trains and evaluates a deep learning model in Python, as in SPC-DLR-302, or equivalent
- Has university-level grounding in one science (biology, chemistry, physics or Earth science) or works with a scientist partner
- Reads research papers fluently

## Topics

### Proteins and molecules

- Protein language and structure models
- Confidence scores and their calibration
- Splits that respect sequence similarity

### Genomics

- Genomic language and sequence-to-function models
- Long-range context and variant effect prediction
- Access rules for human genetic data

### Materials and chemistry

- Machine-learned interatomic potentials
- Predicted stability versus synthesis in the laboratory
- Public materials and catalysis datasets

### Weather, climate and Earth observation

- Data-driven weather models trained on reanalysis
- Persistence, climatology and physical-model baselines
- Neural operators and physics-informed training on small partial differential equation problems
- Earth-observation foundation models and spatial splits

### Validating scientific claims

- Benchmarks versus laboratory and field validation
- Uncertainty, extrapolation and out-of-distribution inputs
- Claims of automated discovery by research agents

# SPC-RSP-404 · Frontier Seminar: Neurosymbolic Methods and AI for Mathematics

- Track: Data Science
- Path: [Research Practice and Frontier](https://sdaiaacademy.github.io/en/paths/SPC-RSP.md)
- Level: Level 400 · Evaluate
- Format: Seminar: six weekly sessions of reading, presentation and hands-on work with solvers, verifiers and proof assistants, rebuilt each term from current conference tutorials
- Total hours: 24 h
- Audience: specialist
- Status: In development

## Description

A reading and hands-on seminar on systems that combine learned models with symbolic tools: language models that call solvers, generated programs checked by verifiers, and proofs checked by a proof assistant. Each week participants read current papers and run a small experiment: proving lemmas with a model, verifying generated code against formal specifications, solving constraint problems with a model plus a solver, and checking whether autoformalised statements say what the informal ones say.

## Learning outcomes

By the end, the participant can:

- Explain the main neurosymbolic patterns: a model proposes and a solver checks, a model guides search, differentiable logic, and learned heuristics inside solvers.
- Use a language model with a proof assistant to prove a set of small lemmas and report success over repeated attempts.
- Build a generate-and-verify loop that writes code with a formal specification and rejects any output the verifier does not accept.
- Evaluate the faithfulness of autoformalised statements against their informal originals.
- Review a neurosymbolic or AI-for-mathematics paper for what its verification guarantees, its contamination risk and its compute budget.

## Prerequisites

- Writes proofs at the level of a discrete mathematics course, as in FND-MTH-105, or equivalent
- Has used search, logic or constraint solving, as in FND-AIC-105, or equivalent
- Calls a language model API from Python and parses structured output
- No proof-assistant experience is assumed; the tracked pre-work introduces one

## Topics

### Neurosymbolic patterns

- Model proposes, solver or verifier checks
- Learned guidance for search and solvers
- Differentiable and probabilistic logic

### Theorem proving and autoformalisation

- Tactic prediction versus whole-proof generation
- Reinforcement learning from verifier feedback
- Misformalisation and human review of statements
- Benchmarks, contamination and success over attempts

### Verified code generation

- Specifications, pre- and postconditions, invariants
- Solver-backed verification-aware languages
- Property-based testing as a weaker check
- What a verified program still does not guarantee

### AI and mathematical research

- Recorded AI contributions to open problems and how they were checked
- Credit and disclosure of AI contributions

# DS-201 · Statistical Inference by Simulation

- Track: Data Science
- Path: [Data Science: courses that help prepare for the Assistant level](https://sdaiaacademy.github.io/en/paths/DS-200.md)
- Level: Level 200 · Apply
- Format: Intensive: 4 teaching days of four sessions and a capstone day, with guided pre-work and a tracked follow-up task
- Total hours: 26 h
- Audience: practitioner
- Status: Available
- Open the course: https://sdaiaacademy.github.io/ds-201/
- The whole course in one file: https://sdaiaacademy.github.io/ds-201/llms-full.txt
- Practice questions: https://sdaiaacademy.github.io/ds-201/practice.html

## Description

Participants learn inference by computing it. On synthetic data from a fictional water utility whose true population is known, they draw repeated samples, build bootstrap intervals, run permutation tests beside classical ones, and report effect sizes with intervals instead of bare p-values. They see how testing 30 districts at once produces false findings and correct for it, then fit and read a first linear regression.

## Learning outcomes

By the end, the participant can:

- Explain what a sampling distribution, a standard error, a confidence interval and a p-value describe, and identify common misreadings.
- Compute bootstrap intervals for a mean, a median and a group difference, resampling the correct unit.
- Implement a permutation test, compare it with the matching classical test and report an effect size with an interval.
- Apply family-wise and false discovery rate corrections to many tests and measure the false findings without them.
- Analyse a linear regression of water consumption on household size and temperature, with slope intervals and residual checks.
- Deliver an inference brief that answers a manager's question with an estimate, an interval, a test, an effect size and stated limits.

## Prerequisites

- [FN-101 · Python for Data and AI Work](https://sdaiaacademy.github.io/en/courses/FN-101.md)
- [FN-103 · Mathematics for Machine Learning: Vectors, Gradients and Probability](https://sdaiaacademy.github.io/en/courses/FN-103.md)
- Filters and groups a table with a dataframe library
- Computes a mean, a standard deviation and a simple probability

## Next courses

- [DS-203 · Exploratory Analysis and Visualisation](https://sdaiaacademy.github.io/en/courses/DS-203.md)
- [DS-204 · Machine Learning for Tabular Data: Baselines and Validation](https://sdaiaacademy.github.io/en/courses/DS-204.md)
- [DS-205 · Designing and Reading Experiments](https://sdaiaacademy.github.io/en/courses/DS-205.md)
- [DS-301 · Regression and Generalised Linear Modelling](https://sdaiaacademy.github.io/en/courses/DS-301.md)
- [DS-302 · Online Experiments and A/B Testing](https://sdaiaacademy.github.io/en/courses/DS-302.md)
- [DS-304 · Forecasting and Time Series](https://sdaiaacademy.github.io/en/courses/DS-304.md)
- [DS-308 · Data Storytelling and Decision Briefings](https://sdaiaacademy.github.io/en/courses/DS-308.md)

## Format and days

### Day 1: Variation

- A sample is one draw of many
- Standard error by simulation and by formula
- Skew, outliers and the median
- Describing a sample honestly

### Day 2: Intervals

- The bootstrap idea
- Coverage is a testable claim
- Resample the right unit
- Intervals for differences and ratios

### Day 3: Tests

- A test is a shuffling rule
- p-values and their misreadings
- Effect size and practical significance
- Thirty districts, many false alarms

### Day 4: Regression and reporting

- Least squares as a summary
- Slopes with intervals
- Residuals and confounding
- Writing an inference brief

### Day 5: Capstone: the inference brief and its defence


## Topics

### Variation and estimation

- Population, sample, parameter and statistic
- Sampling distributions and standard error
- Skew, outliers and the median

### Bootstrap intervals

- Resampling the right unit
- Percentile intervals and coverage
- When the bootstrap fails

### Testing

- The null hypothesis as a shuffling rule
- Classical tests as approximations
- What a p-value is and is not
- Effect size, Type I and Type II errors

### Many comparisons

- Forking paths
- Family-wise error and false discovery rate
- Analysis plans written before the data

### A first regression

- Least squares and slope intervals
- Residual checks
- Confounding and a second variable

---

# DS-202 · Data Acquisition, Preparation and Quality

- Track: Data Science
- Path: [Data Science: courses that help prepare for the Assistant level](https://sdaiaacademy.github.io/en/paths/DS-200.md)
- Level: Level 200 · Apply
- Format: Intensive: 4 teaching days of four sessions and a capstone day, with guided pre-work and a tracked follow-up task
- Total hours: 26 h
- Audience: practitioner
- Status: Available
- Open the course: https://sdaiaacademy.github.io/ds-202/
- The whole course in one file: https://sdaiaacademy.github.io/ds-202/llms-full.txt
- Practice questions: https://sdaiaacademy.github.io/ds-202/practice.html

## Description

Participants assemble an analysis dataset for a fictional food bank network from four sources: registrations with personal data, branch logs, a donations API and open population data. They record provenance, join with key and cardinality checks, clean Arabic and English text, dates and units, write validation rules that rerun on every build, and measure how missing data and measurement error move a headline estimate. Personal data are minimised and pseudonymised, and the dataset rebuilds from raw sources with one command.

## Learning outcomes

By the end, the participant can:

- Describe missing-data mechanisms and kinds of measurement error and the bias each can introduce.
- Prepare a provenance record per source covering origin, owner, coverage, sharing basis, refresh date and limits.
- Implement joins with key checks, cardinality tests and reconciliation counts so that no row is silently lost or duplicated.
- Configure validation rules for types, ranges, uniqueness, completeness and cross-field consistency that run on every rebuild.
- Analyse how complete-case analysis, imputation and a sensitivity range change a headline estimate.
- Build a rebuildable analysis dataset from raw sources with personal data minimised and pseudonymised.

## Prerequisites

- [FN-101 · Python for Data and AI Work](https://sdaiaacademy.github.io/en/courses/FN-101.md)
- [FN-104 · SQL and Data Wrangling](https://sdaiaacademy.github.io/en/courses/FN-104.md)
- [FN-106 · Responsible Data and AI Practice in the Kingdom](https://sdaiaacademy.github.io/en/courses/FN-106.md)
- Writes SQL joins and group-by queries without assistance

## Next courses

- [DS-306 · Text and Unstructured Data for Data Science](https://sdaiaacademy.github.io/en/courses/DS-306.md)
- [DS-311 · Data Quality, Labelling and Pipelines for Analysis](https://sdaiaacademy.github.io/en/courses/DS-311.md)

## Format and days

### Day 1: Find and document the sources

- Start from the question, not the files
- Files, APIs and databases
- Provenance and sharing basis
- Coverage and sampling frames

### Day 2: Join and clean

- Encodings and Arabic text
- Keys and cardinality
- Matching without a clean key
- Types, units and dates

### Day 3: Missing data and measurement

- Why data go missing
- Imputation and its cost
- Sensitivity ranges
- Measurement error and proxies

### Day 4: Validate and protect

- Quality dimensions as rules
- Cross-field and cross-source checks
- Minimise and pseudonymise
- A data-quality report

### Day 5: Capstone project presentations


## Topics

### Sourcing

- Starting from the question
- Files, databases, APIs and open data
- Provenance, licences and coverage

### Joining and cleaning

- Encodings and Arabic text
- Keys, cardinality and reconciliation
- Matching without a clean key
- Types, units and dates

### Missing data and measurement error

- Missingness mechanisms
- Imputation and sensitivity ranges
- Self-report error and proxies

### Validation and personal data

- Quality dimensions as rules on every build
- A data-quality report
- Minimisation and keyed pseudonymisation
- What may leave the analysis environment

# DS-203 · Exploratory Analysis and Visualisation

- Track: Data Science
- Path: [Data Science: courses that help prepare for the Assistant level](https://sdaiaacademy.github.io/en/paths/DS-200.md)
- Level: Level 200 · Apply
- Format: Intensive: 4 teaching days of four sessions and a capstone day, with guided pre-work and a tracked follow-up task
- Total hours: 26 h
- Audience: practitioner
- Status: Available
- Open the course: https://sdaiaacademy.github.io/ds-203/
- The whole course in one file: https://sdaiaacademy.github.io/ds-203/llms-full.txt
- Practice questions: https://sdaiaacademy.github.io/ds-203/practice.html

## Description

Participants answer a fictional regional tourism board's questions by exploring its data, starting every analysis from written questions. They profile tables, examine distributions, relationships and change over time, build charts with a grammar of graphics and scales that do not mislead, and test by resampling whether a pattern could be chance. They repair misleading charts and write findings that state what is and is not shown, in a notebook that reruns from raw data.

## Learning outcomes

By the end, the participant can:

- Distinguish exploratory from confirmatory analysis and explain why a pattern found by exploring needs a fresh test.
- Prepare an analysis plan listing questions, units of observation, variables and the comparison that answers each.
- Analyse distributions, relationships and change over time with summaries and charts suited to each variable type.
- Use a grammar of graphics to map variables to position, colour and facets with honest scales, baselines and labels.
- Test whether an apparent difference or correlation could arise by chance, using permutation or bootstrap resampling.
- Deliver a reproducible exploratory report that states findings, uncertainty, open questions and limits for a non-specialist reader.

## Prerequisites

- [FN-101 · Python for Data and AI Work](https://sdaiaacademy.github.io/en/courses/FN-101.md)
- [FN-104 · SQL and Data Wrangling](https://sdaiaacademy.github.io/en/courses/FN-104.md)
- [DS-201 · Statistical Inference by Simulation](https://sdaiaacademy.github.io/en/courses/DS-201.md)
- Makes a basic chart in any plotting library

## Next courses

- [DS-307 · Metrics, Semantic Models and Dashboards](https://sdaiaacademy.github.io/en/courses/DS-307.md)
- [DS-308 · Data Storytelling and Decision Briefings](https://sdaiaacademy.github.io/en/courses/DS-308.md)

## Format and days

### Day 1: Questions and first looks

- Write the questions first
- Profiling a table
- Distributions
- Summaries that fit the shape

### Day 2: Relationships and time

- Two variables at once
- Counts, rates and denominators
- Change over time
- When the total reverses

### Day 3: Building honest charts

- Marks, encodings and scales
- Small multiples
- Charts that mislead
- Colour, labels and Arabic text

### Day 4: Check and report

- Could it be chance
- Showing uncertainty
- The traps of exploring
- A report that reruns

### Day 5: Capstone: the exploratory report and its defence


## Topics

### Questions before charts

- Analysis plans and units of observation
- Exploratory versus confirmatory work
- Profiling a new table

### Distributions and relationships

- Histograms, density and box plots
- Scatter plots and overplotting
- Rates and denominators
- Change over time and seasonality

### Grammar of graphics

- Marks, encodings and scales
- Small multiples
- Colour-blind-safe palettes
- Arabic and bilingual labels

### Honest charts

- Baselines and axis ranges
- Aggregation and Simpson's paradox
- Showing uncertainty

### Checking and reporting

- Chance patterns and resampling
- Counting the comparisons made
- Findings, limits and next questions

# DS-204 · Machine Learning for Tabular Data: Baselines and Validation

- Track: Data Science
- Path: [Data Science: courses that help prepare for the Assistant level](https://sdaiaacademy.github.io/en/paths/DS-200.md)
- Level: Level 200 · Apply
- Format: Intensive: 4 teaching days of four sessions and a capstone day, with guided pre-work and a tracked follow-up task
- Total hours: 26 h
- Audience: practitioner
- Status: Available
- Open the course: https://sdaiaacademy.github.io/ds-204/
- The whole course in one file: https://sdaiaacademy.github.io/ds-204/llms-full.txt
- Practice questions: https://sdaiaacademy.github.io/ds-204/practice.html

## Description

Participants predict which trainees of a fictional vocational training fund are likely not to complete, so that advisers can offer support early. On synthetic enrolment data with repeated trainees and cohorts, they climb a baseline ladder to tuned gradient-boosted trees, test an automated or pretrained challenger, choose validation that mirrors use, audit for leakage, set a threshold, break errors down by subgroup and write a model card. Deployment is left to AE-205 and AE-305.

## Learning outcomes

By the end, the participant can:

- Identify the leakage type and the fitting validation scheme in short tabular modelling cases.
- Apply a baseline ladder from a constant predictor to tuned gradient-boosted trees, logging every run.
- Implement validation that matches the data structure and measure how far a random split overstates performance.
- Test an automated or pretrained challenger against the tuned model under identical folds and time budget.
- Analyse calibration, the decision threshold and held-out errors by subgroup, with intervals that reflect slice size.
- Build a validated tabular model from framing to model card and defend its validation scheme and limits.

## Prerequisites

- [FN-101 · Python for Data and AI Work](https://sdaiaacademy.github.io/en/courses/FN-101.md)

- [FN-105 · How Machine Learning and Language Models Work](https://sdaiaacademy.github.io/en/courses/FN-105.md)
- [DS-201 · Statistical Inference by Simulation](https://sdaiaacademy.github.io/en/courses/DS-201.md)
- Joins and groups tables with a dataframe library
- Explains overfitting and the purpose of a held-out set

## Next courses

- [DS-305 · Uncertainty, Interpretability and Model Validation](https://sdaiaacademy.github.io/en/courses/DS-305.md)

- [DS-309 · Responsible Data Science: Privacy, Fairness and Documentation](https://sdaiaacademy.github.io/en/courses/DS-309.md)

- Automated and pretrained challengers

# DS-205 · Designing and Reading Experiments

- Track: Data Science
- Path: [Data Science: courses that help prepare for the Assistant level](https://sdaiaacademy.github.io/en/paths/DS-200.md)
- Level: Level 200 · Apply
- Format: Intensive: 3 teaching days of four sessions and a capstone day, with guided pre-work and a tracked follow-up task
- Total hours: 21 h
- Audience: practitioner
- Status: Available
- Open the course: https://sdaiaacademy.github.io/ds-205/
- The whole course in one file: https://sdaiaacademy.github.io/ds-205/llms-full.txt
- Practice questions: https://sdaiaacademy.github.io/ds-205/practice.html

## Description

Participants design randomised experiments for a fictional municipal permits office and read the results without fooling themselves. They turn a decision question into a pre-registration with a hypothesis, primary and guardrail metrics, a stop rule and a unit of randomisation, compute sample size by formula and by simulation, analyse a synthetic experiment log, check that randomisation worked, and measure how peeking, many metrics and a mismatched unit inflate false wins. Variance reduction and sequential tests are left to DS-302.

## Learning outcomes

By the end, the participant can:

- Distinguish a randomised experiment, a quasi-experiment and an observational comparison, and explain the causal claim each supports.
- Draft a pre-registration stating the decision, hypothesis, unit of randomisation, primary and guardrail metrics, stop rule and analysis plan.
- Compute the sample size and run time needed to detect a minimum effect of interest and check it by simulation.
- Analyse a completed two-arm experiment with a difference in proportions, a confidence interval and a sample ratio mismatch test.
- Measure by simulation the false-positive rate caused by peeking, many metrics and analysis at the wrong unit.
- Review a reported experiment and decide whether it supports the decision it claims to support.

## Prerequisites

- [DS-201 · Statistical Inference by Simulation](https://sdaiaacademy.github.io/en/courses/DS-201.md)
- Computes a proportion, a difference in means and a confidence interval
- Writes a simulation loop in Python or R

## Next courses

- [DS-302 · Online Experiments and A/B Testing](https://sdaiaacademy.github.io/en/courses/DS-302.md)
- [DS-303 · Causal Inference from Observational Data](https://sdaiaacademy.github.io/en/courses/DS-303.md)
- [DS-310 · Problem Framing and Analytical Review](https://sdaiaacademy.github.io/en/courses/DS-310.md)

## Format and days

### Day 1: Design

- Which claims need an experiment
- Decision, hypothesis and metrics
- Choosing the unit of randomisation
- Pre-registration

### Day 2: Size and run

- Power and the minimum effect
- Power by simulation
- Cluster randomisation
- Run time and seasonality

### Day 3: Read the result

- Did randomisation work
- Estimate, interval and effect
- False wins by simulation
- Reviewing a reported result

### Day 4: Capstone: the design and analysis pack and its defence


## Topics

### From decision to design

- Decision, hypothesis and estimand
- Primary, secondary and guardrail metrics
- Pre-registration and stop rules

### Randomisation

- Simple, stratified and cluster assignment
- Balance and sample ratio checks
- Interference between units

### Sample size and power

- Minimum effect of interest
- Formula and simulation
- Run time and weekly cycles

### Reading a result

- Differences, intervals and effect sizes
- Practical against statistical significance
- Subgroups read with care

### Common traps

- Peeking
- Many metrics
- Wrong unit of analysis
- Novelty effects and attrition

# DS-206 · Analysis with AI Assistants: Delegate, Verify, Reproduce

- Track: Data Science
- Path: [Data Science: courses that help prepare for the Assistant level](https://sdaiaacademy.github.io/en/paths/DS-200.md)
- Level: Level 200 · Apply
- Format: Intensive: 3 teaching days of four sessions and a capstone day, with guided pre-work and a tracked follow-up task
- Total hours: 21 h
- Audience: practitioner
- Status: Available
- Open the course: https://sdaiaacademy.github.io/ds-206/
- The whole course in one file: https://sdaiaacademy.github.io/ds-206/llms-full.txt
- Practice questions: https://sdaiaacademy.github.io/ds-206/practice.html

## Description

Participants analyse data with a coding assistant or agent in a notebook and stay accountable for every number. For a fictional courier company they decide which steps to delegate, brief the assistant with acceptance checks, prove results by recomputing key numbers another way, measure how answers vary between runs, decide which data may go to which assistant, and package an analysis that a peer reruns from logged prompts, code and data.

## Learning outcomes

By the end, the participant can:

- Identify which analysis steps suit delegation and which need the analyst's own judgement, with a reason for each.
- Prepare a delegation brief stating question, data, definitions, constraints and acceptance checks before the assistant runs.
- Test assisted analyses by recomputing headline numbers another way and checking joins, filters, denominators and chart encodings.
- Measure run-to-run variability by repeating one request five times and comparing code, numbers and conclusions.
- Classify analysis data by sensitivity and assign each table to a local assistant, a hosted assistant or neither.
- Deliver an assisted analysis package that another analyst can rerun and audit from logged prompts, code, data and verification notes.

## Prerequisites

- [FN-101 · Python for Data and AI Work](https://sdaiaacademy.github.io/en/courses/FN-101.md)
- [FN-104 · SQL and Data Wrangling](https://sdaiaacademy.github.io/en/courses/FN-104.md)
- [FN-106 · Responsible Data and AI Practice in the Kingdom](https://sdaiaacademy.github.io/en/courses/FN-106.md)
- Writes SQL joins and dataframe group-bys without assistance
- Has completed one analysis end to end, from raw table to chart

## Format and days

### Day 1: Delegate with intent

- What assistants get wrong in analysis
- Delegate, assist or keep
- The delegation brief
- Context files for a project

### Day 2: Verify

- Recompute it another way
- Joins, filters and denominators
- Charts and words
- Ask it twice

### Day 3: Reproduce and disclose

- Which data may go where
- Logging assisted work
- The peer rerun
- Disclosing assistance

### Day 4: Capstone: the assisted analysis package and its defence


## Topics

### What to delegate

- Where assistants and agents fail in data work
- Evidence that unchecked delegation erodes skill
- Delegate, assist or keep

### Briefing an assistant

- Acceptance checks
- Project context files
- Small steps with checkpoints

### Verification

- Recomputing another way
- Join, filter and denominator checks
- Charts and summaries against the data

### Variability and reproducibility

- Asking twice
- Logging models, settings and prompts

### Data handling and disclosure

- What may go to which assistant
- Disclosing assistance in a report

# DS-207 · Responsible Data Practice and Conduct in Analytical Work

- Track: Data Science
- Path: [Data Science: courses that help prepare for the Assistant level](https://sdaiaacademy.github.io/en/paths/DS-200.md)
- Level: Level 200 · Apply
- Format: Intensive: 3 teaching days of four sessions and a capstone day, with guided pre-work and a tracked follow-up task
- Total hours: 21 h
- Audience: practitioner
- Status: Available
- Open the course: https://sdaiaacademy.github.io/ds-207/
- The whole course in one file: https://sdaiaacademy.github.io/ds-207/llms-full.txt
- Practice questions: https://sdaiaacademy.github.io/ds-207/practice.html

## Description

Participants handle an analytical engagement for a fictional university's student-success unit. They test requests against the Personal Data Protection Law (PDPL), classify the data and decide what may be shared with a government partner, suppress small cells in aggregate outputs, compare outcome and error rates across student groups, keep an analysis log and a datasheet, and handle three stakeholder conversations: scoping, pushing back on an unsafe request and explaining limits. Deeper de-identification and fairness audits are in DS-309.

## Learning outcomes

By the end, the participant can:

- Explain the PDPL principles and the classification and sharing rules an analysis engages, from lawful basis to data subjects' rights and transfer.
- Classify the datasets and outputs of an analysis and decide what may be shared, with whom and in what form.
- Apply aggregation and small-cell suppression to results tables and check that no student can be singled out.
- Analyse referral and error rates across student groups and report differences with their uncertainty and possible causes.
- Prepare a datasheet and an analysis log that let a reviewer trace each result to its data, decisions and approvals.
- Lead a stakeholder conversation that rescopes an unsafe or unclear request into a lawful, answerable question, and record the agreement.

## Prerequisites

- [FN-106 · Responsible Data and AI Practice in the Kingdom](https://sdaiaacademy.github.io/en/courses/FN-106.md)
- Computes rates and a confidence interval for a proportion by group in SQL or a dataframe
- Has written a short analytical report for a non-specialist reader

## Next courses

- Comparing groups
- Naming the bias

### Day 3: Professional conduct

- Datasheets and analysis logs
- Scoping with a sponsor
- Pushing back without obstructing
- Explaining limits

### Day 4: Capstone: the responsible-practice pack

- Lawful basis, purpose and minimisation
- Data subjects' rights and retention
- Secondary use, transfers and breaches

### Classification and sharing

- Sharing requests and conditions
- Small cells and what may go into AI tools

- Rates and errors across groups
- What fairness metrics cannot settle
